title: Night Shift at St. Elm's
hero: Dr. Ayo Bennett, gece nöbetinde aynı gizemli hastalıkla gelen hastaların ardındaki nedeni arıyor.
intro: Saat gece 2. St. Elm's Hastanesi'nin sessiz koridorlarında nöbetçi doktor Ayo Bennett, bu hafta altıncı katta yatan hastaların tuhaf bir hastalığa yakalandığını fark ediyor: ani yüksek ateş, kafa karışıklığı ve hiçbir tetkikte görünmeyen bir neden. Sen de Ayo'nun yanında, ipuçlarını birleştirerek hastanenin sırrını çözeceksin.
outro: Ayo ve ekibi, hastanenin altıncı katındaki gizli tehlikeyi buldu ve doğru kişilere ulaştırdı. Otuz gece boyunca ipuçlarından sonuç çıkardın, tıbbi İngilizceyle okudun ve bir gizemi sonuna kadar takip ettin. Başka bir tefrikaya geçmeye hazırsın.

eps.title: The Fifth Patient
eps.recap: Gece nöbetindeki Dr. Ayo, kalça ameliyatı için yatan Mr. Dunne'ın birden yüksek ateş ve kafa karışıklığıyla kötüleştiğini gördü. Bu, o hafta aynı belirtilerle gelen beşinci hastaydı ve kimse nedenini bilmiyordu.

text: It was two o'clock in the morning. Dr. Ayo Bennett was alone in the night office of St. Elm's Hospital, drinking cold tea. The hospital was quiet.
Then the phone rang. "Doctor, come quickly," said Rosa, the night nurse. "Mr. Dunne is very sick." Ayo ran upstairs.

Mr. Dunne was seventy-eight years old. He came to the hospital on Monday for a new hip, and he felt fine. Now his face was red and his fever was forty degrees. He looked at Ayo and asked, "Where is my mother?"
"This is the fifth patient this week," Rosa said quietly. "Same fever. Same confused words."
Ayo took out her small black notebook. She had five names on one page. Next to each name she had written the same two words: no cause.
A2.proof: This is the fifth patient this week
A2.q: Why was Ayo worried about Mr. Dunne?
o: He was the oldest patient in the whole hospital that night.
Five patients in one week had the same strange illness.
He had not wanted to have a new hip.
Rosa had given him the wrong medicine.
A2.hint: Rosa'nın söylediği sayıya ve 'aynı' kelimesine dikkat et.
A2.why: Rosa bunun bu hafta aynı ateş ve kafa karışıklığıyla gelen beşinci hasta olduğunu söylüyor; Ayo da defterine beş ismi aynı notla yazmış.

text: At two o'clock in the morning, Dr. Ayo Bennett was drinking cold tea in the night office of St. Elm's Hospital when the phone rang. It was Rosa, the night nurse, and she sounded afraid. "Come upstairs, please. It's Mr. Dunne."

Mr. Dunne was seventy-eight and had come in on Monday for a hip operation. The operation had gone well, and until yesterday he had been joking with the nurses. Now his face was red, his fever was forty degrees, and he was staring at the ceiling. "Where is my mother?" he asked Ayo.
She checked his heart, his lungs and his eyes, and found nothing she could explain. "He was perfectly healthy when he arrived," she said. "Healthy enough for surgery, anyway."
Rosa lowered her voice. "This is the fifth patient this week with the same symptoms. High fever, then confusion. And nobody knows why."

Back in her office, Ayo opened her small black notebook. There were five names on the page, and beside each one she had written the same two words: cause unknown. She looked at the list for a long time before she turned off the light.
B1.proof: the fifth patient this week with the same symptoms
B1.q: What can we understand about the patients from the story?
o: They all came to the hospital because of a fever.
They were all having the same kind of operation.
They became ill after arriving at the hospital for other reasons.
They had been joking with the nurses all week.
B1.hint: Mr. Dunne'ın hastaneye neden geldiğini ve ne zaman hastalandığını düşün.
B1.why: Mr. Dunne kalça ameliyatı için gelmişti ve sağlıklıydı; belirtiler hastanede yattığı sırada başladı. Diğer dört hasta için de aynı örüntü söz konusu.

text: At two o'clock in the morning, Dr. Ayo Bennett was finishing a cup of cold tea in the night office of St. Elm's Hospital when the phone rang. It was Rosa, the night nurse, and her voice was tight. "Could you come up? It's Mr. Dunne."

Mr. Dunne was seventy-eight and had been admitted on Monday for a routine hip operation. The surgery had gone smoothly, and until yesterday he had been teasing the nurses about the hospital food. Now his face was flushed, his temperature had reached forty degrees, and he was staring at the ceiling as if he did not recognise it. "Where is my mother?" he asked Ayo.
She examined his heart, his lungs and his eyes, and found nothing that explained what she was seeing. "Healthy enough for surgery on Monday," she murmured, "and now this."
Rosa lowered her voice. "That's the fifth patient this week with exactly the same symptoms. A sudden high fever, then confusion. And every test has come back with nothing."

Back in her office, Ayo opened the small black notebook she kept in her coat pocket. There were five names on the page, and beside each one she had written the same two words: cause unknown. She had told herself that five unrelated cases could happen. Now, looking at the list, she was no longer sure she believed it.
B2.proof: exactly the same symptoms
B2.q: What is Ayo beginning to suspect by the end of the passage?
o: That Rosa has been careless with the patients' records.
That Mr. Dunne's operation was done badly.
That she should ask to change her night shift.
That the five cases may share a cause she has not yet found.
B2.hint: Son cümledeki 'artık emin değildi' kısmına ve 'ilgisiz vakalar' ifadesine bak.
B2.why: Ayo beş vakanın ilgisiz olabileceğini kendine söylemişti, ama listeye bakınca buna artık inanmıyor: ortak ama henüz bulunmamış bir neden olduğundan şüpheleniyor.

text: At two o'clock in the morning, Dr. Ayo Bennett was finishing a cup of cold tea in the night office of St. Elm's Hospital, enjoying the rare luxury of silence, when the phone rang. It was Rosa, the night nurse, and her usual composure had gone. "Could you come up? It's Mr. Dunne."

Mr. Dunne was seventy-eight and had been admitted on Monday for an uncomplicated hip replacement. The surgery had gone smoothly, and until the previous evening he had been teasing the staff about the hospital food. Now his face was flushed, his temperature had climbed to forty degrees, and he stared at the ceiling as though it belonged to somebody else's house. "Where is my mother?" he asked Ayo, with perfect politeness.

She examined his heart, his lungs, his pupils, and found nothing that accounted for the change. "A man fit enough for the theatre on Monday," she murmured, "and by Thursday he's lost the thread of his own life."
Rosa glanced at the door before she spoke. "That's the fifth patient this week with exactly the same picture. A sudden high fever, then confusion. And every test we run comes back clean."

Back in her office, Ayo took the small black notebook from her coat pocket. Five names stood on the page, and beside each she had written the same two words: cause unknown. For days she had told herself that five coincidences were merely unlucky. She noticed now, with some discomfort, that she had stopped writing the word 'coincidence' anywhere at all.
C1.proof: she had stopped writing the word 'coincidence' anywhere at all
C1.q: What does Ayo's change of attitude at the end of the passage imply?
o: She has quietly begun to doubt that the cases are unrelated.
She believes Mr. Dunne is exaggerating his symptoms.
She is certain that the staff have made an error.
She has decided that the illness cannot be treated.
C1.hint: Ayo'nun 'tesadüf' kelimesini artık yazmamasının ne anlama geldiğini düşün.
C1.why: Ayo 'tesadüf' kelimesini yazmayı bırakmış; bu, vakaların ilgisiz olduğuna artık inanmadığını, ortak bir neden aradığını dolaylı olarak gösteriyor.

eps.title: Nothing on the Tests
eps.recap: Ayo, grip, zatürre ve gıda zehirlenmesi ihtimallerini tek tek eledi. Her zamanki antibiyotik de Mr. Dunne'a fayda etmedi; hastalık sıradan bir enfeksiyona benzemiyordu.

text: Ayo worked all night. First she tested Mr. Dunne for the flu. The test was negative. Then she took a picture of his chest. There was a small cloudy place on one lung, but it did not look like a normal infection.
"Maybe it's food poisoning," said Rosa. Ayo shook her head. The five patients had eaten different meals, and the kitchen was clean. Nobody else in the hospital was sick.
In the morning, Ayo gave Mr. Dunne the usual medicine for a lung infection. She waited. At noon his fever was the same. At six o'clock it was a little higher.
"The medicine is not working," Ayo told Rosa. "It is not the flu. It is not food. And it is not a normal lung infection."
Rosa looked at her. "Then what is it?" Ayo did not answer. She did not know.
A2.q: What does the failed medicine tell Ayo?
o: Mr. Dunne did not take the medicine properly.
The hospital pharmacy sent the wrong medicine.
The illness is not the common infection she first thought it was.
Mr. Dunne is getting better more slowly than the others.
A2.hint: Ayo ilacı 'her zamanki akciğer enfeksiyonu' ilacı olarak veriyor; işe yaramaması ne gösterir?
A2.why: Sıradan bir akciğer enfeksiyonuna verilen ilaç işe yaramıyor; Ayo da bunun normal bir enfeksiyon olmadığı sonucuna varıyor.

text: Ayo worked through the night. She tested Mr. Dunne for the flu, and the result was negative. A chest X-ray showed a cloudy patch on one lung, which looked a little like pneumonia, but the shape was wrong, and the blood tests did not fit either.

"Food poisoning?" suggested Rosa. Ayo had already thought of it. The five patients had eaten different meals on different days, the kitchen records were clean, and no one on the other floors had fallen ill.

In the morning she began the standard antibiotic for pneumonia, the one that works in nine cases out of ten. She checked Mr. Dunne at noon and his temperature was unchanged. At six o'clock it had gone up by half a degree.
"It isn't working," she told Rosa in the corridor. "It isn't the flu, it isn't food, and it isn't ordinary pneumonia. Everything I know how to treat has been ruled out."
Rosa folded her arms. "Then it's something you don't know how to treat." Ayo did not argue. She went back to the notebook and, under the five names, wrote a single line: standard drugs fail.
B1.proof: it isn't ordinary pneumonia
B1.q: What is the main problem Ayo faces at the end?
o: The hospital kitchen has refused to share its records.
Rosa does not believe that the patients are ill.
The flu test was done too late to be useful.
The common explanations have all been excluded, but she has no new one.
B1.hint: Ayo'nun elediği ihtimallerin sonunda elinde ne kaldığına bak.
B1.why: Grip, zatürre ve gıda zehirlenmesi eleniyor ve standart tedavi işe yaramıyor; Ayo'nun elinde yeni bir açıklama yok.

text: Ayo worked through the night. She tested Mr. Dunne for the flu and the result was negative. A chest X-ray showed a cloudy patch on one lung, which resembled pneumonia at first glance, yet the shape seemed wrong, and his blood tests did not match the usual picture either.

"Food poisoning?" Rosa suggested. Ayo had already considered it. The five patients had eaten different meals on different days, the kitchen's records were spotless, and nobody on any other floor had fallen ill.

In the morning she started the standard antibiotic for pneumonia, the one that clears the infection in nine cases out of ten. At noon Mr. Dunne's temperature was unchanged. By six o'clock it had risen by half a degree, and he no longer recognised Rosa.
"It isn't working," Ayo told her in the corridor. "It isn't the flu, it isn't food, and it isn't ordinary pneumonia. Everything I know how to treat has been crossed off."

Rosa folded her arms. "Then it's something you don't know how to treat." Ayo did not argue, because the sentence was uncomfortably accurate. She returned to her notebook and wrote one line beneath the five names: standard drugs fail. Then, after a moment, she added a question mark.
B2.proof: Everything I know how to treat has been crossed off
B2.q: What does the final detail, the question mark, suggest about Ayo's state of mind?
o: She is no longer sure that her usual medical knowledge is enough.
She expects the drug to work after a few more hours.
She is asking Rosa to repeat the blood tests.
She believes that the patients are pretending to be ill.
B2.hint: Soru işareti, Ayo'nun yazdığı cümleye karşı duyduğu güveni hakkında ne söylüyor?
B2.why: Ayo, bildiği her tedavinin elendiğini söylüyor ve 'standart ilaçlar işe yaramıyor' notuna soru işareti ekliyor; bildiği tıbbın yetmeyebileceğinden emin olmadığını gösteriyor.

text: Ayo worked through the night with a methodical calm she did not feel. The flu test came back negative. A chest X-ray revealed a cloudy patch on one lung, which resembled pneumonia at first glance, though its margins were wrong and Mr. Dunne's blood work refused to follow the textbook pattern. She ordered every test the hospital could run before sunrise.

"Food poisoning?" Rosa ventured. Ayo had considered it hours earlier. The five patients had eaten different meals on different days, the kitchen's records were immaculate, and not one person on any other floor had so much as a headache. Whatever this was, it was choosing its victims with care.

At dawn she started the standard antibiotic for pneumonia, the one that clears the infection in nine cases out of ten. By noon Mr. Dunne's temperature was unchanged. By six in the evening it had crept up half a degree, and he no longer recognised Rosa, whom he had been calling 'love' since Monday.
"It isn't working," Ayo told her in the corridor. "It isn't flu, it isn't food, and it isn't ordinary pneumonia. Everything I know how to treat has been crossed off the list."

Rosa folded her arms. "Then it's something you don't know how to treat." Ayo did not argue, because the sentence was uncomfortably precise. She returned to the notebook and wrote one line beneath the five names: standard drugs fail. After a moment she added a question mark, and then, more slowly, she underlined it.
C1.proof: Everything I know how to treat has been crossed off the list
C1.q: What can be inferred from the fact that Ayo underlines the question mark?
o: She has decided that the antibiotic should be given in a larger dose.
She now treats the unanswered question as the central problem.
She is annoyed that Rosa interrupted her work.
She believes the X-ray was read incorrectly.
C1.hint: Ayo, soru işaretini silmek yerine altını çiziyor; bu davranış neyi önemli saydığını gösterir.
C1.why: Soru işaretinin altını çizmek, cevapsız sorunun artık işin merkezi olduğunu gösteriyor; Ayo bilinen açıklamaların bittiğini kabul etmiş durumda.

eps.title: Room Numbers
eps.recap: Ayo, beş hastanın odalarını bir tahtaya yazdı ve hepsinin aynı katta, koridorun aynı tarafında olduğunu gördü. Rosa bunun tesadüf olduğunu söyledi, ama hastalığın hastalarda değil, katta olabileceği fikri ortaya çıktı.

text: The next night, Ayo took a marker and wrote on the white board in the office. She wrote the five names. Next to each name, she wrote a room number: 602, 605, 608, 611, 614.
She stood back and looked at the numbers. They all started with six. "Rosa," she said, "come here. Look."
Rosa looked. "The sixth floor," she said. "So? The old people stay there. Many people on the sixth floor get sick."
"Not like this," said Ayo. "Nobody had a fever when they arrived. They all got sick here. And all of them slept in the same part of the same floor."
Rosa did not say 'coincidence' this time. She stared at the board. Then, very slowly, she said, "All the rooms are on the east side."
A2.proof: all of them slept in the same part of the same floor
A2.q: What new idea does the board give Ayo?
o: The old patients should not stay in the hospital.
Rosa has been giving the same medicine to everyone.
The numbers on the doors are wrong.
The cause may be something on the sixth floor, not in the patients.
A2.hint: Odaların hepsinin aynı katta ve aynı tarafta olması neyi düşündürür?
A2.why: Hastaların hiçbiri ateşle gelmedi; hepsi aynı katın aynı bölümünde yattı. Bu, nedenin hastalardan çok o yerde olabileceğini düşündürüyor.

text: The next night, Ayo wrote the five names on the white board in her office. Beside each name she added a room number: 602, 605, 608, 611, 614. She stepped back and frowned. "Rosa, come and look at this."
Rosa studied the board. "The sixth floor. So what? That's where the older patients stay. Of course they get sick."
"Not like this," said Ayo. "None of them had a fever when they were admitted. They were all well on Monday, and they all became ill here. And every one of them slept in the same wing."

For once Rosa did not say the word 'coincidence'. She picked up the marker and drew a line along the corridor on the floor plan pinned beside the board. "The east side," she said slowly. "All five rooms are on the east side. The rooms on the west side have been fine."
Neither of them spoke for a moment. Somewhere below them, the old building made a low, steady, rattling sound, like a machine that had been running too long.
B1.proof: the east side
B1.q: What is the most important thing the room numbers show?
o: All the sick patients stayed in the same part of the same floor.
The oldest patients were given the best rooms.
The hospital has too few rooms on the west side.
Rosa moved the patients to the wrong rooms.
B1.hint: Rosa'nın çizdiği çizgi ve 'batı tarafındaki odalar iyiydi' cümlesine dikkat et.
B1.why: Beş oda da aynı katın doğu tarafında; batı tarafındaki odalar sağlam. Bu, ortak bir nedenin o bölgede olabileceğini gösteriyor.

text: The next night Ayo wrote the five names on the white board in her office and added a room number beside each: 602, 605, 608, 611, 614. She had spent the whole afternoon looking through the files, and she had not slept. She stepped back, frowned, and called, "Rosa, come and look at this."
Rosa studied the board. "The sixth floor. And? That's where the older patients stay. It's hardly surprising they get sick."
"Not like this," said Ayo. "None of them had a fever when they were admitted. They were all well on Monday, and they all deteriorated here. And every one of them has slept in the same wing."

For once Rosa did not say the word 'coincidence'. She took the marker and drew a line along the corridor on the floor plan pinned beside the board. "The east side," she said slowly. "All five rooms are on the east side. The rooms at the other end have been perfectly fine."

Neither of them spoke. Somewhere beneath their feet the old building let out a low, rhythmic rattle, like a machine that had been running for too long, and the lights above the board flickered once. Ayo realised she was no longer looking for a sick patient. She was looking for a sick place.
B2.proof: She was looking for a sick place
B2.q: What change in Ayo's thinking does the last sentence describe?
o: She has decided to move all patients to the west wing.
She has moved from blaming individual patients to suspecting the environment.
She has begun to suspect that Rosa is hiding something.
She now believes the illness will disappear by itself.
B2.hint: 'Hasta bir kişi' ile 'hasta bir yer' arasındaki farkı düşün.
B2.why: Ayo artık hasta bir kişiyi değil, hasta bir yeri arıyor; yani nedenin hastalardan çok ortamda olabileceğini düşünüyor.

text: The following night Ayo wrote the five names on the white board in her office and added a room number beside each: 602, 605, 608, 611, 614. She had spent the afternoon cross-checking admission files instead of sleeping, and her handwriting showed it. She stepped back, frowned, and called, "Rosa, come and look at this."
Rosa studied the board with the air of someone preparing to be unconvinced. "The sixth floor. And? That's where the elderly patients are placed. It's hardly remarkable that they fall ill."
"Not like this," said Ayo. "None of them had a fever on admission. They were all well on Monday, and they all deteriorated here. Every one of them has slept in the same wing."

For once Rosa did not reach for the word 'coincidence'. Instead she took the marker and drew a line along the corridor on the floor plan pinned beside the board. "The east side," she said slowly. "All five rooms are on the east side. The rooms at the other end have been perfectly fine."

Neither of them spoke. Somewhere beneath their feet the old building let out a low, rhythmic rattle, like a machine that had been running a little too long, and the lights above the board flickered once and steadied. Ayo found that she had stopped looking for a sick patient. She was looking, instead, for a sick place, and the thought made the back of her neck prickle. Somewhere in this building, she decided, there was an answer, and it was hiding in plain sight.
C1.proof: She was looking, instead, for a sick place
C1.q: What does the author suggest by mentioning the rattling sound beneath the building?
o: That the hospital is about to be closed for repairs.
That Rosa is nervous about working alone at night.
That the hidden cause may be connected to the building's own equipment.
That the patients are being disturbed by noise.
C1.hint: Binanın altından gelen 'çok uzun süre çalışan makine' sesinin neye işaret ettiğini düşün.
C1.why: Yazar, uzun süredir çalışan bir makineye benzeyen sesi 'hasta yer' fikriyle yan yana koyuyor; bu, nedenin binanın kendi teknik donanımıyla ilgili olabileceğini sezdiriyor.

eps.title: A Daughter's Question
eps.recap: İlk hasta Mr. Hale'in durumu ağırlaştı. Kızı Claire, babasının sadece kırık bir bilek için yattığını ve hastanede hastalandığını söyleyerek Ayo'ya zor sorular sordu; Ayo yanıt veremedi ve araştırmaya söz verdi.

text: Mr. Hale was the first patient with the strange fever. He was eighty-two years old. On Wednesday, he was much worse. He slept all day, and his breathing was loud.
His daughter, Claire, sat beside the bed. She was a teacher. She looked tired. When Ayo came in, Claire stood up.
"Doctor, my father came here with a broken wrist," she said. "Only a wrist. He was happy and he talked all the time. Now he cannot even know my name."
"I am very sorry," said Ayo. "We are doing everything."
"What is this illness?" asked Claire. "Please tell me the truth." Ayo looked at the floor. She could not say "I don't know." But she could not lie. "I will find out," she said. "I promise."
A2.proof: my father came here with a broken wrist
A2.q: What does Claire's question make Ayo think about?
o: Her father became sick because of something in the hospital.
Her father was already sick before he came.
Her father does not want to stay in the hospital.
Claire does not trust the nurses.
A2.hint: Claire babasının hastaneye neden geldiğini ve şimdi nasıl olduğunu söylüyor.
A2.why: Mr. Hale sadece kırık bilek için gelmişti ve sağlıklıydı; hastalık hastanede başladı. Bu, nedenin hastanede olabileceğini düşündürüyor.

text: Mr. Hale had been the first patient with the strange fever. He was eighty-two years old, and by Wednesday he was much worse. He slept almost all day, and his breathing had become loud and shallow.
His daughter, Claire, a schoolteacher, sat beside the bed with dark circles under her eyes. When Ayo came into the room, she stood up at once.

"Doctor, my father came here with a broken wrist," she said. "A wrist. He was laughing and complaining about the food. Now he doesn't know my name. People don't catch things like this by breaking a wrist."
"I'm very sorry," said Ayo. "We're doing everything we can."

"That's what everybody says. What is this illness? Please, tell me the truth." Ayo looked at the floor. She could not say "I don't know" and she would not tell a lie. "I will find out," she said at last. "I promise you." It was a promise she did not know how to keep.
B1.proof: People don't catch things like this by breaking a wrist.
B1.q: What is Claire really suggesting with her last remark?
o: That her father should have stayed at home.
That her father caught the illness while he was inside the hospital.
That the broken wrist was caused by the illness.
That the doctors have misunderstood the operation.
B1.hint: Claire'in 'bileği kırarak böyle bir şey kapılmaz' sözünün altında yatan fikri düşün.
B1.why: Claire, babasının hastalığı bilek kırığı yüzünden değil, hastanede yattığı sırada kaptığını ima ediyor.

text: Mr. Hale had been the first patient with the strange fever. He was eighty-two years old, and by Wednesday he was much worse. He slept almost all day, and his breathing had become loud and shallow.
His daughter, Claire, a schoolteacher, sat beside the bed with dark circles under her eyes. When Ayo came into the room she stood up at once.

"Doctor, my father came here with a broken wrist," she said. "A wrist. He was laughing and complaining about the food. Now he doesn't know my name. People don't catch something like this by breaking a wrist."
"I'm very sorry," said Ayo. "We're doing everything we can."

"That's what everyone says. What is this illness? Please, just tell me the truth." Ayo looked at the floor. She could not say "I don't know," and she would not tell a lie. She thought of the five names in her notebook, and of the sixth floor, and of the fact that nobody in charge seemed to want to ask the obvious question. "I will find out," she said at last. "I promise you." It was a promise she did not yet know how to keep.
B2.proof: nobody in charge seemed to want to ask the obvious question
B2.q: What does Ayo's thought about 'nobody in charge' imply?
o: She believes the nurses are hiding information.
She thinks Claire is asking the wrong question.
She feels the hospital management is not taking the cases seriously.
She plans to leave the hospital the next day.
B2.hint: Ayo 'sorumlu kimse' derken kimleri kastediyor olabilir?
B2.why: Ayo, yönetimdeki kimsenin bariz soruyu sormak istemediğini düşünüyor; yani yönetimin vakaları ciddiye almadığını hissediyor.

text: Mr. Hale had been the first patient with the strange fever. He was eighty-two years old, and by Wednesday he was much worse. He slept almost all day, and his breathing had become loud and shallow, like a man climbing stairs in his sleep.
His daughter, Claire, a schoolteacher, sat beside the bed with dark circles under her eyes. When Ayo came into the room she stood up at once, as though a verdict were about to be read.

"Doctor, my father came here with a broken wrist," she said. "A wrist. He was laughing and complaining about the food. Now he doesn't know my name. People don't catch something like this by breaking a wrist."
"I'm very sorry," said Ayo. "We are doing everything we can."

"That's what everyone says. What is this illness? Please, just tell me the truth." Ayo looked at the floor. She could not say "I don't know," and she refused to tell a lie. She thought of the five names in her notebook, of the east corridor, and of the fact that nobody in charge seemed to want the obvious question asked. "I will find out," she said at last. "I promise you." It was a promise made with no plan behind it, which was exactly why she meant it.
C1.proof: It was a promise made with no plan behind it
C1.q: Why does the narrator say Ayo 'meant' her promise?
o: Because she already knows the cause of the illness.
Because she wants to calm Claire quickly and leave.
Because the hospital has ordered her to promise it.
Because she makes it from conviction, not from a ready solution.
C1.hint: 'Planı olmayan bir söz' neden içtenlikle verilmiş olabilir?
C1.why: Ayo'nun elinde bir plan yok ama sözü içtenlikle veriyor; yani söz bir çözüm bilmekten değil, kararlılıktan geliyor.

eps.title: Nothing Will Grow
eps.recap: Laboratuvar teknisyeni Pete, hastalardan aldığı örnekleri sıradan besiyerlerinde 48 saat üretmeye çalıştı ama hiçbir şey üremedi. Mikroskopta bir şey gördü; bu, özel koşullarda büyüyen alışılmadık bir bakteriye işaret ediyordu.

text: Pete worked in the hospital laboratory. He was thin and quiet, and he loved his microscope. For two days, he tried to grow bacteria from the patients' samples. He put them on special plates and in a warm box.
On Thursday morning, he called Ayo. "Come down," he said. "I want to show you something."
Ayo went to the lab. Pete showed her the plates. They were clean. There was nothing on them. "Nothing grew," he said. "Not after forty-eight hours."
"Then the patients are not sick with bacteria?" Ayo asked. Pete shook his head. "No. Look." He gave her the microscope. She saw tiny thin shapes in the sample.
"They are bacteria," said Pete. "But they do not grow on normal food. Only a few bacteria are like this. I do not want to say the name yet."
A2.proof: they do not grow on normal food
A2.q: What does Pete's result tell us?
o: The patients are not ill at all.
The patients have a special kind of bacteria that is hard to grow.
The microscope is broken.
The samples were too old.
A2.hint: Plakalar boş ama mikroskopta bakteri görünüyor; bu nasıl bir bakteri olabilir?
A2.why: Sıradan besiyerinde bir şey üremedi ama mikroskopta bakteri görünüyor; yani bu bakteriler normal koşullarda üremeyen özel bir tür.

text: Pete worked in the hospital laboratory. He was thin and quiet, and he loved his microscope more than most people. For two days he had been trying to grow bacteria from the patients' samples on the standard plates, in the warm incubator.
On Thursday morning he called Ayo. "Come down," he said. "I want to show you something."
She went to the lab. Pete showed her the plates. They were perfectly clean. "Nothing has grown," he said. "Not after forty-eight hours. By now the usual infections would be covering the plate."
"So it isn't bacteria?" asked Ayo. Pete shook his head. "I didn't say that. Look." He gave her the microscope. In the sample she saw tiny, thin, rod-shaped bodies, pale against the glass.
"They're bacteria," said Pete quietly. "But they refuse to grow on ordinary food. Only a few kinds behave like that. I don't want to say the name until I'm sure."
B1.proof: I didn't say that.
B1.q: Why are the plates clean although bacteria are present?
o: The incubator was switched off.
The bacteria died when Pete opened the samples.
The bacteria need special conditions that the ordinary plates do not give.
Pete used the wrong patient samples.
B1.hint: Bakteri var ama sıradan plakada üremiyor; bunun nedeni ne olabilir?
B1.why: Bakteriler sıradan besiyerinde üremiyor, yani özel koşullara ihtiyaç duyan, zor üreyen bir tür olmalı.

text: Pete worked in the hospital laboratory. He was thin and quiet, and he loved his microscope more than most people. For two days he had been trying to grow bacteria from the patients' samples on the standard plates, in the warm incubator.
On Thursday morning he called Ayo. "Come down," he said. "I want to show you something."
She went to the lab. Pete showed her the plates, which were perfectly clean. "Nothing has grown," he said. "Not after forty-eight hours. By now an ordinary infection would be covering the plate."
"So it isn't bacteria?" asked Ayo. Pete shook his head. "I didn't say that. Look." He handed her the eyepiece. In the sample she saw tiny, thin, rod-shaped bodies, pale against the glass.

"They're bacteria," said Pete quietly. "But they refuse to grow on ordinary food. Only a few kinds behave like that, and most of them live in places where nobody expects to find them. I don't want to say the name until I'm sure." He rubbed his tired eyes. "I have been awake since Tuesday, and I would like to be wrong."
B2.proof: most of them live in places where nobody expects to find them
B2.q: What does Pete's last sentence hint at?
o: That the bacteria were brought by a visitor.
That the infection can be cured with food.
That the laboratory is not clean enough.
That the source of the bacteria may be somewhere unusual.
B2.hint: 'Kimsenin beklemediği yerlerde yaşarlar' ifadesi kaynak hakkında ne söylüyor?
B2.why: Pete bu bakterilerin çoğunun kimsenin beklemediği yerlerde yaşadığını söylüyor; yani kaynak olağandışı bir yerde olabilir.

text: Pete worked in the hospital laboratory. He was thin and quiet, and he loved his microscope more than most people loved their families. For two days he had been trying to grow bacteria from the patients' samples on the standard plates, in the warm incubator.
On Thursday morning he called Ayo. "Come down," he said. "I want to show you something."

She went to the lab. Pete showed her the plates, which were perfectly clean. "Nothing has grown," he said. "Not after forty-eight hours. By now an ordinary infection would be covering the plate like a carpet."

"So it isn't bacteria?" asked Ayo. Pete shook his head. "I didn't say that. Look." He handed her the eyepiece. In the sample she saw tiny, thin, rod-shaped bodies, pale against the glass, as if somebody had drawn them there with a very fine pencil.

"They're bacteria," said Pete quietly. "But they refuse to grow on ordinary food. Only a few kinds behave like that, and most of them live in places where nobody expects to find them. I don't want to say the name until I'm sure. If I'm right, then we haven't been looking at the patients. We've been looking at the wrong thing."
C1.proof: We've been looking at the wrong thing
C1.q: What is Pete's final sentence implying about the investigation so far?
o: That the doctors have been searching in the wrong place for the cause.
That the patients are not really ill.
That the microscope gives false results.
That the sample numbers were mixed up.
C1.hint: 'Hastalara bakıyorduk, yanlış şeye bakıyorduk' cümlesi ne anlatıyor?
C1.why: Pete, kaynağın hastalarda değil başka bir yerde (örneğin ortamda) olabileceğini, şimdiye kadar yanlış yere baktıklarını ima ediyor.

eps.title: Don't Tell Anyone
eps.recap: Tesis müdürü Mr. Garrow, Ayo'yu şafakta odasına çağırdı ve vakaları dışarıdaki kimseye anlatmamasını istedi. Ayo, Garrow'un Pete'in test sonucunu henüz kimse söylemeden bildiğini fark etti.

text: On Friday morning, before the sun came up, Ayo's phone rang. It was Mr. Garrow, the facilities manager. He ran the building: the pipes, the heating and the air.
"Dr. Bennett," he said. "Please come to my office. Now." Ayo was surprised. She had spoken to Mr. Garrow only two times in a year.

His office was warm and neat. Mr. Garrow smiled, but his eyes did not smile. "I hear you are worried about some patients," he said. "I understand. But this is a hospital. People get sick. Please do not talk about this outside. A rumour can close a whole floor."
"I have not talked to anyone outside," said Ayo.
"Good," he said. "And you must not ask the laboratory for strange tests." Ayo stood still. She had told nobody about Pete's work. How did he know about the laboratory?
A2.proof: How did he know about the laboratory?
A2.q: Why does Ayo become suspicious of Mr. Garrow?
o: He smiled too much during the conversation.
He called her at a strange hour.
He knows about the laboratory tests, and she told nobody.
He asked her to talk to the newspapers.
A2.hint: Garrow'un laboratuvardan söz etmesi Ayo'yu neden şaşırttı?
A2.why: Ayo laboratuvar çalışmasını kimseye söylememişti ama Garrow bunu biliyor; bu onun bilgi aldığını ve bir şey saklıyor olabileceğini gösteriyor.

text: On Friday morning, before sunrise, Ayo's phone rang. It was Mr. Garrow, the facilities manager, the man who ran the building: its pipes, its heating, its air.
"Dr. Bennett," he said. "Please come to my office. Now." Ayo was surprised. In a whole year she had spoken to Mr. Garrow only twice.

His office was warm and tidy. Mr. Garrow smiled, but the smile did not reach his eyes. "I hear you are worried about some patients," he said. "I understand. But this is a hospital, and sick people are what hospitals are for. Please don't discuss this outside. A rumour can close an entire floor, and then where would our patients go?"
"I haven't discussed it with anyone outside," said Ayo.

"Good. And I'd prefer that you didn't ask the laboratory for any unusual tests." Ayo stood very still. She had told nobody about Pete's work, nobody at all. So how did the facilities manager know what was happening in the laboratory?
B1.proof: So how did the facilities manager know what was happening in the laboratory?
B1.q: What can be inferred from Garrow's last remark?
o: He is the head of the laboratory.
He wants Ayo to be promoted.
He is trying to protect Pete's job.
He has been informed about the lab work, so someone is reporting to him.
B1.hint: Garrow'un laboratuvar işini bilmesi, birilerinin ona haber verdiğini düşündürür mü?
B1.why: Ayo kimseye söylememişti; Garrow'un laboratuvar çalışmasını bilmesi, birinin ona bilgi verdiğini ya da onun bu işi gözlediğini gösteriyor.

text: On Friday morning, before sunrise, Ayo's phone rang. It was Mr. Garrow, the facilities manager, the man who ran the building: its pipes, its heating, its air.
"Dr. Bennett," he said. "Please come to my office. Now." Ayo was surprised. In a whole year she had spoken to Mr. Garrow only twice.

His office was warm and tidy. Mr. Garrow smiled, but the smile did not reach his eyes. "I hear you are worried about some patients," he said. "I understand. But sick people are what hospitals are for. Please don't discuss this outside. A rumour can close an entire floor, and then where would our patients go?"
"I haven't discussed it with anyone outside," said Ayo.

"Good. And I would prefer that you didn't ask the laboratory for any unusual tests." Ayo stood very still. She had told nobody about Pete's work, not even Rosa. So how did the man responsible for the pipes and the air know what was happening in the laboratory? And why did he care? She thanked him politely and left, and in the lift she realised her hands were cold.
B2.proof: And why did he care?
B2.q: Why does the narrator mention that Garrow is responsible for the pipes and the air?
o: To hint that his work may be connected to the cause of the illness.
To explain why he is so busy in the mornings.
To show that he has no medical knowledge.
To suggest that he enjoys talking to doctors.
B2.hint: Garrow'un sorumlu olduğu şeyler (boru, ısıtma, hava) ile hastalık arasındaki olası bağlantıyı düşün.
B2.why: Yazar Garrow'u 'boruların ve havanın' sorumlusu olarak anıyor ve neden ilgilendiğini soruyor; bu, hastalığın binanın teknik sistemleriyle ilgili olabileceğini sezdiriyor.

text: On Friday morning, before sunrise, Ayo's phone rang. It was Mr. Garrow, the facilities manager, the man who ran the building: its pipes, its heating, its air.
"Dr. Bennett," he said. "Please come to my office. Now." Ayo was surprised. In a whole year she had spoken to Mr. Garrow only twice, and both times about parking.

His office was warm and tidy. Mr. Garrow smiled, but the smile stopped well short of his eyes. "I hear you are worried about some patients," he said. "I quite understand. But sick people are what hospitals are for. I'd ask you not to discuss this outside these walls. A rumour can close an entire floor, and then where would our patients go?"
"I haven't discussed it with anyone outside," said Ayo.

"Good. And I would prefer that you didn't ask the laboratory for any further unusual tests." Ayo stood very still. She had told nobody about Pete's work, not even Rosa. So how did the man responsible for the pipes and the air know what was happening in the laboratory? And why, when it was no part of his job, did he care so much? She kept her face blank and thanked him politely, the way one thanks a person one has just begun to distrust.
C1.proof: the way one thanks a person one has just begun to distrust
C1.q: How does Ayo react at the end of the scene, and why?
o: She openly accuses Garrow of lying.
She hides her suspicion so that Garrow will not know she noticed.
She agrees to stop the investigation.
She leaves without saying anything to him.
C1.hint: Ayo'nun 'kibar teşekkürü' ve 'boş yüz ifadesi' neyi gizlemek için?
C1.why: Ayo yüzünü boş tutuyor ve nazikçe teşekkür ediyor; çünkü Garrow'dan şüphelenmeye başladığını ona belli etmek istemiyor.

eps.title: The Calendar
eps.recap: Ayo, hastaların yatış ve hastalanma tarihlerini bir takvime çizdi. Hepsi hastaneye geldikten iki ila beş gün sonra hastalanmıştı; bu, hastalığın hastane içinde kapıldığını güçlendiriyordu.

text: On Saturday night, Ayo took a big sheet of paper and drew a calendar. She wrote the name of each patient. Under each name, she put two dates: the day the patient came to the hospital, and the day the fever began.
She worked slowly. Mr. Hale came on a Monday. His fever began on Thursday. Mr. Dunne came on Monday, and his fever began on Thursday too. Another patient came on Tuesday, and she was sick on Friday.
Ayo counted the days between the two dates. Then she counted again. It was always the same: two days, three days, four days or five days. Never one day. Never ten days.
She called Pete. "Pete, these people were well when they came," she said. "The fever started after some days. It looks like they caught something here."
"In the hospital?" Pete asked. "Yes," said Ayo. "And always after a few days. Like waiting time."
A2.proof: Never one day. Never ten days.
A2.q: What does the pattern in the calendar show?
o: The patients were sick before they came.
The fever began on the same day for everybody.
The patients came to the hospital on different weeks.
The patients became sick a few days after they arrived.
A2.hint: Yatış ve ateş tarihleri arasındaki gün sayısının hep benzer olmasına bak.
A2.why: Ateş her zaman geldikten iki-beş gün sonra başlıyor; yani hastalar hastanede bir şey kapıp birkaç gün sonra hastalanıyor.

text: On Saturday night Ayo took a large sheet of paper and drew a calendar. She wrote the name of every sick patient down the left side, and beside each name she put two dates: the day the patient was admitted and the day the fever began.

She worked slowly. Mr. Hale had been admitted on a Monday, and his fever began on Thursday. Mr. Dunne had also come in on a Monday, and his fever began on Thursday as well. A third patient had arrived on Tuesday and fallen ill on Friday.
Ayo counted the days between the two dates, then counted them again. The result was always the same: two, three, four or five days. Never one day. Never ten.

She called Pete at the laboratory. "Pete, they were all healthy when they arrived. The fever starts after a few days, and the gap is almost the same every time. It looks as if they caught something here."
"In the hospital?" Pete asked quietly. "Yes," said Ayo. "And whatever it is, it needs a few days to make them ill. Like a delay on a fuse."
B1.proof: whatever it is, it needs a few days to make them ill
B1.q: What can we conclude from the calendar?
o: The patients were exposed after admission, and the illness has a short delay.
The illness was brought into the hospital by visitors.
The patients were all infected before surgery.
The illness appears only on Thursdays.
B1.hint: Hep iki-beş günlük bir aralık olması neyi düşündürür?
B1.why: Belirtiler hep kabulden birkaç gün sonra başlıyor; hastalar hastanede maruz kalmış ve hastalığın kısa bir kuluçka süresi var.

text: On Saturday night Ayo took a large sheet of paper and drew a calendar. She wrote the name of every sick patient down the left side, and beside each name she put two dates: the day the patient was admitted and the day the fever began.

She worked slowly. Mr. Hale had been admitted on a Monday, and his fever began on Thursday. Mr. Dunne had also come in on a Monday, and his fever began on Thursday as well. A third patient had arrived on Tuesday and fallen ill on Friday.

Ayo counted the days between the two dates, then counted them again. The result never changed: two, three, four or five days. Never one day. Never ten. When she plotted the numbers, the points formed a narrow band, as neat as a row of teeth.

She called Pete at the laboratory. "Pete, they were all healthy when they arrived. The fever starts after a few days, and the gap is almost identical every time. It looks as if they caught something here."
"In the hospital?" Pete asked quietly. "Yes," said Ayo. "And whatever it is, it needs a few days to make them ill. If it were already in their bodies when they arrived, we'd see a much wider spread."
B2.proof: If it were already in their bodies when they arrived, we'd see a much wider spread
B2.q: Why does Ayo say the cases would be more spread out if the infection were already present?
o: Because older patients get ill more slowly.
Because people would become ill at very different times if they came infected.
Because the fever would start before admission.
Because every patient has a different doctor.
B2.hint: Hastalar zaten hasta gelseydi hastalanma zamanları nasıl olurdu?
B2.why: Hastalar enfeksiyonlu gelselerdi hastalanma zamanları çok farklı olurdu. Dar bir aralıkta toplanmaları hastanede ortak bir maruziyet olduğunu gösteriyor.

text: On Saturday night Ayo took a large sheet of paper and drew a calendar. She wrote the name of every sick patient down the left side, and beside each name she put two dates: the day the patient was admitted and the day the fever began. The office was silent, and the single lamp made a small yellow island on the desk.

She worked slowly. Mr. Hale had been admitted on a Monday, and his fever began on Thursday. Mr. Dunne had also come in on a Monday, and his fever began on Thursday as well. A third patient had arrived on Tuesday and fallen ill on Friday.

Ayo counted the days between the two dates, then counted them again. The result never changed: two, three, four or five days. Never one day. Never ten. When she plotted the numbers, the points formed a narrow band, as neat as a row of teeth.

She called Pete at the laboratory. "Pete, they were all healthy when they arrived. The fever starts after a few days, and the gap is almost identical every time. It looks as if they caught something here."

"In the hospital?" Pete asked quietly. "Yes," said Ayo. "And whatever it is, it needs a few days to make them ill. If it were already in their bodies when they arrived, we'd see a far wider spread, with some people ill on the first night and others a fortnight later. Instead we see a clock. Something started that clock for each of them, and I want to know what."
C1.proof: Instead we see a clock
C1.q: What does Ayo mean by 'a clock'?
o: A broken machine in the ward that stops at night.
The schedule of the nurses' shifts.
A regular delay between exposure and illness that points to a common cause.
A piece of equipment used for operations.
C1.hint: Ayo 'saat' derken düzenli bir gecikmeyi mi, gerçek bir saati mi kastediyor?
C1.why: Ayo'nun 'saat' benzetmesi, maruziyetten hastalığa kadar geçen düzenli süreyi anlatıyor; bu düzenlilik ortak bir nedeni işaret ediyor.

eps.title: After the Shower
eps.recap: Eski pratisyen hekim Dr. Moyo, hastalığın duştan sonra başladığını ve buharlı suyu soluduğunu söyledi. Ayo, enfeksiyonun solunan su buharıyla bulaşmış olabileceğini düşünmeye başladı.

text: One of the patients on the sixth floor was a doctor. His name was Dr. Moyo, and he was seventy. He was a retired family doctor. He came to the hospital for heart tests. Now he had a fever, but his mind was still clear.
Ayo sat beside his bed. "Tell me exactly what you remember," she said. "Everything. Even small things."

Dr. Moyo closed his eyes. "I felt well on Tuesday," he said. "On Wednesday evening, I had a shower. The water was only a little warm, and there was a lot of mist in the bathroom. I breathed it for ten minutes. I remember the smell. Like old, wet earth."
"And then?" asked Ayo. "That night, I felt very hot," he said. "By morning, I could not think well. A doctor knows when something is wrong, and I knew."
Ayo wrote in her notebook: shower, mist, wet-earth smell. Then she looked up. "Did the others take a shower too?" she asked.
A2.proof: I breathed it for ten minutes
A2.q: What idea does Dr. Moyo's story give Ayo?
o: The infection may come from breathing tiny drops of water.
The infection may come from heart tests.
The infection is caused by old books.
The infection is caused by eating late at night.
A2.hint: Doktorun banyoda sis soluduğunu ve kokuyu tarif ettiğine dikkat et.
A2.why: Dr. Moyo duştan çıkan sisi on dakika solumuş ve kokuyu hatırlıyor; bu, enfeksiyonun suyun küçük damlacıklarını solumakla bulaşmış olabileceğini düşündürüyor.

text: One of the patients on the sixth floor was a doctor. Dr. Moyo, seventy years old, was a retired family physician who had come in for some heart tests. Now he had the same high fever as the others, but his mind was still mostly clear.
Ayo sat beside his bed. "Tell me exactly what you remember," she said. "Everything, even the small things."

Dr. Moyo closed his eyes. "I felt well on Tuesday. On Wednesday evening I had a shower. The water was only lukewarm, and the bathroom filled with mist. I stood in it for ten minutes, breathing it in. I remember the smell, like wet earth after a long drought."
"And then?" asked Ayo. "That night I became very hot. By morning I couldn't think straight. A doctor knows when something is wrong, Dr. Bennett. I knew."

Ayo wrote in her notebook: shower, lukewarm, mist, smell of wet earth. Then she looked up. "Did you use the same bathroom as the other patients?" she asked. "The one at the east end of the corridor? We all did," said Dr. Moyo.
B1.proof: breathing it in
B1.q: Which detail in Dr. Moyo's story is most important for Ayo's investigation?
o: He was a retired doctor.
He breathed mist from lukewarm water in a shared bathroom.
He felt well on Tuesday.
He had a heart test.
B1.hint: Sıcak olmayan su, sis ve ortak banyo birlikte neyi düşündürür?
B1.why: Ilık suyun sisinin solunması ve herkesin aynı banyoyu kullanması, ortak bir kaynağı ve soluma yoluyla bulaşı düşündürüyor.

text: One of the patients on the sixth floor was a doctor. Dr. Moyo, seventy years old, was a retired family physician who had come in for some heart tests. Now he had the same high fever as the others, but his mind was still mostly clear, and Ayo was grateful for it.
She sat beside his bed. "Tell me exactly what you remember," she said. "Everything, even the small things."

Dr. Moyo closed his eyes. "I felt well on Tuesday. On Wednesday evening I had a shower. The water was only lukewarm, and the bathroom filled with mist. I stood in it for ten minutes, breathing it in. I remember the smell, like wet earth after a long drought."
"And then?" asked Ayo. "That night I became very hot. By morning I couldn't think straight. A doctor knows when something is wrong, Dr. Bennett. I knew."

Ayo wrote in her notebook: shower, lukewarm, mist, smell of wet earth. Then she looked up. "Did you use the same bathroom as the other patients, the one at the east end of the corridor?" "We all did," said Dr. Moyo. "There's only one on this side, and it has always been a little too cold. I complained to the nurses about it on my first day."
B2.proof: it has always been a little too cold
B2.q: What does the temperature of the shower water suggest?
o: That the bathroom was newly built.
That the patients preferred cold showers.
That tepid water may have helped bacteria to survive and spread.
That the nurses were responsible for the water.
B2.hint: Su hiçbir zaman yeterince sıcak olmamış; bu bakteriler için ne anlama gelir?
B2.why: Sürekli ılık kalan su bazı bakteriler için ideal ortam olabilir; hasta bu suyun solunan sisiyle enfekte olmuş olabilir.

text: One of the patients on the sixth floor was a doctor. Dr. Moyo, seventy years old, was a retired family physician who had come in for some heart tests. Now he had the same high fever as the others, but his mind was still mostly clear, and Ayo was grateful for it: a doctor, she reasoned, was a witness who could think.
She sat beside his bed. "Tell me exactly what you remember," she said. "Everything, even the small things."

Dr. Moyo closed his eyes. "I felt well on Tuesday. On Wednesday evening I had a shower. The water was only lukewarm, and the bathroom filled with mist. I stood in it for ten minutes, breathing it in. I remember the smell, like wet earth after a long drought."
"And then?" asked Ayo. "That night I became very hot. By morning I couldn't think straight. A doctor knows when something is wrong, Dr. Bennett. I knew."

Ayo wrote in her notebook: shower, lukewarm, mist, smell of wet earth. Then she looked up. "Did you use the same bathroom as the other patients, the one at the east end of the corridor?" "We all did," said Dr. Moyo. "There's only one on this side, and the water has always been a little too cold. I complained about it on my first day. The nurse said, 'Everyone complains, doctor. Nobody fixes it.'" The sentence stayed in Ayo's mind long after she left the room.
C1.proof: Nobody fixes it.
C1.q: Why does the last sentence stay in Ayo's mind?
o: It shows that the nurses are unfriendly.
It proves that the patients were rude.
It means the bathroom was closed.
It suggests that a known problem with the water was ignored.
C1.hint: 'Herkes şikâyet ediyor, kimse düzeltmiyor' cümlesi bir sorun hakkında ne söylüyor?
C1.why: Su sorunu biliniyormuş ama kimse çözmemiş; bu, ihmal edilmiş teknik bir sorunun hastalıkla ilgili olabileceğini düşündürüyor.

eps.title: Rosa's Daughter
eps.recap: Rosa'nın kızı Lina, geçen pazar annesini ziyaret edip altıncı kattaki doğu banyosunu kullanmıştı. Şimdi başı ağrıyor ve öksürüyordu; Rosa korku içindeydi.

text: On Sunday night, Rosa came to Ayo's office. Her eyes were red. She was a strong woman, and Ayo had never seen her cry. "Doctor," she said, "I need to tell you something."

"Sit down, Rosa," said Ayo. Rosa did not sit. "My daughter Lina is nine years old," she said. "Last Sunday, she came to the hospital. I was working. She stayed with me for two hours. She played in the corridor, and she washed her hands in the bathroom at the east end."
Ayo felt cold. "The east end of the sixth floor?" "Yes. That bathroom." Rosa's voice was very small. "This morning, Lina had a headache. Tonight she has a cough. She says her legs hurt."
"It may be a normal cold," said Ayo gently. "Children get colds all the time."
"Maybe," said Rosa. "But I do not believe in 'maybe' any more. Not on this floor."
A2.proof: I do not believe in 'maybe' any more
A2.q: Why is Rosa so afraid?
o: Her daughter has failed an exam at school.
Her daughter may have been exposed in the same place as the patients.
Her daughter broke the bathroom door.
Rosa is angry with her daughter.
A2.hint: Lina'nın nerede vakit geçirdiğine ve şimdi nasıl olduğuna dikkat et.
A2.why: Lina geçen pazar hastalıkla ilişkilendirilen doğu banyosunu kullanmıştı ve şimdi belirtiler gösteriyor; Rosa aynı yerde maruz kalmış olmasından korkuyor.

text: On Sunday night Rosa came to Ayo's office with red eyes. She was a strong woman, and Ayo had never once seen her cry. "Doctor," she said, "I need to tell you something."

"Sit down, Rosa." Rosa remained standing. "My daughter Lina is nine. Last Sunday she came to the hospital because I was working a double shift. She stayed with me for two hours. She played in the corridor, and she washed her hands in the bathroom at the east end."

Ayo felt a coldness spread through her chest. "The east end of the sixth floor?" "That bathroom." Rosa's voice was very small. "This morning Lina had a headache. Tonight she's coughing, and she says her legs hurt."
"It could be an ordinary cold," Ayo said gently. "Children catch them all the time."

"It could be. But I don't believe in 'could be' any more. Not on that floor." Ayo looked at the calendar on her wall. Counting from last Sunday, the days between the visit and the first symptoms were exactly the days she had been writing down all week.
B1.proof: exactly the days she had been writing down all week
B1.q: What does Ayo realise by counting the days?
o: Lina is too young to catch the illness.
Lina has already recovered.
Lina's timing matches the pattern seen in the patients.
Rosa visited the bathroom more often than Lina.
B1.hint: Lina'nın ziyaretten semptomlara kadar geçen günlerini hastaların günleriyle karşılaştır.
B1.why: Ziyaretten belirtilere kadar geçen süre, Ayo'nun hastalarda bulduğu aralıkla tam örtüşüyor; Lina'nın durumu aynı örüntüye uyuyor.
