B1.proof: A new year of work was beginning.
B1.q: What does the sunrise symbolise in the story?
o: The end of all work.
A broken clock.
A warning.
A fresh start after a dark period of secrecy and danger.
B1.hint: Gün doğumu hikâyede neyi sembolize ediyor?
B1.why: Gizlilik ve tehlike dolu karanlık bir dönemden sonra yeni bir başlangıcı.

text: After four long months of darkness the sun came back. Nika stood at the station window in her warm sweater. The sky was pink and gold, and a thin line of light moved slowly across the white ice. It was the first sunrise of the year, and it seemed to her that the whole continent was exhaling.
Behind her the station was waking up. She could hear Kit singing in the kitchen, Tomas laughing at something, and Brandt's slow footsteps in the corridor.
Nika sat down at her desk and opened a new notebook. She wrote the date. Then she wrote one big question on the first page:
'What did the life in the lake know before we came?'

She looked at the sentence for a long time and smiled. Outside the light was growing stronger. A new year of work was beginning. Then she closed the notebook and went to the kitchen, where the smell of fresh bread and the sound of Kit's singing were waiting for her. Kit's voice rose and fell in the corridor, off key and very happy.
B2.proof: the whole continent was exhaling
B2.q: What does the phrase 'the whole continent was exhaling' express?
o: A feeling of relief and release after the long dark winter.
That the continent was sick.
That the wind was strong.
That the station was closing.
B2.hint: 'Kıta nefes veriyordu' ifadesi neyi anlatıyor?
B2.why: Uzun ve karanlık kıştan sonra duyulan rahatlama ve ferahlama hissini.

text: After four long months of darkness the sun came back. Nika stood at the station window in her warm sweater. The sky was pink and gold, and a thin line of light moved slowly across the white ice. It was the first sunrise of the year, and it seemed to her that the whole continent was exhaling.
Behind her the station was waking up. She could hear Kit singing in the kitchen, Tomas laughing at something, and Brandt's slow footsteps in the corridor.
Nika sat down at her desk and opened a new notebook. She wrote the date. Then she wrote one big question on the first page:
'What did the life in the lake know before we came?'

She looked at the sentence for a long time and smiled. Outside the light was growing stronger. A new year of work was beginning. It occurred to her that the previous winter had begun with a number that seemed to be wrong and had ended with a question that could not be answered yet, and that this was probably what science was: a way of replacing small mistakes with larger and more beautiful uncertainties. She turned the page and, in a firmer hand, began to plan the second drill.
C1.proof: replacing small mistakes with larger and more beautiful uncertainties
C1.q: What definition of science does Nika arrive at?
o: That science is only about measurement.
That science is a process that turns errors into deeper, more interesting questions.
That science eliminates all uncertainty.
That science is a kind of luck.
C1.hint: Nika bilimi sonunda nasıl tanımlıyor kendi sözleriyle?
C1.why: Bilim, küçük hataları daha büyük ve daha güzel belirsizliklere dönüştüren bir süreçtir.

title: The Letter in the Archive
hero: Arşiv asistanı Ivo Marsh, 1994'teki fabrika yangınıyla ilgili gizlenmiş bir mektup buluyor ve kasabanın bildiği hikâyeyi sorgulamaya başlıyor.
intro: Küçük bir kasabanın arşivinde, eski gazete ciltlerinin arasında unutulmuş bir mektup. Arşiv asistanı Ivo Marsh, otuz yıl önceki Redmill fabrikası yangınının kasabanın bildiği gibi olmadığına dair ilk ipucunu buluyor. Tarih, hukuk, gazetecilik ve toplum üzerine İngilizce okuyacağın bir entrika seni bekliyor.
outro: Ivo gerçeği buldu ve yıllarca haksız yere suçlanan bir adamın adını temize çıkardı. Otuz gün boyunca belgelerden, tanıklıklardan ve eski haberlerden sonuç çıkardın. Başka bir tefrikaya geçmeye hazırsın.

eps.title: Upside Down
eps.recap: Arşiv asistanı Ivo, 1994 gazete cildini raflarken yangın haberinin sayfasına saklanmış, katlanmış eski bir mektup buldu. Mektup, cildin ters konulmuş olmasına rağmen tam bu sayfanın arasındaydı ve ilk satırı yaklaşan bir felaketten söz ediyordu.

text: Ivo Marsh worked in the town archive. It was a small room under the library. Every day he put old newspapers on the shelves. The job was quiet, and Ivo liked it.
On Friday afternoon, he found a big book on the wrong shelf. It was the Redmill Gazette for 1994. It was upside down. "Who does this?" Ivo said. He turned it over and opened it.
A letter fell out. It was old and yellow, and someone had folded it three times. Ivo looked at the page where the letter was. It was the story about the big fire at the Redmill factory.
Ivo did not know much about the fire. Everybody in the town knew it, but nobody talked about it. Thirty people lost their jobs. A worker, Tom Hale, was blamed.
Ivo opened the letter. The first line said: "By the time you read this, the factory will be gone."
A2.q: Why is Ivo suspicious about the letter?
o: The letter was written by a worker he knew.
The book was in the wrong place, and the letter was inside the page about the fire.
The book was the only one in the archive from 1994.
He had been looking for the letter all week.
A2.hint: Cildin nasıl durduğuna ve mektubun hangi sayfada çıktığına bak.
A2.why: Cilt yanlış rafta ve ters duruyordu; mektup da yangın haberinin tam sayfasının arasındaydı. Bu, onun bilerek oraya saklandığını düşündürüyor.

text: Ivo Marsh worked in the town archive, a small, dusty room underneath the public library. Every day he catalogued old newspapers and put them back on the shelves. It was quiet work, and he liked it that way.

On Friday afternoon he found a heavy volume on the wrong shelf. It was the Redmill Gazette for 1994, and someone had put it back upside down. "Careless," Ivo muttered. He lifted it onto the table and opened it.

A folded letter slid out onto the table. The paper was yellow and soft, and it had been folded three times. Ivo looked at the page where it had been lying. It was the front page about the great fire at the Redmill factory.

He knew only the outline of the story. Everyone in town did. Thirty people had lost their jobs that night, and the blame had fallen on one man, a worker called Tom Hale. After that, nobody in Redmill liked to talk about it.
Ivo unfolded the letter carefully. The handwriting was neat and nervous. The first line read: "By the time you read this, the factory will be gone."
B1.proof: someone had put it back upside down
B1.q: What makes Ivo think the letter did not end up there by accident?
o: The handwriting was the same as his own.
The paper was in perfect condition.
The volume was misplaced and the letter lay on the page about the fire.
Tom Hale had worked in the archive.
B1.hint: Cildin durumu ve mektubun bulunduğu sayfa arasındaki bağlantıyı düşün.
B1.why: Cilt ters ve yanlış yerdeydi, mektup da yangını anlatan sayfanın arasındaydı. Bu iki ayrıntı mektubun bilinçli olarak saklandığını düşündürüyor.

text: Ivo Marsh worked in the town archive, a small, dusty room beneath the public library. Every day he catalogued old newspapers and returned them to the shelves. It was quiet work, and he liked it that way.

On Friday afternoon he noticed a heavy volume on the wrong shelf. It was the Redmill Gazette for 1994, and somebody had put it back upside down. "Careless," Ivo muttered. He lifted it onto the table and opened it.

A folded letter slid out across the wood. The paper was yellow and soft, and it had been creased in three places. Ivo looked at the page where it had been resting. It was the front page about the great fire at the Redmill factory.

He knew only the outline of that story, as everyone in town did. Thirty people had lost their jobs that night, and the blame had fallen on a single man, a worker called Tom Hale. Since then, nobody in Redmill had liked to discuss it.

Ivo unfolded the letter with the tips of his fingers. The handwriting was neat but nervous, as if the writer had been afraid of being interrupted. The first line read: "By the time you read this, the factory will be gone."
B2.proof: as if the writer had been afraid of being interrupted
B2.q: What does the description of the handwriting suggest about the writer?
o: That the writer was a professional journalist.
That the writer wanted the letter to be found quickly.
That the writer was very old.
That the writer was frightened or in a hurry when writing it.
B2.hint: 'Düzgün ama gergin' yazı, yazarın hangi ruh halini yansıtır?
B2.why: Yazı düzgün ama gergin; sanki biri yazarı bölecekmiş gibi. Bu, yazarın korktuğunu ya da acele ettiğini düşündürüyor.

text: Ivo Marsh worked in the town archive, a small, dusty room beneath the public library, where the ceiling pipes hummed and the light never changed with the weather. Every day he catalogued old newspapers and returned them to the shelves. It was quiet work, and he had chosen it for exactly that reason.

On Friday afternoon he noticed a heavy volume on the wrong shelf. It was the Redmill Gazette for 1994, and somebody had put it back upside down. "Careless," Ivo muttered. He lifted it onto the table and opened it with the reluctance of a man about to correct someone else's mistake.

A folded letter slid out across the wood. The paper was yellow and soft, and it had been creased in three places. Ivo looked at the page where it had been resting. It was the front page about the great fire at the Redmill factory.

He knew only the outline of that story, as everyone in town did. Thirty people had lost their jobs that night, and the blame had fallen on a single man, a worker called Tom Hale. Since then, nobody in Redmill had cared to discuss the matter, and nobody had asked why.

Ivo unfolded the letter with the tips of his fingers. The handwriting was neat but nervous, as though the writer had feared being interrupted. The first line read: "By the time you read this, the factory will be gone." He read it again. A fire could not be a surprise to someone who had written those words beforehand.
C1.proof: A fire could not be a surprise to someone who had written those words beforehand
C1.q: What does Ivo conclude from the first line of the letter?
o: That the writer knew about the fire before it happened.
That the writer was one of the workers who lost a job.
That the letter was written to a newspaper editor.
That the fire was only a small accident.
C1.hint: Mektup yangından önce yazılmışsa yazar hakkında ne söylenebilir?
C1.why: Mektup 'fabrika yok olmuş olacak' diyor; yani yazarı yangından önce bunu biliyordu. Ivo bunu açıkça fark ediyor.

eps.title: Three Days Before
eps.recap: Mektubun tarihi yangından üç gün öncesiydi ve altındaki imza bilerek silinmişti. Ivo, mektubu yazan kişinin yangını önceden bildiğini ya da korktuğunu anladı.

text: Ivo read the letter again. It was short. The writer said: "I have told them many times. The old machines are dangerous. Nobody listens. By the time you read this, the factory will be gone."
He looked at the date at the top. It said: 11 March 1994. Ivo opened the newspaper. The fire was on the night of 14 March.
"Three days," he said. "The writer wrote this three days before the fire."

Then he looked at the end of the letter. There was a name there, but someone had rubbed it out with a pencil eraser. Ivo held the paper up to the light. He could see only one thing: a capital letter, maybe an R, maybe a B.
Ivo sat very still. Someone had written a warning. Someone else had hidden it and rubbed out the name.
A2.q: Why is the date on the letter important?
o: It proves the fire started because of the letter.
It shows the letter was written by Tom Hale.
It shows the writer was worried about danger before the fire happened.
It means the newspaper printed the date wrongly.
A2.hint: Mektubun tarihi ile yangının tarihi arasındaki farka bak.
A2.why: Mektup yangından üç gün önce yazılmış ve tehlikeden söz ediyor; yazar yangından önce endişeliydi.

text: Ivo read the letter again. It was short and direct: "I have warned them many times that the old machines are dangerous. Nobody listens. By the time you read this, the factory will be gone."
He looked at the date at the top of the page: 11 March 1994. Then he opened the newspaper and found the report of the fire. It had started on the night of 14 March.
"Three days," he whispered. "This was written three days before the fire."

He turned to the bottom of the letter. There had once been a signature there, but someone had rubbed it out with an eraser, so hard that the paper had almost worn through. Ivo held the page up to the lamp. He could make out only a single capital letter, perhaps an R, perhaps a B.
He sat very still. Somebody had written a warning. Somebody else, later, had gone to the trouble of hiding it and removing the writer's name.
B1.proof: three days before the fire
B1.q: What can we understand from the rubbed-out signature?
o: The writer forgot to sign the letter.
The ink had faded over thirty years.
The writer signed with only an initial.
Someone wanted the writer's identity to stay unknown.
B1.hint: İmzanın 'o kadar sert silinmiş ki kâğıt neredeyse delinmiş' olduğunu düşün.
B1.why: İmza, kâğıdı neredeyse delecek kadar sert silinmiş; biri yazarın kimliğinin bilinmesini istememiş.

text: Ivo read the letter again. It was short and direct: "I have warned them many times that the old machines are dangerous, and I have been ignored every time. By the time you read this, the factory will be gone."
He checked the date at the top of the page: 11 March 1994. Then he found the newspaper report of the fire. It had broken out on the night of 14 March.
"Three days," he whispered. "This was written three days before the fire."

He turned to the bottom of the letter. There had once been a signature there, but someone had rubbed it out with an eraser, so hard that the paper had almost worn through. Ivo held the page up to the lamp and made out a single capital letter, perhaps an R, perhaps a B, and nothing more.

He sat very still. Somebody had written a warning. Somebody else, at some later point, had gone to the trouble of concealing it and removing the writer's name. He had spent six years at the archive without ever finding a document that someone had tried to hide, and he felt, to his own surprise, afraid.
B2.proof: someone had rubbed it out with an eraser
B2.q: What is the most reasonable conclusion about the letter's history?
o: Two different people were involved: one who warned and one who hid it.
The writer erased his own name by accident.
The letter was written after the fire.
The archive has always hidden its oldest documents.
B2.hint: Mektubu yazan ile imzayı silen kişinin aynı olması mantıklı mı?
B2.why: Biri uyarıyı yazmış, başka biri daha sonra onu saklayıp imzayı silmiş; yani metinde iki farklı kişi söz konusu.

text: Ivo read the letter again. It was short and direct: "I have warned them many times that the old machines are dangerous, and I have been ignored every time. By the time you read this, the factory will be gone."

He checked the date at the top of the page: 11 March 1994. Then he found the newspaper's account of the fire. It had broken out on the night of 14 March, and the report named one man as responsible without quoting a single witness.
"Three days," he whispered. "This was written three days before the fire."

He turned to the bottom of the letter. There had once been a signature there, but someone had rubbed it out with an eraser, so forcefully that the paper had nearly worn through. Ivo held the page up to the lamp and made out a single capital letter, perhaps an R, perhaps a B, and nothing more.

He sat very still. Somebody had written a warning. Somebody else, at some later point, had gone to the trouble of concealing it and removing the writer's name. In six years at the archive he had never found a document that someone had tried to hide, and he felt, to his own surprise, afraid, not of the letter itself but of whoever had thought it dangerous enough to bury.
C1.proof: without quoting a single witness
C1.q: Which detail in the passage most weakens the newspaper's account of the fire?
o: It was printed on the front page.
It named one man as responsible without quoting a single witness.
It described the fire as breaking out at night.
It was kept in a volume on a high shelf.
C1.hint: Bir haberi güvenilmez yapan şey tanık olmaması mıdır, sayfa konumu mu?
C1.why: Rapor tek bir kişiyi sorumlu tutuyor ama hiçbir tanıktan alıntı yapmıyor; bu, haberin dayanaksız olabileceğini düşündürüyor.

eps.title: Everybody Knows
eps.recap: Kasabadaki herkes yangını işçi Tom Hale'in ihmaline bağlıyordu ve gazete de öyle yazmıştı. Ivo, haberin altındaki imzayı okuyunca muhabirin adını fark etti ve bu ismi tanıdığını düşündü.

text: On Saturday, Ivo went to the market. He asked an old man about the fire. "Oh, that," said the man. "Tom Hale smoked in the storeroom. Everybody knows that."
Ivo asked a woman at the bakery. "Tom Hale," she said. "He was careless. Poor family. His daughter left town after that."
Everybody said the same thing. Nobody said, "I saw it." Nobody said, "I was there." They only said, "Everybody knows."
That evening, Ivo went back to the archive. He read the newspaper report again. It blamed Tom Hale. It said he was alone in the building that night.
At the end of the article, there was a small name: "By R. Okafor." Ivo looked at the letter on his desk. Then he looked at the name again. The same letter, R.
A2.q: What does Ivo notice about what the townspeople say?
o: They all remember the fire very clearly.
They are afraid to talk about Tom Hale.
They disagree about who was responsible.
They repeat the same story, but nobody saw the fire themselves.
A2.hint: İnsanların 'Herkes biliyor' demesi ile 'Ben gördüm' dememesi arasındaki farka dikkat et.
A2.why: Herkes aynı şeyi söylüyor ama kimse olayı kendi gözüyle gördüğünü söylemiyor; bilgi başkasından duyulmuş.

text: On Saturday Ivo went to the market and asked an old man about the fire. "Oh, that," the man said. "Tom Hale smoked in the storeroom. Everybody knows that."
At the bakery he asked a woman. "Tom Hale," she said, shaking her head. "Careless man. Poor family. His daughter left town after that and never came back."
Everyone gave him the same answer, in almost the same words. Nobody said, "I saw it." Nobody said, "I was there that night." They only said, "Everybody knows."
That evening Ivo went back to the archive and read the newspaper report again. It blamed Tom Hale. It claimed he had been alone in the building when the fire started.
At the bottom of the article was a small line in grey type: "By R. Okafor." Ivo looked at the letter on his desk. Then he looked at the name again. The same capital letter, R.
B1.proof: Nobody said, "I saw it."
B1.q: What problem does Ivo see in the town's version of the story?
o: It is based on repeated opinion, not on people who saw what happened.
It is based on documents that nobody can read.
It is told differently by every person he asks.
It was invented by the newspaper last year.
B1.hint: Herkesin aynı sözleri tekrarlamasının güvenilir bir kanıt olup olmadığını düşün.
B1.why: Kimse olayı görmemiş, herkes sadece 'herkes biliyor' diyor. Hikâye görgü tanıklığına değil, tekrarlanan söylentiye dayanıyor.

text: On Saturday Ivo walked through the market and asked an old man about the fire. "Oh, that," the man said. "Tom Hale smoked in the storeroom. Everybody knows that."
At the bakery he asked a woman behind the counter. "Tom Hale," she said, shaking her head. "Careless man. Poor family. His daughter left town after that and never came back."

Everyone gave him the same answer in almost the same words. Nobody said, "I saw it." Nobody said, "I was there that night." They only said, "Everybody knows," which seemed to Ivo a very different thing from knowing.
That evening he returned to the archive and reread the newspaper report. It blamed Tom Hale, and it claimed he had been alone in the building when the fire started.

At the bottom of the article, in small grey type, was the reporter's name: "By R. Okafor." Ivo looked at the letter on his desk, at the one capital letter left behind by the eraser, and then back at the byline. It might mean nothing. It might mean everything.
B2.proof: which seemed to Ivo a very different thing from knowing
B2.q: What is Ivo's attitude toward the phrase 'Everybody knows'?
o: He believes it is the strongest evidence in the case.
He thinks it is not a reliable proof of the truth.
He has heard it only from the baker.
He is angry because nobody will talk to him.
B2.hint: 'Herkes biliyor' ile 'bilmek' arasında Ivo'nun yaptığı ayrımı değerlendir.
B2.why: Ivo 'herkes biliyor' ifadesini gerçekten bilmekten çok farklı buluyor; yani bunu güvenilir bir kanıt saymıyor.

text: On Saturday Ivo walked through the market and asked an old man about the fire. "Oh, that," the man said, without looking up. "Tom Hale smoked in the storeroom. Everybody knows that."
At the bakery he put the same question to a woman behind the counter. "Tom Hale," she said, shaking her head. "Careless man. Poor family. His daughter left town soon after, and she never came back."

Everyone gave him the same answer in almost the same words. Nobody said, "I saw it." Nobody said, "I was there that night." They only said, "Everybody knows," which struck Ivo as a very different thing from actually knowing. A story repeated for thirty years, he thought, acquires the authority of fact without ever having been checked.

That evening he returned to the archive and reread the newspaper's report. It blamed Tom Hale and claimed that he had been alone in the building when the fire started. There was no quotation from the fire brigade and no statement from the owner.

At the bottom of the article, in small grey type, was the reporter's name: "By R. Okafor." Ivo looked at the letter on his desk, at the single capital letter the eraser had failed to destroy, and then back at the byline. It might mean nothing. He had a feeling that it did not.
C1.proof: acquires the authority of fact without ever having been checked
C1.q: What is the main point of Ivo's reflection about the story told in town?
o: A newspaper article is always more reliable than local memory.
People in small towns are unwilling to help strangers.
A claim repeated for long enough can seem true even if nobody has verified it.
Old reports should be destroyed after thirty years.
C1.hint: Ivo'nun 'otuz yıl tekrarlanan hikâye' hakkındaki düşüncesinin ana fikrini belirle.
C1.why: Ivo, otuz yıl boyunca tekrarlanan bir hikâyenin hiç doğrulanmadan gerçek gibi kabul edildiğini düşünüyor; ana fikir bu.

eps.title: Mrs. Okafor
eps.recap: Ivo, yangını haberleştiren eski muhabir Mrs. Okafor'u ziyaret edip mektubu gösterdi. Mrs. Okafor, haberdeki 'Tom Hale tek başınaydı' cümlesini kendisinin yazmadığını, yazısının değiştirildiğini söyledi.

text: On Sunday, Ivo took the bus to the end of the town. Mrs. Okafor lived in a small yellow house with a garden full of flowers. She was seventy-six years old. Thirty years ago, she was a reporter at the Redmill Gazette.
She made tea and listened. Then Ivo took the letter out of his bag. "I found this in the 1994 book," he said. "On the page of your article about the fire."
Mrs. Okafor read the letter slowly. Her hand began to shake. She put the cup down. "Mr. Marsh," she said, "I never saw this before. But I must tell you something."

Ivo waited. "In my article, I did not write that Tom Hale was alone in the building," she said. "I wrote that the police were still asking questions. Somebody changed my words before the newspaper was printed."
"Who?" asked Ivo. Mrs. Okafor looked out of the window. "My editor," she said. "He gave me the new article and said: 'Print it. This is the story.'"
A2.proof: Somebody changed my words before the newspaper was printed.
A2.q: What does Mrs. Okafor's statement suggest?
o: The newspaper story about Tom Hale may not be true.
The newspaper printed too many copies.
Mrs. Okafor wrote the letter herself.
Tom Hale was a reporter at the Gazette.
A2.hint: Mrs. Okafor makalesinin ne olduğunu ve değiştirildiğini anlatıyor.
A2.why: Makaledeki ana suçlama onun yazdığı şey değil; biri sözlerini değiştirmiş. Bu, kasabanın bildiği hikâyenin doğru olmayabileceğini düşündürüyor.

text: On Sunday Ivo took the bus to the far end of town. Mrs. Okafor lived in a small yellow house with a garden full of flowers. She was seventy-six, and thirty years earlier she had been a reporter at the Redmill Gazette.
She made tea and listened. Then Ivo took the letter out of his bag. "I found this inside the 1994 volume," he said, "on the page with your article about the fire."
Mrs. Okafor read slowly. Her hand began to shake, and she put down her cup. "Mr. Marsh, I have never seen this letter in my life. But there is something you ought to know."

Ivo waited. "In my article," she said, "I never wrote that Tom Hale was alone in the building. I wrote that the police were still asking questions. Somebody changed my words before the paper went to print."

"Who?" asked Ivo. Mrs. Okafor looked out at her flowers. "My editor. He gave me a different article and said, 'Print this. This is the story.' I was young, and I needed the job. I have not forgiven myself since."
B1.proof: Somebody changed my words before the paper went to print.
B1.q: What can we understand about Mrs. Okafor's feelings?
o: She is proud of the article she wrote.
She feels guilty because she accepted a false version of her article.
She is angry with Ivo for finding the letter.
She is afraid of the police.
B1.hint: 'Kendimi hâlâ affetmedim' cümlesi hangi duyguyu anlatıyor?
B1.why: Mrs. Okafor genç olduğu ve işe ihtiyacı olduğu için değiştirilmiş yazıyı kabul etmiş; bunun için suçluluk duyuyor.

text: On Sunday Ivo took the bus to the far end of town. Mrs. Okafor lived in a small yellow house with a garden full of flowers. She was seventy-six, and thirty years earlier she had been a reporter at the Redmill Gazette.
She made tea and listened. Then Ivo took the letter out of his bag. "I found this inside the 1994 volume," he said, "on the page with your article about the fire."
Mrs. Okafor read slowly. Her hand began to tremble, and she put down her cup. "Mr. Marsh, I have never seen this letter in my life. But there is something you ought to know."

Ivo waited. "In my article," she said, "I never wrote that Tom Hale was alone in the building. I wrote that the police were still asking questions. Somebody changed my words before the paper went to print."

"Who?" asked Ivo. Mrs. Okafor looked out at her flowers. "My editor. He handed me a different article and said, 'Print this. This is the story.' I was young, and I needed the job, so I put my name on it. I have not forgiven myself since, and I never knew who had asked him to do it."
B2.proof: I never knew who had asked him to do it
B2.q: What question is raised by the last sentence?
o: Who delivered the newspaper to the town?
Why did Mrs. Okafor leave the newspaper?
Who wanted the article changed, and why?
Why did Ivo visit the archive?
B2.hint: Editörü kimin ya da neyin değişikliğe yönelttiği belli değil.
B2.why: Mrs. Okafor editörünün yazıyı değiştirdiğini ama bunu kimin istediğini hiç öğrenmediğini söylüyor; bu, asıl sorumlunun kim olduğu sorusunu açıyor.

text: On Sunday Ivo took the bus to the far end of town. Mrs. Okafor lived in a small yellow house with a garden crowded with flowers. She was seventy-six, and thirty years earlier she had been a young reporter at the Redmill Gazette, with a reputation for being stubborn.
She made tea and listened. Then Ivo took the letter out of his bag. "I found this inside the 1994 volume," he said, "on the page with your article about the fire."
Mrs. Okafor read slowly. Her hand began to tremble, and she put down her cup. "Mr. Marsh, I have never seen this letter in my life. But there is something you ought to know."

Ivo waited. "In my article," she said, "I never wrote that Tom Hale was alone in the building. I wrote that the police were still asking questions. Somebody changed my words before the paper went to print."

"Who?" asked Ivo. Mrs. Okafor looked out at her flowers. "My editor. He handed me a different article and said, 'Print this. This is the story.' I was young, and I needed the job, so I put my name on it. I have not forgiven myself since. And I never learned who had asked him to do it, which is a strange thing for a reporter to admit."
C1.proof: which is a strange thing for a reporter to admit
C1.q: Why does Mrs. Okafor call her admission 'strange'?
o: Because she has never talked to an editor.
Because she is proud of her reputation.
Because she wrote the story without help.
Because a reporter is expected to discover who is behind a story.
C1.hint: Bir muhabirin neyi bilmesi beklenir? Mrs. Okafor neden bunu garip buluyor?
C1.why: Bir muhabirin bir haberin arkasında kimin olduğunu araştırması beklenir; Mrs. Okafor bunu yapmadığını kabul ederken kendi mesleki başarısızlığını vurguluyor.

eps.title: The Second Page
eps.recap: Ivo mektubun ikinci sayfasında fabrikanın sigortasının bu yıl üç kez artırıldığını yazan bir satır buldu. Mrs. Okafor, yangından kısa süre önce bir kişinin telefonla ona 'sigortaya bakın' dediğini hatırladı.

text: Mrs. Okafor made more tea. Ivo turned the letter over, because he had not looked at the back of the page. There were four more lines in the same nervous handwriting.
He read them aloud: "The machines are old, and the alarms are switched off at night. And the factory insurance has gone up three times this year. Nobody asks why."
Mrs. Okafor closed her eyes. "Insurance," she said. "Oh, my God. I remember now."

"What do you remember?" asked Ivo. "A week before the fire, a man phoned me," she said. "He did not say his name. He said, 'Look at the factory insurance.' I laughed. I said, 'Why would I do that?' He put down the phone."
She looked at the letter. "I never looked," she said. "I forgot. Then the fire happened, and then they gave me the new article."
A2.proof: the factory insurance has gone up three times this year
A2.q: Why is the line about the insurance important?
o: It shows that the factory was very rich.
It may give the factory owner a reason to want a fire.
It proves that Tom Hale wrote the letter.
It explains why the alarms made noise.
A2.hint: Sigorta bedeli yükselmiş ve alarmlar gece kapalıymış: bunlar birlikte neyi düşündürür?
A2.why: Sigortanın yükseltilmesi ve alarmların kapalı olması, fabrika sahibinin yangından çıkar sağlamış olabileceğini düşündürüyor.

text: Mrs. Okafor poured more tea. Ivo turned the letter over, because he had not looked at the back of the page. There were four more lines in the same nervous handwriting.
He read them aloud: "The machines are old, and the alarms are switched off at night. And the factory insurance has gone up three times this year. Nobody asks why."
Mrs. Okafor closed her eyes. "Insurance," she whispered. "Oh, my goodness. I remember now."

"Remember what?" asked Ivo. "A week before the fire, a man telephoned me at the newspaper. He wouldn't give his name. He just said, 'Look at the factory's insurance.' I thought it was a joke. I asked why on earth I should, and he hung up."
She stared at the letter. "I never looked. And then the fire happened, and then my editor gave me the new article, and I let it go. For thirty years I let it go."
B1.proof: Nobody asks why.
B1.q: How does the letter and the phone call fit together?
o: Both show that the factory was closed before the fire.
Both were written by Mrs. Okafor.
Both point to the insurance as something worth investigating.
Both are about the weather before the fire.
B1.hint: Mektuptaki sigorta satırı ile telefondaki 'sigortaya bakın' arasındaki ortak noktayı bul.
B1.why: Mektup da arayan kişi de sigortaya dikkat çekiyor; yani aynı ipucunu işaret ediyorlar ve bu araştırılmaya değer.

text: Mrs. Okafor poured more tea. Ivo turned the letter over, because he had not looked at the back of the page. There were four more lines in the same nervous handwriting.
He read them aloud: "The machines are old, and the alarms are switched off at night. And the factory insurance has gone up three times this year. Nobody asks why."
Mrs. Okafor closed her eyes. "Insurance," she whispered. "Oh, my goodness. I remember now."

"Remember what?" asked Ivo. "A week before the fire, a man telephoned me at the newspaper. He wouldn't give his name. He just said, 'Look at the factory's insurance.' I thought it was a joke, and I asked why on earth I should. He hung up."

She stared at the letter. "I never looked. Then the fire happened, and then my editor gave me his article, and I let it go. For thirty years I let it go. But whoever telephoned me and whoever wrote this were saying the same thing, weren't they? They wanted someone to follow the money."
B2.proof: They wanted someone to follow the money.
B2.q: What does the expression 'follow the money' mean here?
o: Find out who paid for the newspaper.
Check how much the workers earned.
Count the money the factory lost.
Investigate who gained financially from the fire.
B2.hint: 'Parayı takip et' ifadesi bir suçta neye bakmayı önerir?
B2.why: 'Follow the money' parayla ilgili çıkarın kimde olduğunu araştırmak demek; yani yangından kimin maddi olarak kazanç sağlayacağına bakılmalı.

text: Mrs. Okafor poured more tea. Ivo turned the letter over, because he had not looked at the back of the page. There were four more lines in the same nervous handwriting.
He read them aloud: "The machines are old, and the alarms are switched off at night. And the factory insurance has gone up three times this year. Nobody asks why."
Mrs. Okafor closed her eyes. "Insurance," she whispered. "Oh, my goodness. I remember now."

"Remember what?" asked Ivo. "A week before the fire, a man telephoned me at the newspaper. He wouldn't give his name. He just said, 'Look at the factory's insurance.' I thought it was a joke, and I asked why on earth I should. He hung up."

She stared at the letter. "I never looked. Then the fire happened, and then my editor gave me his article, and I let it go. For thirty years I let it go. But whoever telephoned me and whoever wrote this were saying the same thing, weren't they? They wanted someone to follow the money." Ivo said nothing. He was thinking that a factory that is insured for more each year, with its alarms silenced at night, is not an unlucky building. It is a prepared one.
C1.proof: It is a prepared one.
C1.q: What does Ivo's final thought imply?
o: That the fire may have been planned rather than accidental.
That the factory was protected by good luck.
That the alarms were switched off by the workers.
That the building was too old to be insured.
C1.hint: 'Şanssız bina' ile 'hazırlıklı bina' arasındaki fark ne?
C1.why: Artan sigorta ve gece kapalı alarmlar Ivo'ya binanın şanssız değil, 'hazırlıklı' olduğunu düşündürüyor; yani yangın planlanmış olabilir.

eps.title: Mr. Pell Wants It Back
eps.recap: Arşiv müdürü Mr. Pell, Ivo'dan mektubu ve gazete cildini hemen geri istedi. Ivo, Pell'in telefonda 'Evet Mr. Varley, halledilecek' dediğini duydu.

text: On Monday morning, Mr. Pell was waiting for Ivo at the door of the archive. Mr. Pell was the archive director. He was a small grey man who rarely spoke.
"Mr. Marsh," he said. "I hear you moved the 1994 book. Please bring it to my office. And I want everything you found inside it."
Ivo's heart jumped. He did not remember telling Mr. Pell about the letter. He said, "There is nothing special, sir."
"Please do not lie to me," said Mr. Pell. "The letter belongs to the archive. I will put it in the safe. Today."
At that moment, the phone on Mr. Pell's desk rang. Ivo was standing in the open door. He heard Mr. Pell say, very quietly: "Yes, Mr. Varley. It will be done."
A2.proof: Yes, Mr. Varley. It will be done.
A2.q: What does the telephone call suggest?
o: Mr. Pell is calling a friend about his lunch.
Mr. Pell wants to give the letter to the police.
Mr. Pell is taking orders from the owner of the factory.
Mr. Pell is angry with Mr. Varley.
A2.hint: Varley fabrikanın sahibi; Pell onunla nasıl konuşuyor?
A2.why: Pell, fabrika sahibi Varley'e 'yapılacak' diyor; yani ondan talimat alıyor ve mektubu bu yüzden istiyor olabilir.

text: On Monday morning Mr. Pell was waiting for Ivo at the archive door. Mr. Pell, the director, was a small grey man who rarely spoke and almost never came down to the basement.
"Mr. Marsh," he said. "I understand you moved the 1994 volume. Please bring it to my office, and everything you found inside it."
Ivo's heart jumped. He had not told anyone at the archive about the letter, not one person. "There was nothing special, sir," he said.
"Please don't insult me," said Mr. Pell. "Any document in this building belongs to the archive. I will keep it in the safe. Today." He held out his hand and waited.
At that moment the telephone on Mr. Pell's desk rang. Ivo, still standing in the open doorway, heard him answer in a quite different voice, low and respectful. "Yes, Mr. Varley. It will be done."
B1.proof: He had not told anyone at the archive about the letter
B1.q: What does Ivo notice about Mr. Pell's knowledge?
o: Mr. Pell has found the letter in the safe.
Mr. Pell has read the 1994 volume.
Mr. Pell has spoken to Mrs. Okafor.
Mr. Pell knows about the letter although Ivo told nobody at the archive.
B1.hint: Ivo mektuptan arşivde kimseye bahsetmedi; Pell nasıl biliyor?
B1.why: Ivo arşivde kimseye mektuptan söz etmemişti ama Pell biliyor; bu, birinin ona haber verdiğini ya da Ivo'yu izlediğini gösteriyor.

text: On Monday morning Mr. Pell was waiting for Ivo at the archive door. Mr. Pell, the director, was a small grey man who rarely spoke and almost never came down to the basement.
"Mr. Marsh," he said. "I understand you moved the 1994 volume. Please bring it to my office, along with everything you found inside it."
Ivo's heart jumped. He had not told anyone at the archive about the letter, not one person. "There was nothing special, sir," he said.

"Please don't insult me," said Mr. Pell. "Any document in this building belongs to the archive. I shall keep it in the safe. Today." He held out his hand and waited, and the silence in the basement was very long.

At that moment the telephone on Mr. Pell's desk rang. Ivo, still standing in the open doorway, heard him answer in a quite different voice, low and respectful. "Yes, Mr. Varley. It will be done." Ivo knew only one Varley in Redmill: the man whose name had once been written above the gates of the factory that burned.
B2.proof: the man whose name had once been written above the gates of the factory that burned

o: It links the archive director to the owner of the burned factory.
It shows that Varley is a famous journalist.

It explains why the archive is in the basement.

eps.title: The Policy
eps.recap: Ivo, belediye kayıtlarında Redmill fabrikasının sigorta poliçesinin yangından bir ay önce dokuz yüz bin sterline yükseltildiğini ve poliçeyi Alan Varley'nin imzaladığını buldu.

text: On Tuesday, Ivo went to the town hall. In the basement, there was a room with old records of the town. A tired clerk gave him a key. "Take what you want," she said. "Nobody comes here."
Ivo looked for papers about the Redmill factory. He found a grey box with the year 1994 on it. Inside, there were letters, plans and forms. One form said: Fire Insurance Policy.
He read it slowly. In 1993, the factory was insured for two hundred thousand pounds. Then he saw a new date: February 1994. The new amount was nine hundred thousand pounds.
Ivo counted. The factory was burned one month later, in March. At the bottom of the page, there was a signature in thick black ink: Alan Varley.
He took out his notebook. "The owner made the factory four times more valuable," he wrote. "And one month later, it was gone."
A2.proof: The owner made the factory four times more valuable
A2.q: Why is the increase in the policy important?
o: The factory was growing very quickly.
The workers asked for a bigger factory.
The town hall wanted to buy the factory.
The owner would receive much more money if the factory burned.
A2.hint: Sigorta bedeli dört kat arttı ve bir ay sonra fabrika yandı: bunun bir anlamı var mı?
A2.why: Poliçe yangından bir ay önce dört katına çıkarılmış; yangın çıkarsa sahibi çok daha fazla para alacaktı. Bu bir saik olabilir.

text: On Tuesday Ivo went to the town hall. In the basement there was a records room, and a tired clerk handed him the key. "Help yourself," she said. "Nobody comes down here."
Ivo looked for papers about the Redmill factory and found a grey box marked 1994. Inside lay letters, building plans and forms. One of them was headed: Fire Insurance Policy.
He read it slowly. In 1993 the factory had been insured for two hundred thousand pounds. Then he noticed a new date, February 1994, and a new figure: nine hundred thousand pounds.
Ivo counted on his fingers. The fire had happened only one month later, in March. At the bottom of the page, in thick black ink, was a signature: Alan Varley.

He took out his notebook. "The owner made the factory worth four times more," he wrote. "And one month later it burned down. I don't know whether this is a motive, but it is certainly an opportunity."
B1.proof: a motive, but it is certainly an opportunity

o: The insurance change gives a possible reason for the fire, but he has no proof yet.
The insurance change proves that Varley started the fire.

The insurance change was approved by Tom Hale.
B1.hint: Ivo 'saik' ve 'fırsat' arasında nasıl bir ayrım yapıyor?
B1.why: Ivo poliçe artışını olası bir neden olarak görüyor ama henüz kesin kanıt olmadığını da biliyor.

text: On Tuesday Ivo went to the town hall. In the basement there was a records room, and a tired clerk handed him the key. "Help yourself," she said. "Nobody comes down here. Nobody has for years, as far as I know."

Ivo looked for papers about the Redmill factory and found a grey box marked 1994. Inside lay letters, building plans and forms. One of them was headed: Fire Insurance Policy. The paper was thin and soft, and it smelled of cellars.
He read it slowly. In 1993 the factory had been insured for two hundred thousand pounds. Then he noticed a new date, February 1994, and a new figure: nine hundred thousand pounds.

Ivo counted on his fingers. The fire had happened only one month later, in March. At the bottom of the page, in thick black ink, was a signature: Alan Varley. A man does not usually quadruple the insurance on a factory with old machines, unless he believes the factory is worth more, or has begun to believe it is worth more burnt.

He took out his notebook. "The owner made the factory worth four times more," he wrote. "And one month later it burned down. I don't know whether this is a motive, but it is certainly an opportunity."
B2.proof: unless he believes the factory is worth more, or has begun to believe it is worth more burnt

o: That the factory had valuable burned materials.

That the fire improved the factory.

B2.why: Yüksek sigorta bedeli nedeniyle fabrikanın yanması sahibine daha çok para getirebilirdi; ifade bu olası kazancı anlatıyor.

text: On Tuesday Ivo went to the town hall. In the basement there was a records room, and a tired clerk handed him the key. "Help yourself," she said. "Nobody comes down here. Nobody has for years, as far as I know, and I have never been inclined to ask why."

Ivo looked for papers about the Redmill factory and found a grey box marked 1994. Inside lay letters, building plans and forms. One of them was headed: Fire Insurance Policy. The paper was thin and soft, and it smelled of cellars and old rain.
He read it slowly. In 1993 the factory had been insured for two hundred thousand pounds. Then he noticed a new date, February 1994, and a new figure: nine hundred thousand pounds.

Ivo counted on his fingers. The fire had happened only one month later, in March. At the bottom of the page, in thick black ink, was a signature: Alan Varley. A man does not usually quadruple the insurance on a factory full of ageing machines unless he believes the building is worth far more than it seems, or has begun to believe that it is worth more burnt than standing.

He took out his notebook. "The owner made the factory worth four times more," he wrote. "And one month later it burned down. I do not know whether this is a motive, but it is certainly an opportunity." He underlined the last word twice, and then, being an archivist, he wrote the box number beneath it so that nobody could ever claim he had invented the page.
C1.proof: so that nobody could ever claim he had invented the page
C1.q: Why does Ivo write the box number in his notebook?
o: To remember where he left his key.
To tell the clerk which box to return.
To make his discovery verifiable by others.
To hide the page from the town hall.

C1.why: Ivo kutu numarasını yazarak belgenin gerçekten orada olduğunu başkalarının da doğrulayabilmesini sağlıyor.

eps.title: Sarah Hale
eps.recap: Ivo, Tom Hale'in kızı Sarah'nın küçük dükkânına gitti. Sarah konuşmayı reddetti ama kapıyı kapatırken babasının hayatında hiç sigara içmediğini söyledi.

text: Tom Hale's daughter, Sarah, was now forty-two years old. She had a small shop in the old part of town. It sold bread and newspapers. On Wednesday morning, Ivo went there.
She was putting bread on a shelf when he came in. Ivo said his name. He said that he worked in the archive. He said that he wanted to talk about the fire.

Sarah stopped. She put down the bread very slowly. Her face became hard. "Please go," she said. "For thirty years, people have talked about my father. They said he was careless. They said he was a fool."
"I do not think he was a fool," said Ivo. "I think someone was not honest." Sarah looked at him. For a second, her eyes were soft. Then she turned away.
"I cannot help you," she said. At the door, she added quietly: "My father never smoked. Never. Not one cigarette in his whole life."
A2.q: Why is Sarah's last sentence important?
o: It contradicts the story that he caused the fire with a cigarette.
It proves that she owns a shop.
It shows that she likes Ivo.
It means that she cannot read.
A2.hint: Kasabada 'Tom depoda sigara içti' deniyordu; Sarah ne diyor?
A2.why: Kasaba yangını Tom'un depoda sigara içmesine bağlıyor; Sarah babasının hiç sigara içmediğini söylüyor. Bu, resmî açıklamayla çelişiyor.

text: Tom Hale's daughter, Sarah, was now forty-two. She ran a small shop in the old part of town that sold bread and newspapers, and on Wednesday morning Ivo walked in.
She was stacking loaves on a shelf. Ivo said his name, explained that he worked in the archive, and said that he wanted to talk about the fire.
Sarah stopped. She put down the bread very slowly, and her face hardened. "Please go. For thirty years people have talked about my father. Careless, they said. A fool."
"I don't think he was a fool," said Ivo. "I think somebody wasn't honest." Sarah looked at him, and for a second her eyes softened. Then she turned away.
"I can't help you," she said. At the door she added, so quietly that he almost missed it: "My father never smoked. Not once in his whole life. Ask yourself who said he did."
B1.proof: Ask yourself who said he did.
B1.q: What does Sarah's last sentence encourage Ivo to do?
o: To buy a newspaper from her shop.
To find out who started the story about the cigarette.
To ask her father directly.
To leave the town.

B1.why: Sarah, sigara hikâyesini kimin ortaya attığını araştırmasını öneriyor; çünkü babası hiç sigara içmemiş.

text: Tom Hale's daughter, Sarah, was now forty-two. She ran a small shop in the old part of town that sold bread and newspapers, and on Wednesday morning Ivo walked in, carrying nothing but his notebook and a speech he had rehearsed on the bus.
She was stacking loaves on a shelf. Ivo said his name, explained that he worked in the archive, and said that he wanted to talk about the fire. The speech, he noticed, had already abandoned him.

Sarah stopped. She put down the bread very slowly, and her face hardened. "Please go. For thirty years people have talked about my father. Careless, they said. A fool. My mother never recovered, and I left school at sixteen."
"I don't think he was a fool," said Ivo. "I think somebody wasn't honest." Sarah looked at him, and for a second her eyes softened. Then she turned away.

"I can't help you," she said. At the door she added, so quietly that he almost missed it: "My father never smoked. Not once in his whole life. Ask yourself who said he did, and why nobody ever asked me."

o: That she is angry with her mother.

That she wrote the newspaper article.

text: Tom Hale's daughter, Sarah, was now forty-two. She ran a small shop in the old part of town that sold bread and newspapers, and on Wednesday morning Ivo walked in, carrying nothing but his notebook and a speech he had rehearsed on the bus.

She was stacking loaves on a shelf. Ivo said his name, explained that he worked in the archive, and said that he wanted to talk about the fire. The speech, he noticed, had already abandoned him, as speeches tend to do when they meet a real face.

Sarah stopped. She put down the bread very slowly, and her face hardened. "Please go. For thirty years people have talked about my father. Careless, they said. A fool. My mother never recovered, and I left school at sixteen to work."

"I don't think he was a fool," said Ivo. "I think somebody wasn't honest." Sarah looked at him, and for a second her eyes softened. Then she turned away, as if kindness were something she could not afford.

"I can't help you," she said. At the door she added, so quietly that he almost missed it: "My father never smoked. Not once in his whole life. Ask yourself who said he did, and why nobody ever asked me." The door closed. Ivo stood on the pavement and understood that the most important sentence in the whole conversation had been spoken by someone who had said she could not help.
C1.proof: had been spoken by someone who had said she could not help

C1.hint: Yardım edemeyeceğini söyleyen kişi aslında ne yapmış?
C1.why: Sarah yardım edemeyeceğini söylerken en önemli bilgiyi vermiş: babasının hiç sigara içmediğini ve kimsenin ona hiç sormadığını.

eps.title: Mr. Reed's Office
eps.recap: Ivo, kasabanın yaşlı avukatı Mr. Reed'i ziyaret etti. Reed 1994 dosyalarının yıllar önce imha edildiğini söyledi, ama masasının arkasında üzerinde 'Hale 94' yazan bir kutu görünüyordu.

text: On Thursday afternoon, Ivo visited Mr. Reed, the oldest lawyer in Redmill. His office was above a bakery. It was dark and full of paper. Mr. Reed was a thin old man with white hair and a gentle voice.
"I am looking for the old files from 1994," said Ivo. "About the factory fire. About Tom Hale. Did you work on his case?"
Mr. Reed took off his glasses and cleaned them slowly. "I helped a little," he said. "But those files are gone. We destroyed all the old papers many years ago. It is the rule."
"I see," said Ivo. He looked around the office. There were boxes on every shelf. Behind Mr. Reed's chair, there was a small grey box with a white label.
The label said, in black letters: 'HALE 94'. Ivo said nothing. He smiled politely and thanked the lawyer for his time.
A2.proof: Behind Mr. Reed's chair, there was a small grey box
A2.q: Why is Mr. Reed's answer suspicious?
o: He does not remember Tom Hale.
He says the files were destroyed, but a box with the name is in his office.
He is too old to work.
His office is above a bakery.
A2.hint: Reed 'dosyalar yok' diyor ama Ivo ne görüyor?
A2.why: Reed 1994 dosyalarının imha edildiğini söylüyor ama arkasında 'HALE 94' yazan bir kutu duruyor; bu iki şey çelişiyor.

text: On Thursday afternoon Ivo visited Mr. Reed, the oldest lawyer in Redmill. His office was above a bakery, dark and crowded with paper, and Mr. Reed himself was a thin old man with white hair and a gentle voice that made every sentence sound like a kindness.

eps.title: The Alarms Were Off
eps.recap: Emekli işçi Dennis Pike, kasabadaki bir barda Ivo'ya yangın gecesi alarmların kapalı olduğunu söyledi. Alarmlar, komşuları uyandırıyor diye Ocak'tan beri her gece kapatılıyordu.

text: On Friday night, Mrs. Okafor took Ivo to the old pub, The Anchor. Many retired workers of the factory met there on Fridays. "They will talk to me," she said. "I wrote about them when they were young."

At a table in the corner sat a big man with white hair. His name was Dennis Pike. He worked at the factory for twenty years. When Mrs. Okafor asked about the fire, he looked into his beer for a long time.
"Everyone says it was Tom Hale," he said at last. "Tom was not stupid. He checked the machines every night. And you know what? That night, the alarms did not ring."
"Why not?" asked Ivo. "They were switched off," said Dennis. "At night. Every night, since January. The boss said the alarms woke the neighbours. He said it was a waste of money."
Mrs. Okafor stopped writing. "The alarms were switched off every night?" she asked. "Every night," said Dennis. "And I never told anyone. Nobody asked."
A2.q: What does Dennis's story tell us?
o: The workers liked the noise of the alarms.
The alarms were broken by Tom Hale.
The fire could burn without the alarms warning anyone.
The neighbours asked for more alarms.
A2.hint: Alarmlar yangın gecesi neden çalmadı?
A2.why: Alarmlar Ocak'tan beri her gece kapalıydı; yani yangın çıktığında kimseyi uyaracak bir sistem yoktu.
