eps.title: Order 4471
eps.recap: Ivo, alarm şirketinin eski kayıtlarında 3 Ocak 1994 tarihli 4471 numaralı iş emrini buldu: gece alarmını devre dışı bırakma talimatı Alan Varley tarafından imzalanmıştı.

text: On Saturday, Ivo found the name of the old alarm company: Bright Alarm Services. The company was still in business. Ivo telephoned them and asked for old papers. A friendly woman answered. "We keep everything," she said. "Come tomorrow."
On Sunday, in a small office, she brought him a thin folder. "This is the factory," she said. "Redmill. Work orders for 1994."
Ivo opened the folder. There were six papers. The fourth one was number 4471. It was dated the third of January 1994. The words at the top were: 'Night alarm: disconnect.'
At the bottom of the page, there was a signature he knew now very well. It was thick, black and proud: Alan Varley.
"He signed it himself," said Ivo. "Yes," said the woman. "That is unusual. Normally, the manager signs. The owner never does."
A2.q: What does the work order prove?
o: The alarm company turned off the alarm by mistake.
Tom Hale ordered the alarm to be repaired.
The factory was closed in January.
The factory owner personally ordered the night alarm to be turned off.
A2.hint: İş emrinin altındaki imza kime ait ve ne yapılmasını istiyor?
A2.why: İş emrinde gece alarmının kapatılması isteniyor ve imza Alan Varley'e ait; yani alarmı kapatma talimatını fabrika sahibi bizzat vermiş.

text: On Saturday Ivo found the name of the old alarm company: Bright Alarm Services. It was still in business, and when he telephoned, a friendly woman answered. "We keep everything," she said. "Come tomorrow."
On Sunday, in a small office, she brought him a thin folder. "This is your factory," she said. "Redmill. All the work orders for 1994."
Ivo opened it. There were six pages. The fourth was numbered 4471 and dated the third of January 1994. The words at the top read: 'Night alarm: disconnect.'
At the bottom was a signature he now knew very well, thick, black and proud: Alan Varley.

"He signed it himself," said Ivo. "Yes," said the woman. "Which is unusual. Normally the works manager signs for things like this. The owner never does." "Unless he wants to be sure it's done," Ivo said quietly.
B1.proof: Unless he wants to be sure it's done
B1.q: What does Ivo imply with his last remark?
o: That Varley personally wanted to make sure the alarm was disabled.
That Varley was too busy to sign papers.
That the woman made a mistake.
That the works manager was on holiday.
B1.hint: Sahibin normalde imzalamadığı bir kâğıdı imzalaması neyi gösterir?
B1.why: Genelde müdür imzalarmış, bu kez sahibi imzalamış; Ivo, Varley'in alarmın gerçekten kapatıldığından emin olmak istediğini ima ediyor.

text: On Saturday Ivo found the name of the old alarm company: Bright Alarm Services. It was still in business, and when he telephoned, a friendly woman answered. "We keep everything," she said. "Come tomorrow, and bring some identification."
On Sunday, in a small office, she brought him a thin folder. "This is your factory," she said. "Redmill. All the work orders for 1994."

Ivo opened it. There were six pages. The fourth was numbered 4471 and dated the third of January 1994. The words at the top read: 'Night alarm: disconnect.' Beneath them, in smaller print, someone had added: 'Customer accepts full responsibility.'
At the bottom was a signature he now knew very well, thick, black and proud: Alan Varley.

"He signed it himself," said Ivo. "Yes," said the woman. "Which is unusual. Normally the works manager signs for things like this. The owner never does." "Unless he wants to be sure it's done," Ivo said quietly. "And unless he wants the paper to say, in his own handwriting, that nobody else is to blame."
B2.proof: Customer accepts full responsibility
B2.q: Why is the sentence 'Customer accepts full responsibility' significant?
o: It proves that the alarm company was careless.
It shows that Varley, not Tom Hale, took responsibility for the disabled alarm.
It shows that the alarm cost a lot of money.
It means that the customer was a worker.
B2.hint: Sorumluluğu kabul eden 'müşteri' kim?
B2.why: Müşteri fabrikanın sahibi olan Varley; yani alarmın kapatılmasının sorumluluğu onda, Tom Hale'de değil.

text: On Saturday Ivo found the name of the old alarm company: Bright Alarm Services. It was still in business, and when he telephoned, a friendly woman answered. "We keep everything," she said. "Come tomorrow, and bring some identification."
On Sunday, in a small office, she brought him a thin folder. "This is your factory," she said. "Redmill. All the work orders for 1994."

Ivo opened it. There were six pages. The fourth was numbered 4471 and dated the third of January 1994. The words at the top read: 'Night alarm: disconnect.' Beneath them, in smaller print, someone had added: 'Customer accepts full responsibility.'
At the bottom was a signature he now knew very well, thick, black and proud: Alan Varley.

"He signed it himself," said Ivo. "Yes," said the woman. "Which is unusual. Normally the works manager signs for things like this. The owner never does." "Unless he wants to be sure it's done," Ivo said quietly. "And unless he wants the paper to say, in his own handwriting, that nobody else is to blame." Ivo photographed the page three times, once for himself, once for Mrs. Okafor, and once for the person he did not yet know he would need to show it to. A fire without alarms was no longer a story about one careless man, but about a decision, taken in January, by someone who had known exactly what he was switching off.
C1.proof: someone who had known exactly what he was switching off
C1.q: How does the final sentence change the nature of the story?
o: It proves that the fire was an accident.
It suggests that the alarm company is responsible.
It turns the fire from a worker's mistake into the result of an owner's deliberate decision.
It shows that Ivo wants to leave the archive.
C1.hint: 'Bir kişinin ihmali' ile 'bir kararın sonucu' arasındaki fark ne?
C1.why: Alarmı kapatan karar Ocak'ta ve bilinçli olarak alınmış; yangın artık tek bir işçinin ihmali değil, sahibin kararının sonucu gibi görünüyor.

eps.title: The Candidate
eps.recap: Ivo, arşivin girişinde 'Redmill için Varley' yazan bir seçim afişi gördü. Alan Varley artık belediye meclisi başkan adayıydı ve geçmişin açığa çıkması onun için büyük bir tehlikeydi.

text: On Monday morning, Ivo walked to the archive. He was very tired. He had not slept well for three nights. He was thinking about the alarm paper in his pocket.

At the front door of the library, someone had put a new poster. It was big and bright. A man with silver hair was smiling at him. He wore a blue suit and a warm smile. Under the picture were three words: 'VARLEY FOR REDMILL.'
Ivo stopped. He read the small letters at the bottom of the poster. 'Alan Varley, candidate for the Chairman of the Town Council. Vote on Friday. A man you can trust.'
Ivo looked at the smiling face. He thought of the signature on the alarm paper. He thought of Tom Hale, who died without a name.
"Friday," he said to himself. "The election is on Friday. In four days."
A2.q: Why does the poster worry Ivo?
o: The man who may have planned the fire wants to become a powerful leader.
The poster is ugly and too big.
The election is next year.
The library does not allow posters.
A2.hint: Afişteki adam kim ve neye aday?
A2.why: Afişteki Alan Varley, olası olarak yangını planlayan kişi ve şimdi belediye meclisi başkanı adayı; Ivo bu yüzden endişeleniyor.

text: On Monday morning Ivo walked to the archive. He was exhausted; he hadn't slept properly for three nights, and the photograph of the alarm order seemed to weigh a great deal in his pocket.

On the front door of the library someone had stuck a new poster, big and bright. A man with silver hair and a blue suit smiled out of it with great warmth. Under the picture were three words: VARLEY FOR REDMILL.
Ivo stopped. He read the small print at the bottom. 'Alan Varley, candidate for Chairman of the Town Council. Polling day: Friday. A man you can trust.'
He looked at the smiling face, and then he thought of the thick black signature on the alarm order. He thought of Tom Hale, who had died with a ruined name.
"Friday," he said to himself. "In four days, the man who switched off the alarms could become the most important person in this town."
B1.proof: A man you can trust.
B1.q: Why is the slogan on the poster ironic?
o: Because the poster is in a library.
Because the man may have hidden the truth and blamed another person.
Because the slogan is badly written.
Because Ivo does not like blue suits.
B1.hint: 'Güvenebileceğiniz biri' sloganı Ivo'nun bildikleriyle nasıl çelişiyor?
B1.why: Ivo Varley'in alarmı kapattığını ve suçu bir işçiye yıktığını düşünüyor; bu yüzden 'güvenilir adam' sloganı ironik.

text: On Monday morning Ivo walked to the archive. He was exhausted; he hadn't slept properly for three nights, and the photograph of the alarm order seemed to weigh a great deal in his pocket.

On the front door of the library someone had stuck a new poster, big and bright. A man with silver hair and a blue suit smiled out of it with great warmth. Under the picture were three words: VARLEY FOR REDMILL.

Ivo stopped. He read the small print at the bottom. 'Alan Varley, candidate for Chairman of the Town Council. Polling day: Friday. A man you can trust.' There were identical posters on the lamp posts all the way down the street.
He looked at the smiling face, and then he thought of the thick black signature on the alarm order. He thought of Tom Hale, who had died with a ruined name.

"Friday," he said to himself. "In four days, the man who switched off the alarms could become the most important person in this town." He understood now why Mr. Pell had been so quick to ask for the letter. A man about to be elected does not want his past found. He wants it filed.
B2.proof: A man about to be elected does not want his past found. He wants it filed.
B2.q: What does 'He wants it filed' mean in this context?
o: He wants his past published in a newspaper.
He wants to organise the papers himself.
He wants his past kept hidden in the archive where nobody reads it.
He wants to give the archive a gift.
B2.hint: Bir şeyi 'dosyalamak' o şeyin akıbeti hakkında ne söyler?
B2.why: 'Filed' burada arşivde, kimsenin okumayacağı bir yerde saklanmış anlamında; Varley geçmişinin ortaya çıkmasını değil, gömülmesini istiyor.

text: On Monday morning Ivo walked to the archive. He was exhausted; he hadn't slept properly for three nights, and the photograph of the alarm order seemed to weigh a great deal in his pocket.

On the front door of the library someone had stuck a new poster, big and bright. A man with silver hair and a blue suit smiled out of it with great warmth. Under the picture were three words: VARLEY FOR REDMILL.

Ivo stopped. He read the small print at the bottom. 'Alan Varley, candidate for Chairman of the Town Council. Polling day: Friday. A man you can trust.' There were identical posters on the lamp posts all the way down the street, and on the windows of the bakery, and, he noticed with a small cold shock, on the door of Mr. Reed's office.
He looked at the smiling face, and then he thought of the thick black signature on the alarm order. He thought of Tom Hale, who had died with a ruined name.

"Friday," he said to himself. "In four days, the man who switched off the alarms could become the most important person in this town." He understood now why Mr. Pell had been so quick to ask for the letter, and why Mr. Reed's grey box had been so carefully guarded. A man about to be elected does not want his past found. He wants it filed, and he has friends with keys to the drawers.
C1.proof: he has friends with keys to the drawers
C1.q: What does the final sentence suggest about Varley?
o: That he is a locksmith by profession.
That he is afraid of drawers.
That he has lost the keys to his office.
That he has influential allies who help him keep documents hidden.
C1.hint: 'Çekmecelerin anahtarına sahip arkadaşlar' kimleri ima ediyor?
C1.why: Pell ve Reed gibi kişiler belgeleri saklamak için Varley'e yardım ediyor gibi görünüyor; Ivo onun nüfuzlu müttefikleri olduğunu düşünüyor.

eps.title: Three Pages Missing
eps.recap: Ivo, Redmill yangın dosyasını yeniden açtı ve içinden üç belgenin eksik olduğunu fark etti: itfaiye raporu, alarm kaydı ve bir tanık ifadesi. Dosyanın kapağındaki liste belgelerin bir zamanlar orada olduğunu gösteriyordu.

text: On Monday, Ivo went down to the archive basement. It was cold and quiet. He took the grey box with the label: 'Redmill Fire, 1994'. He put it on the table and opened it.
Inside, there was a thick folder. On the front of the folder, there was a list. It was typed on an old typewriter. The list said that the folder had eleven documents.
Ivo counted the papers one by one. One, two, three... eight. Only eight. He counted again. Eight.
He looked at the list. Three lines had a small pencil mark next to them. They were: 'Fire Brigade Report', 'Alarm Record' and 'Witness Statement, night guard'.
Ivo stood up slowly. "Someone took them," he said to the empty room. "Someone took the three most important papers."
A2.q: What is the problem with the folder?
o: It has too many papers.
It should have eleven documents, but three important ones are missing.
It is in the wrong box.
The list is new.
A2.hint: Klasörde kaç belge olması gerekiyordu ve kaç tane var?
A2.why: Listeye göre on bir belge olmalıydı ama yalnızca sekiz var; üç önemli belge eksik.

text: On Monday Ivo went down to the archive basement, a cold, quiet place smelling of old paper. He lifted down the grey box labelled 'Redmill Fire, 1994', set it on the table and opened it.
Inside was a thick folder with a typed list pinned to its cover. The list had been produced on an old typewriter, and it said the folder contained eleven documents.
Ivo counted the papers one by one. One, two, three... eight. Only eight. He counted again, more slowly, with the same result.
He studied the list. Three of the lines had a small pencil mark beside them: 'Fire Brigade Report', 'Alarm Record' and 'Witness Statement, night guard'.

Ivo straightened up. "Somebody took them," he said to the empty room. "Somebody removed the three most important papers in the whole file." He did not touch anything else, and he wrote down the date and the time.
B1.proof: Somebody removed the three most important papers in the whole file.
B1.q: Why are the missing documents significant?
o: They are the oldest papers.
They are in a foreign language.
They are exactly the papers that could explain how the fire started.
They are the pages with the pictures.
B1.hint: Eksik üç belgenin türü neden önemli?
B1.why: İtfaiye raporu, alarm kaydı ve tanık ifadesi, yangının nasıl çıktığını açıklayabilecek en önemli belgelerdi.

text: On Monday Ivo went down to the archive basement, a cold, quiet place that smelled of old paper and dust. He lifted down the grey box labelled 'Redmill Fire, 1994', set it on the table and opened it.

Inside was a thick folder with a typed list pinned to its cover. The list had been produced on an old typewriter, and it said the folder contained eleven documents. Somebody, thirty years ago, had been careful enough to count them.
Ivo counted the papers one by one. One, two, three... eight. Only eight. He counted again, more slowly, with the same result.
He studied the list. Three of the lines had a small pencil mark beside them, as if a later hand had ticked them off: 'Fire Brigade Report', 'Alarm Record' and 'Witness Statement, night guard'.

Ivo straightened up. "Somebody took them," he said to the empty room. "Somebody removed the three most important papers in the whole file, and tried to make it look as if they had never been there." But the typist's list, he realised, was an honest witness: it had not been altered.
B2.proof: the typist's list, he realised, was an honest witness
B2.q: What does Ivo realise about the typed list?
o: That it was written by the thief.
That it contains false information.
That it is the only paper left.
That it proves the documents existed, even though they are gone.
B2.hint: Daktilo ile yazılmış bu liste neyi ispatlıyor?
B2.why: Liste, belgelerin bir zamanlar dosyada olduğunu kanıtlıyor; yani silinen izler tamamen yok edilememiş.

text: On Monday Ivo went down to the archive basement, a cold, quiet place that smelled of old paper and dust. He lifted down the grey box labelled 'Redmill Fire, 1994', set it on the table and opened it.

Inside was a thick folder with a typed list pinned to its cover. The list had been produced on an old typewriter, and it said the folder contained eleven documents. Somebody, thirty years ago, had been careful enough to count them, and had probably never imagined that anybody would ever need to.
Ivo counted the papers one by one. One, two, three... eight. Only eight. He counted again, more slowly, with the same result.
He studied the list. Three of the lines had a small pencil mark beside them, as if a later hand had ticked them off: 'Fire Brigade Report', 'Alarm Record' and 'Witness Statement, night guard'.

Ivo straightened up. "Somebody took them," he said to the empty room. "Somebody removed the three most important papers in the whole file, and tried to make it look as if they had never been there." But the typist's list, he realised, was an honest witness: it had not been altered, and it was the one piece of evidence that its author had never thought to destroy, because he had never thought of it as evidence at all.
C1.proof: it was the one piece of evidence that its author had never thought to destroy
C1.q: Why does the list survive when the documents do not?
o: Because the person who removed the papers did not consider the list to be important evidence.
Because the list was hidden in a safe.
Because the list was written in code.
Because Ivo made it himself.
C1.hint: Liste neden hâlâ yerinde duruyor?
C1.why: Belgeleri alan kişi, listeyi bir delil olarak görmediği için ona dokunmamış.

eps.title: The Delivery Slips
eps.recap: Ivo, arşivin teslim defterinde eksik üç belgenin 1994 sonbaharında çıkarıldığını gösteren fişleri buldu. Fişler, belgeleri 'A. V. adına' Mr. Pell'in aldığını gösteriyordu.

text: Every archive has a second book. It is the book of delivery slips. When someone takes a paper from the archive, he must sign a small slip. The slips are kept in a drawer for fifty years.
Ivo opened the old drawer. It was full of yellow papers. He searched for 1994. He searched for October. His fingers stopped on three slips with the same date: 24 October 1994.
On each slip there was a number, the name of a document, and a signature. The signature was the same on all three: 'R. Pell'.
Under the signature, there were two small letters in a different pen: 'for A.V.'
Ivo looked at the letters for a long time. A.V. He knew only one man in Redmill with these letters. And that man was now standing for mayor.
A2.q: Who is A.V.?
o: Ivo's old teacher.
The night guard of the archive.
Alan Varley, the factory owner who is now standing for mayor.
A famous writer.
A2.hint: 'A.V.' harfleri kimin adını ima ediyor?
A2.why: A.V., fabrika sahibi ve şimdi belediye başkanı adayı olan Alan Varley'i ima ediyor.

text: Every archive keeps a second book: the book of delivery slips. Whenever somebody takes a paper out, he must sign a small slip, and the slips are kept in a drawer for fifty years.
Ivo opened the old drawer, which was crammed with yellow papers. He searched for 1994, then for October. His fingers stopped on three slips with the same date: 24 October 1994.
Each slip carried a number, the name of a document, and a signature. The signature was identical on all three: 'R. Pell'.
Beneath the signature, in a different pen, someone had added two small words: 'for A.V.'

Ivo stared at the letters. A.V. He knew only one man in Redmill with those initials, and that man was now campaigning to become mayor. He took a pencil and wrote down the numbers of the slips, one by one, and put the notebook in his pocket.
B1.proof: campaigning to become mayor
B1.q: What does Ivo conclude from the slips?
o: That Mr. Pell stole them for himself.
That the papers were lost by mistake.
That Varley wrote the slips.
That Mr. Pell took the papers on behalf of Alan Varley.
B1.hint: Fişlerdeki imza ve 'for A.V.' notu birlikte neyi gösteriyor?
B1.why: Pell belgeleri Alan Varley adına almış; yani Varley belgelerin kaybolmasında rol oynamış.

text: Every archive keeps a second book: the book of delivery slips. Whenever somebody takes a paper out, he must sign a small slip, and the slips are kept in a drawer for fifty years, a rule that nobody ever questions because nobody ever reads them.
Ivo opened the old drawer, which was crammed with yellow papers. He searched for 1994, then for October. His fingers stopped on three slips with the same date: 24 October 1994.
Each slip carried a number, the name of a document, and a signature. The signature was identical on all three: 'R. Pell'.
Beneath the signature, in a different pen, someone had added two small words: 'for A.V.'

Ivo stared at the letters. A.V. He knew only one man in Redmill with those initials, and that man was now campaigning to become mayor. It struck him as a curious thing, that a person so careful to remove the papers had not been careful enough to remove the slips. He copied the numbers of the slips into his notebook, one by one, and put the notebook carefully in his inside pocket.
B2.proof: had not been careful enough to remove the slips
B2.q: What irony does Ivo notice?
o: That the thief removed the main papers but forgot the records of the removal.
That the slips were new.
That nobody signed them.
That the drawer was locked.
B2.hint: Ivo hangi çelişkiyi fark ediyor?
B2.why: Belgeleri alan kişi asıl kâğıtları temizlemiş ama kimin aldığını gösteren teslim fişlerini unutmuş.

text: Every archive keeps a second book: the book of delivery slips. Whenever somebody takes a paper out, he must sign a small slip, and the slips are kept in a drawer for fifty years, a rule that nobody ever questions because nobody ever reads them.
Ivo opened the old drawer, which was crammed with yellow papers. He searched for 1994, then for October. His fingers stopped on three slips with the same date: 24 October 1994.
Each slip carried a number, the name of a document, and a signature. The signature was identical on all three: 'R. Pell'.
Beneath the signature, in a different pen, someone had added two small words: 'for A.V.'

Ivo stared at the letters. A.V. He knew only one man in Redmill with those initials, and that man was now campaigning to become mayor. It struck him as a curious thing, that a person so careful to remove the papers had not been careful enough to remove the slips. Perhaps he had simply never imagined that a bureaucratic drawer, full of forgotten forms, could ever testify against him. Bureaucracy, Ivo thought, is the memory that nobody bothers to corrupt. He photographed all three slips with his phone before he left the basement.
C1.proof: Bureaucracy, Ivo thought, is the memory that nobody bothers to corrupt.
C1.q: What does Ivo mean by his final remark?
o: That bureaucracy is always corrupt.
That routine paperwork often preserves the truth because no one thinks it matters.
That memory is unreliable.
That archives should be destroyed.
C1.hint: 'Bürokrasi, kimsenin bozmaya zahmet etmediği hafızadır' ne anlama gelir?
C1.why: Sıradan evrak kimse önem vermediği için çoğu zaman gerçeği korur; bu yüzden fişler hâlâ duruyor.

eps.title: Leave It Alone
eps.recap: Ivo'yu gece yarısı isimsiz bir telefon aradı. Ses kısıktı ve 'Bu işi bırak, yoksa işini kaybedersin' dedi. Ivo arşivdeki fişlerin fotokopisini yanına almıştı.

text: At midnight, Ivo's phone rang. He was in bed. The number on the screen was hidden. He answered. "Hello?"
Nobody spoke for a moment. Then a low voice said, "Leave it alone."
"Who is this?" asked Ivo. His heart started to beat faster.
"You are a young man with a good job," said the voice. "You work in a quiet place with old papers. It is a nice life. Do not make it difficult. Stop looking at the fire of 1994."
The line went dead. Ivo sat in the dark for a long time. Then he got up and put the photocopies of the slips under his mattress.
A2.q: What is the purpose of the call?
o: Someone wants to offer Ivo a new job.
Someone wants to say hello.
Someone is selling a phone.
Someone wants to frighten Ivo so that he stops his research.
A2.hint: Gizemli telefon görüşmesinin asıl amacı nedir?
A2.why: Biri Ivo'yu korkutup 1994 yangını hakkındaki araştırmayı bırakmasını istiyor.

text: At midnight Ivo's phone rang. He was in bed, and the number on the screen was hidden. He answered. "Hello?"
For a moment nobody spoke. Then a low voice said, "Leave it alone."
"Who is this?" asked Ivo, his heart beating faster.
"You're a young man with a good job," said the voice. "You work somewhere quiet, among old papers. It's a pleasant life. Don't make it difficult. Stop looking at the fire of 1994."

The line went dead. Ivo sat in the dark for a long time. Then he got up and slid the photocopies of the delivery slips under his mattress. He could not sleep any more. He lay there for hours and listened to every sound in the house, and every car that passed in the street made him look at the window. At six o'clock he finally made coffee and decided that he would tell Mrs. Okafor in the morning.
B1.proof: You work somewhere quiet, among old papers.
B1.q: What does the caller's description of Ivo's life imply?
o: That the caller knows where Ivo works and could threaten his job.
That the caller admires old papers.
That the caller wants to be Ivo's friend.
That the caller is a teacher.
B1.hint: Arayanın Ivo'nun işini bilmesi neyi gösteriyor?
B1.why: Arayan Ivo'nun nerede çalıştığını biliyor ve işini tehdit edebileceğini ima ediyor.

text: At midnight Ivo's phone rang. He was in bed, and the number on the screen was hidden. He answered. "Hello?"
For a moment nobody spoke. Then a low voice said, "Leave it alone."
"Who is this?" asked Ivo, his heart beating faster.

"You're a young man with a good job," said the voice. "You work somewhere quiet, among old papers. It's a pleasant life, and it would be a shame if it became less pleasant. Stop looking at the fire of 1994."

The line went dead. Ivo sat in the dark for a long time. The voice had not shouted, and it had not made a single open threat; it had simply described his life back to him, gently, as one describes a house to a person who is about to lose it. He got up and slid the photocopies of the delivery slips under his mattress. He could not sleep any more, and at six o'clock he made coffee and decided to tell Mrs. Okafor everything in the morning. The cold from the floor came up through his feet, and he did not move for a very long time.
B2.proof: it had simply described his life back to him, gently
B2.q: How is the threat delivered?
o: By shouting angry words.
Politely and indirectly, by describing what Ivo could lose.
By a written letter.
By a physical attack.
B2.hint: Bu tehdit hangi biçimde ve nasıl yapılıyor?
B2.why: Arayan bağırmadan, nazik bir tonla Ivo'nun kaybedebileceği şeyleri sayarak dolaylı bir tehdit yapıyor.

"You're a young man with a good job," said the voice. "You work somewhere quiet, among old papers. It's a pleasant life, and it would be a shame if it became less pleasant. Stop looking at the fire of 1994."

The line went dead. Ivo sat in the dark for a long time. The voice had not shouted, and it had not made a single open threat; it had simply described his life back to him, gently, as one describes a house to a person who is about to lose it. He got up and slid the photocopies of the delivery slips under his mattress. What frightened him most was not the threat but the timing: he had told no one about the slips except the old journalist, and he had made the copies only that afternoon. At six o'clock he made coffee and decided to tell Mrs. Okafor everything, because he suspected that he would need a witness.
C1.proof: he had told no one about the slips except the old journalist
C1.q: What disturbs Ivo most about the call?
o: That the caller was rude.
That the call was too long.
That it came very soon after he found the slips, so someone must be watching him.
That the phone was old.
C1.hint: Ivo'yu en çok korkutan şey nedir burada?
C1.why: Aramanın fişleri bulduktan hemen sonra gelmesi; biri onu izliyor ya da bilgi sızıyor olmalı.

eps.title: Three Witnesses, Three Stories
eps.recap: Mrs. Okafor eski gazete notlarını açtı. 1994'te yangını gören üç kişiyle konuşmuştu ve üçünün anlattıkları birbiriyle uyuşmuyordu; bu da gerçeğin değiştirildiğini gösteriyordu.

text: On Tuesday, Mrs. Okafor made tea for Ivo in her small kitchen. On the table, she put a brown box full of notebooks. "My notes from 1994," she said. "I never threw anything away."
She opened one notebook. "I talked to three people about the fire," she said. "The night guard, a neighbour and a young fireman."

She read the first note. "The guard says: the fire started on the ground floor, near the machines." She read the second. "The neighbour says: the fire started on the roof. I saw red light up there." She read the third. "The fireman says: the fire started in the storeroom at the back."
Ivo looked at her. "Three people. Three different places."
"Exactly," said Mrs. Okafor. "One fire cannot start in three places. Somebody was not telling the truth. Or somebody told them what to say."
A2.proof: One fire cannot start in three places.
A2.q: What is the problem with the three stories?
o: They are different, so at least one person was lying or was told what to say.
They are exactly the same.
They are about three different fires.
They are written in different languages.
A2.hint: Üç tanığın anlattığı yerlerin farklı olması ne gösterir?
A2.why: Tek bir yangın üç ayrı yerde başlayamaz; birileri yalan söylemiş ya da onlara ne diyecekleri söylenmiş olabilir.

text: On Tuesday Mrs. Okafor made tea for Ivo in her small kitchen and put a brown box full of notebooks on the table. "My notes from 1994," she said. "I never throw anything away."

Ivo looked at her. "Three people, three different places."
"Exactly," said Mrs. Okafor. "A fire cannot start in three places at once. Either someone was mistaken, or someone had been told what to say." Ivo wrote the three names in his own notebook.

B1.q: What does Mrs. Okafor suspect?
o: That the fire started three times.
That the witnesses were influenced before they spoke to her.
That she wrote the notes wrongly.
That the witnesses were children.
B1.hint: Mrs. Okafor üç farklı ifadenin nedenini ne olarak düşünüyor?
B1.why: Tanıkların kendilerine ne söyleyeceği önceden söylenmiş olabileceğinden şüpheleniyor.

eps.title: My Father Found Something
eps.recap: Sarah Hale sonunda Ivo ile konuşmayı kabul etti. Babasının yangından önceki hafta tuhaf davrandığını ve 'bir şey buldum, Varley bilmek zorunda' dediğini anlattı.

text: Sarah Hale had a small bakery in the main street. The smell of warm bread filled the shop. When Ivo came in, she was putting loaves on a shelf. She did not look at him.
"Mrs. Okafor sent me," said Ivo. "I want to ask about your father."
"I do not talk about my father," said Sarah. "The whole town says he burned the factory. I was a child. I heard the words every day at school."

Ivo waited. After a minute, Sarah put the bread down. Her voice was very quiet. "There is one thing," she said. "The week before the fire, my father came home late every night. He was nervous. One evening he said to my mother: I found something. Varley must know. He will have to listen to me."
She looked at Ivo for the first time. "My father never smoked. Never. Not even once in his life."
A2.q: What did Tom Hale say before the fire?
o: That he wanted to burn the factory.
That he had found something and that Mr. Varley must know about it.
That he would leave the town.
That he was going on holiday.
A2.hint: Tom Hale yangından önce ne söylemiş?
A2.why: Bir şey bulduğunu ve Varley'in bunu bilmesi gerektiğini söylemiş.

B2.why: Soruşturmanın aileyi dinlemediğini, yani dikkatsiz ya da kasıtlı olarak tek yönlü yürütüldüğünü düşündürüyor.

eps.title: The Kitchen Table
eps.recap: Sarah, babasının mutfak masasının hâlâ evde durduğunu ve çekmecesinde yazılmamış gibi görünen bir mektup taslağı bulunduğunu söyledi. Ivo taslağın ilk satırını okuyunca dondu.

text: That evening, Sarah took Ivo to her mother's house. It was an old house at the end of a quiet street. In the kitchen, there was a wooden table with a small drawer.
"My mother never moved this table," said Sarah. "She never opened the drawer. She said it was too painful."
Sarah pulled out the drawer. It was stiff. Inside, there were pencils, a ruler and a yellow paper, folded twice. She gave it to Ivo.
Ivo opened it carefully. It was a letter, but it was not finished. The handwriting was big and round. Many words were crossed out.

He read the first line. Then he read it again. 'Dear Mr. Varley, I am writing to tell you that I have seen the insurance papers.' Ivo knew the handwriting. It was the same as the secret letter in the archive.
A2.proof: I have seen the insurance papers.
A2.q: What does the draft show?
o: That Tom Hale wrote a love letter.
That Sarah wrote the letter.
That Tom Hale knew about the insurance papers and wanted to speak to Varley.
That the letter is about bread.
A2.hint: Taslak mektubun ilk satırı neyi gösteriyor?
A2.why: Tom Hale'in sigorta belgelerini gördüğünü ve Varley'e yazmak istediğini; el yazısı arşivdeki gizli mektupla aynı.

That the handwriting belongs to the mother.

text: That evening Sarah took Ivo to her mother's house, an old house at the end of a quiet street. In the kitchen stood a wooden table with one small drawer.

He read the first line, and then read it again. 'Dear Mr. Varley, I am writing to tell you that I have seen the insurance papers.' Ivo knew that handwriting. eps.title: The Whole Draft
eps.recap: Ivo ve Mrs. Okafor taslağın tamamını okudu. Mektubun yazarı Tom Hale'di ve Varley'e sigorta belgelerindeki rakamları gördüğünü, yangından endişe ettiğini yazmıştı. Arşivdeki mektup bu taslağın temiz kopyasıydı.

text: On Saturday morning, Ivo and Mrs. Okafor sat in her kitchen. Ivo put the yellow draft on the table next to the unsigned letter from the archive. They read both papers, line by line.
The letter from the archive was clean and neat. The draft was messy. But the sentences were almost the same.

Mrs. Okafor put her finger on a line. "The draft says: 'I saw the new insurance papers in the office. The number is very big. I am afraid something will happen to the factory.' And the neat letter says the same thing, only shorter."
"So the neat letter is the second version," said Ivo. "Tom Hale copied it from the draft. He cleaned it. He wanted to send it."
"Yes," said Mrs. Okafor slowly. "And the signature at the bottom was not forgotten. Somebody erased it later. Somebody who did not want us to know who wrote it."
A2.q: What do the two letters show?
o: Mrs. Okafor wrote both letters.
The letters are about bread.
The draft is a different story.
Tom Hale wrote the archive letter, and someone erased his name afterward.
A2.hint: İki mektup birlikte neyi gösteriyor?
A2.why: Arşivdeki mektubu Tom Hale yazmış ve biri imzayı sonradan silmiş.

text: On Saturday morning Ivo and Mrs. Okafor sat in her kitchen. Ivo laid the yellow draft on the table beside the unsigned letter from the archive, and they read both papers line by line.

B1.q: Why would someone erase the signature?
o: To hide that the warning came from Tom Hale before the fire.
To make the letter prettier.
To save ink.
Because the signature was too long.

B1.why: Uyarının yangından önce Tom Hale'den geldiğini gizlemek için silinmiş olabilir.

text: On Saturday morning Ivo and Mrs. Okafor sat in her kitchen. Ivo laid the yellow draft on the table beside the unsigned letter from the archive, and they read both papers line by line, as two doctors read the same x-ray.

B2.proof: a warning written by the man later blamed for the fire is a warning that should never be read

eps.title: A Man Who Wanted to Warn
eps.recap: Sarah, annesinin eski bir takvimini buldu. Yangından önceki günün sayfasında Tom'un el yazısıyla 'Varley ile görüşme, 9:00' yazıyordu. Hale, mektubu yangın gecesinden bir gün önce Varley'e vermeyi planlamıştı.

text: On Sunday, Sarah came to Mrs. Okafor's house. She was holding an old calendar with pictures of flowers. The year on it was 1994.
"My mother kept this calendar in a box," she said. "I never looked inside. Today I looked."
She opened it at March. There was a small square for each day. Most of them were empty. But on the thirteenth, there was a note in pencil. The handwriting was big and round. Sarah read it aloud.
"'Varley. Nine o'clock. Give him the letter.'"

Nobody in the kitchen moved. The thirteenth of March was the day before the fire. Tom Hale had planned to give the letter to Varley himself, the very next morning. And in the middle of that night, the factory burned.
A2.q: Why is the calendar note important?
o: It shows that Tom planned to warn Varley the day before the fire.
It shows that Tom planned a holiday.
It shows that Tom was late.
It shows that Sarah likes flowers.
A2.hint: Takvimdeki bu not neyi gösteriyor bize?
A2.why: Tom'un yangından önceki gün mektubu Varley'e vermeyi planladığını gösteriyor.

text: On Sunday Sarah came to Mrs. Okafor's house holding an old calendar decorated with flowers. The year printed on it was 1994.
"My mother kept this in a box," she said. "I never looked inside it. Today I did."

"'Varley. Nine o'clock. Give him the letter.'"

Nobody in the kitchen moved. The thirteenth of March was the day before the fire. Tom Hale had intended to hand the letter to Varley himself the next morning, and in the middle of that night the factory burned. Mrs. Okafor made tea, and nobody drank it. They sat there for a long time, and outside the window the afternoon light slowly turned gold.
B1.proof: The thirteenth of March was the day before the fire.
B1.q: What does the timing suggest?
o: That the fire happened a year later.
That the fire happened just before Tom could deliver his warning.
That Tom was on holiday.
That the fire was an accident.

B1.why: Yangın, Tom uyarısını iletmeden hemen önce çıkmış; bu bir tesadüf olmayabilir.

B2.hint: Ivo 'tesadüf' kelimesine neden şüpheyle yaklaşıyor?
B2.why: Varley'in sigortası, anahtarları ve nedeni vardı; bu kadar elverişli bir tesadüf inandırıcı değil.

text: On Sunday Sarah came to Mrs. Okafor's house holding an old calendar decorated with flowers. The year printed on it was 1994.
"My mother kept this in a box," she said. "I never looked inside it. Today I did."
She opened it at March. Each day had a small square, and most of them were empty. But on the thirteenth there was a note in pencil, in big round handwriting. Sarah read it aloud.
"'Varley. Nine o'clock. Give him the letter.'"

Nobody in the kitchen moved. The thirteenth of March was the day before the fire. Tom Hale had intended to hand the letter to Varley himself the next morning, and in the middle of that night the factory burned. It would be reasonable, Ivo thought, to call this a coincidence, if the same man had not also owned the insurance policy, the keys and the motive. Sarah closed the calendar very gently, as one closes a door on a sleeping child. "He wasn't a criminal," she said. "He was an honest man who went to warn his boss. And for that, they took his name." Nobody touched the tea that Mrs. Okafor had made. The tea went cold on the table, and the flowers on the calendar looked suddenly very bright.
C1.proof: He was an honest man who went to warn his boss.
C1.q: What is the main point of Sarah's final statement?
o: That her father was a criminal.
That her father was the boss.
That her father enjoyed warnings.
That her father was honest and was wrongly punished for trying to do the right thing.
C1.hint: Sarah babasının hikâyesini nasıl özetliyor?
C1.why: Babası dürüst biriydi ve doğru olanı yapmaya çalıştığı için haksız yere cezalandırıldı.

eps.title: A Letter from the Lawyer
eps.recap: Pazartesi sabahı Ivo'nun masasında resmî bir mektup vardı. Varley'in avukatı, arşivdeki 'yetkisiz araştırma' nedeniyle Ivo'nun yangın dosyasına erişimini yasaklıyordu. Arşiv müdürü kapıda bekliyordu.

text: On Monday morning, Ivo came to work and found a white envelope on his desk. It was thick and expensive. In the corner, there was the name of a law firm.
He opened it. The letter was two pages long. The words were cold and polite. 'Unauthorised research.' 'Misuse of public records.' 'Immediate action.'
At the end, one sentence was in bold: 'Mr. Marsh is not allowed to touch the 1994 fire file.'
Ivo looked up. The director of the archive was standing in the doorway. He was a thin man with a grey face. He did not look into Ivo's eyes.
"I am sorry, Ivo," he said. "I have to take the key to the basement. And your computer. Please go home."
A2.q: What does the lawyer's letter try to do?
o: Offer Ivo a promotion.
Stop Ivo from investigating by using legal pressure.
Invite Ivo to dinner.
Thank Ivo for his work.
A2.hint: Avukatın mektubu ne yapmaya çalışıyor?
A2.why: Ivo'yu hukuki baskıyla araştırmasını durdurmaya zorluyor.

text: On Monday morning Ivo arrived at work and found a white envelope on his desk. It was thick and expensive-looking, with the name of a law firm in the corner.

Ivo looked up. The director of the archive stood in the doorway, a thin man with a grey face, avoiding his eyes.

"I'm sorry, Ivo," he said. "I have to take the key to the basement, and your computer. Please go home." He picked up his coat and his bag and walked out of the building past the empty desks, and nobody looked up. On the street, the rain had started. He stood there for a minute and then took out his phone to call Mrs. Okafor.
B1.proof: I have to take the key to the basement
B1.q: What does the director's behaviour show?
o: That he is happy to fire Ivo.
That he wrote the letter.
That he is under pressure and is uncomfortable carrying out the order.
That he is a lawyer.

B1.why: Baskı altında ve emri uygulamaktan rahatsız; gözlerinin içine bakmaması bunu gösteriyor.

text: On Monday morning Ivo arrived at work and found a white envelope on his desk. It was thick and expensive-looking, with the name of a law firm embossed in the corner.

o: The letter has the client's name.

He recognises the pattern of pressure from the same person who wants the fire file closed.

B2.why: Yangın dosyasının kapatılmasını isteyen kişiyle aynı baskı örüntüsünü tanıyor; Varley olduğunu tahmin ediyor.

text: On Monday morning Ivo arrived at work and found a white envelope on his desk. It was thick and expensive-looking, with the name of a law firm embossed in the corner.
He opened it. The letter was two pages long, written in cold and polite language. 'Unauthorised research.' 'Misuse of public records.' 'Immediate action.'

He looked up. The director of the archive stood in the doorway, a thin man with a grey face, avoiding his eyes.

"I'm sorry, Ivo," he said. "I have to take the key to the basement, and your computer. Please go home." Ivo noticed that the threat had arrived exactly three days after he found the slips, and that it was precisely as well-organised as a man with a great deal to lose would make it. He took out his phone and called Mrs. Okafor.

That Varley is generous.

C1.why: Yanlış bir hikâye için avukat tutulmaz; bu hareket hikâyenin doğru ve Varley için tehlikeli olduğunu gösteriyor.

eps.title: Mr. Reed's Conscience
eps.recap: Ivo işsiz kaldığı akşam Mr. Reed kapısını çaldı. Yaşlı avukat otuz yıldır sakladığı bir dosyayı getirmişti: yangın soruşturmasında kapatılan üç tanık ifadesinin kopyaları ve bir mahkeme yazışması.

text: On Monday evening, someone knocked on Ivo's door. He opened it. An old man in a brown coat was standing in the rain. He held a heavy bag in both hands. It was Mr. Reed, the lawyer.
"May I come in?" he asked. His voice was weak. "I have not slept well for thirty years. Tonight, I want to sleep."
Mr. Reed sat at Ivo's table. He put the bag on it. Inside, there was a dusty grey file with the words 'Hale Defence, 1994'.

"I was Tom Hale's lawyer," he said. "The court gave me his case. I read three statements. All three said that the alarms were turned off by Mr. Varley's order. I put them in my file. But then Mr. Varley's people came to me. They said: be quiet, and your career will be fine."
He looked at his old hands. "I was afraid. I was a coward. I never used the statements in court."
A2.q: What does Mr. Reed confess?
o: He stole money from Tom Hale.
He lost the file.
He knew of evidence that could have helped Tom Hale but stayed silent.
He wrote the three statements.
A2.hint: Mr. Reed ne itiraf ediyor?
A2.why: Tom Hale'e yardım edebilecek kanıtları bildiği halde korkudan susmuş.

text: On Monday evening somebody knocked on Ivo's door. An old man in a brown coat stood in the rain holding a heavy bag in both hands. It was Mr. Reed, the lawyer.
"May I come in?" he asked in a weak voice. "I haven't slept properly for thirty years. Tonight I would like to."
Mr. Reed sat at Ivo's table and laid the bag in front of him. Inside was a dusty grey file marked 'Hale Defence, 1994'.

"I was Tom Hale's lawyer," he said. "I read three witness statements, all saying the alarms had been switched off on Mr. Varley's orders. I put them in my file. Then Varley's people came to see me. They said: stay quiet, and your career will be perfectly safe."
He looked at his old hands. "I was afraid. I was a coward. I never used those statements in court."
B1.proof: stay quiet, and your career will be perfectly safe
B1.q: Why did Mr. Reed not use the statements?
o: Because he forgot them.
Because they were in French.
Because the judge refused.
Because Varley's people threatened or bribed him to stay silent.
B1.hint: Mr. Reed ifadeleri neden mahkemede kullanmadı?
B1.why: Varley'in adamları ona sessiz kalırsa kariyerinin güvende olacağını söyleyerek baskı yapmış.

text: On Monday evening somebody knocked on Ivo's door. An old man in a brown coat stood in the rain holding a heavy bag in both hands. It was Mr. Reed, the lawyer, looking ten years older than the last time Ivo had seen him.
"May I come in?" he asked in a weak voice. "I haven't slept properly for thirty years. Tonight I would like to."
Mr. Reed sat at Ivo's table and laid the bag in front of him. Inside was a dusty grey file marked 'Hale Defence, 1994'.

"I was Tom Hale's lawyer," he said. "I read three witness statements, all saying the alarms had been switched off on Mr. Varley's orders. I put them in my file. Then Varley's people came to see me. They said: stay quiet, and your career will be perfectly safe."

He looked at his old hands. "I was afraid. I was a coward. I never used those statements in court. A defence lawyer who hides his best evidence is no longer a defence lawyer, Mr. Marsh. He is merely an expensive witness to an injustice."
B2.proof: an expensive witness to an injustice
B2.q: How does Mr. Reed judge his own behaviour?
o: As a failure of professional duty that allowed an injustice.
As a heroic act.
As a normal job.
As a perfect defence.
B2.hint: Mr. Reed kendi davranışını nasıl değerlendiriyor?
B2.why: Mesleki görevini yerine getirmediğini ve bir haksızlığın sessiz tanığı olduğunu kabul ediyor.

He looked at his old hands. "I was afraid. I was a coward. I never used those statements in court. A defence lawyer who hides his best evidence is no longer a defence lawyer, Mr. Marsh. eps.title: To the Newspaper
eps.recap: Salı sabahı Ivo ve Mrs. Okafor, Reed'in dosyasını, mektubu, taslağı ve teslim fişlerinin kopyalarını 'Redmill Herald' gazetesine götürdü. Genç bir muhabir olan Priya her şeyi dikkatle okudu.

text: On Tuesday morning, Ivo and Mrs. Okafor walked to the building of the local newspaper, the Redmill Herald. Ivo carried the grey file. Mrs. Okafor carried the old calendar in a plastic bag.
At the front desk, a young woman looked up. She had short black hair and a pen behind her ear. Her name card said: 'Priya Nair, Reporter'.

"Can I help you?" she asked. "I hope so," said Mrs. Okafor, and her voice was very strong. "I used to work for this newspaper. I wrote the story about the Redmill fire in 1994. Now I think it was wrong."
Priya took them to a small meeting room. They put everything on the table: the file, the letters, the calendar, the slips.
Priya read for two hours without saying a word. When she finished, she was pale. "This is not a small story," she said.
A2.proof: This is not a small story
A2.q: What does Priya think of the evidence?
o: She thinks it is boring.
She thinks it is a joke.
She thinks it is old news.
She thinks it is very important and serious.
A2.hint: Priya kanıtlar hakkında ne düşünüyor?
A2.why: Çok önemli ve ciddi bir haber olduğunu düşünüyor.

text: On Tuesday morning Ivo and Mrs. Okafor walked to the offices of the local newspaper, the Redmill Herald. Ivo carried the grey file, and Mrs. Okafor carried the old calendar in a plastic bag.
At the front desk a young woman with short black hair and a pen behind her ear looked up. Her name card read: 'Priya Nair, Reporter'.

"Can I help you?" she asked. "I hope so," said Mrs. Okafor, her voice very firm. "I used to work for this paper. I wrote the original story about the Redmill fire in 1994. I now believe it was wrong."
Priya led them to a small meeting room, where they laid everything out: the file, the letters, the calendar, the delivery slips.
Priya read for two hours without a word. When she had finished she was pale. "This is not a small story," she said.
B1.proof: I now believe it was wrong.
B1.q: What courage does Mrs. Okafor show?
o: She admits that her own earlier reporting may have been mistaken.
She blames Priya.
She leaves the room.
She refuses to talk.
B1.hint: Mrs. Okafor nasıl bir cesaret gösteriyor?
B1.why: Kendi eski haberinin yanlış olabileceğini açıkça kabul ediyor.

text: On Tuesday morning Ivo and Mrs. Okafor walked to the offices of the local newspaper, the Redmill Herald. Ivo carried the grey file, and Mrs. Okafor carried the old calendar in a plastic bag, as carefully as if it were a sleeping bird.
At the front desk a young woman with short black hair and a pen behind her ear looked up. Her name card read: 'Priya Nair, Reporter'.

"Can I help you?" she asked. "I hope so," said Mrs. Okafor, her voice very firm. "I used to work for this paper. I wrote the original story about the Redmill fire in 1994. I now believe it was wrong, and I would like to correct it, thirty years late."
Priya led them to a small meeting room, where they laid everything out: the file, the letters, the calendar, the delivery slips.
Priya read for two hours without a word. When she had finished she was pale. "This is not a small story," she said. It was a quiet moment, and she did not say anything else.
B2.proof: I would like to correct it, thirty years late.
B2.q: What does Mrs. Okafor want?
o: To get her job back.
To publicly correct an old error, even after a very long time.
To become famous.
To forget the story.
B2.hint: Mrs. Okafor gazeteden tam olarak ne istiyor?
B2.why: Uzun zaman geçmiş olsa da eski hatasını kamuoyu önünde düzeltmek istiyor.

text: On Tuesday morning Ivo and Mrs. Okafor walked to the offices of the local newspaper, the Redmill Herald. Ivo carried the grey file, and Mrs. Okafor carried the old calendar in a plastic bag, as carefully as if it were a sleeping bird.
At the front desk a young woman with short black hair and a pen behind her ear looked up. Her name card read: 'Priya Nair, Reporter'.

"Can I help you?" she asked. "I hope so," said Mrs. Okafor, her voice very firm. "I used to work for this paper. I wrote the original story about the Redmill fire in 1994. I now believe it was wrong, and I would like to correct it, thirty years late."

Priya led them to a small meeting room, where they laid everything out: the file, the letters, the calendar, the delivery slips. The pile looked modest on the table, a few yellowing papers and a book of flowers, and it was difficult to believe that it could shake a town.

Priya read for two hours without a word. When she had finished she was pale. "This is not a small story," she said. "It's the kind of story that a newspaper exists to tell. And it's also the kind that a newspaper in a small town is tempted to forget."
C1.proof: the kind that a newspaper in a small town is tempted to forget
C1.q: What worry does Priya express?
o: That the story is too small.
That the newspaper is too big.
That a small-town paper may avoid publishing a story that threatens powerful people.
That nobody reads newspapers.
C1.hint: Priya hangi endişeyi dile getiriyor?
C1.why: Küçük bir kasaba gazetesinin, güçlü kişileri rahatsız edecek bir haberi yayımlamaktan çekinebileceğinden endişe ediyor.

eps.title: The Advertiser
eps.recap: Priya haberi yazıp editör Mr. Collins'e götürdü. Editör yüzünü buruşturdu: 'Varley bu gazetenin en büyük reklam verenidir. Bu haberi yayımlarsak yarın kapanırız.'

text: On Wednesday morning, Priya finished the article. It was three pages long. The title was strong: 'The Letter That Was Never Read: Redmill, 1994'.
She walked to the editor's office. Mr. Collins was a big man with a red face and a loud voice. He read her article standing up. At first he said nothing. His face became redder and redder.
"Priya," he said at last. "Sit down. I want to tell you something about this newspaper."

He pointed to a large poster on the wall. The poster said: 'Varley Industries. Proud Sponsor of Redmill.' "Mr. Varley pays for forty per cent of our advertising," said Mr. Collins. "If I print this, he will take his money away. We will close in three months."
Priya held the article against her chest. "Then maybe," she said, "it is time to find out what this newspaper is for."
A2.proof: Mr. Varley pays for forty per cent of our advertising
A2.q: What is the problem for the editor?
o: Varley supplies much of the newspaper's income, so publishing could ruin it.
Varley is the editor's brother.
The article is badly written.
The poster is ugly.
A2.hint: Editör haberi yayımlamaktan neden çekiniyor?
A2.why: Varley gazetenin reklam gelirinin büyük kısmını sağlıyor; haber yayımlanırsa gazete kapanabilir.

text: On Wednesday morning Priya finished the article. It ran to three pages, under a strong title: 'The Letter That Was Never Read: Redmill, 1994'.
She walked into the editor's office. Mr. Collins, a big man with a red face and a loud voice, read the article standing up. At first he said nothing, but his face grew redder and redder.
"Priya," he said at last. "Sit down. I want to tell you something about this newspaper."

He pointed to a large poster on the wall: 'Varley Industries. Proud Sponsor of Redmill.' "Mr. Varley pays for forty per cent of our advertising," said Mr. Collins. "If I print this, he'll withdraw his money and we'll be closed within three months."
Priya held the article against her chest. "Then perhaps," she said, "it's time we found out what this newspaper is for."
B1.proof: it's time we found out what this newspaper is for
B1.q: What is Priya suggesting?
o: That the newspaper should sell flowers.
That a newspaper's purpose is to tell the truth, even at a cost.
That the editor should resign for no reason.
That the poster should be bigger.
B1.hint: Priya 'bu gazete ne için var' derken neyi kastediyor?
B1.why: Bir gazetenin amacı, bedeli ne olursa olsun gerçeği anlatmaktır.

text: On Wednesday morning Priya finished the article. It ran to three pages, under a strong title: 'The Letter That Was Never Read: Redmill, 1994'.
She walked into the editor's office. Mr. Collins, a big man with a red face and a loud voice, read the article standing up. At first he said nothing, but his face grew redder and redder.

"If I print this, he'll withdraw his money and we'll be closed within three months. Twenty-two people work here. Do you want to explain to them that their jobs were the price of your principles?"

Priya held the article against her chest. "Then perhaps," she said, "it's time we found out what this newspaper is for." Mr. Collins said nothing. Mr. Collins said nothing for a while, and Priya heard the clock ticking loudly on the wall behind his desk.

B2.q: What dilemma is described here?
o: Between buying and selling flowers.

Between publishing the truth and protecting the newspaper's staff and income.
Between two editors.
B2.hint: Bu sahnede hangi ikilem anlatılıyor yazar tarafından?
B2.why: Gerçeği yayımlamak ile gazetenin gelirini ve çalışanlarını korumak arasında bir ikilem var.

text: On Wednesday morning Priya finished the article. It ran to three pages, under a strong title: 'The Letter That Was Never Read: Redmill, 1994'.
She walked into the editor's office. Mr. Collins, a big man with a red face and a loud voice, read the article standing up. At first he said nothing, but his face grew redder and redder.
"Priya," he said at last. "Sit down. I want to tell you something about this newspaper."

He pointed to a large poster on the wall: 'Varley Industries. Proud Sponsor of Redmill.' "Mr. Varley pays for forty per cent of our advertising," said Mr. Collins. "If I print this, he'll withdraw his money and we'll be closed within three months. Twenty-two people work here. Do you want to explain to them that their jobs were the price of your principles?"

Priya held the article against her chest. "Then perhaps," she said, "it's time we found out what this newspaper is for." Mr. Collins did not answer. He looked at the poster for a long time, and then, strangely, at the empty desk by the window that had once been Mrs. Okafor's. It occurred to Priya that the editor had not once said the story was false. He had only said it was expensive, and that, in her experience, was how the truth is usually refused.
C1.proof: He had only said it was expensive
C1.q: What does Priya notice about the editor's argument?
o: That he proved the story false.

C1.why: Editör haberin yanlış olduğunu söylemiyor, yalnızca maliyetinden çekiniyor; yani haber doğru.

eps.title: Printed at Midnight
eps.recap: Mr. Collins gece boyunca düşündü ama cesaret edemedi. Priya, haberi kendi adıyla ve belgelerin taranmış kopyalarıyla bağımsız bir haber sitesine gönderdi. Sabaha kadar on bin kişi okudu; sabah Collins gazetenin ön sayfasını değiştirdi.

text: On Wednesday night, Priya did not go home. She sat in the empty newsroom with the grey file and her laptop. Mr. Collins had gone home. He had said: 'I need to think.' She knew what that meant.

At eleven, she made a decision. She scanned every document: the letter, the draft, the slips, Mr. Reed's statements. She wrote one clear article, with her own name at the top. She sent it to an independent news website that was not afraid of anybody.
At midnight, the article appeared on the internet. It had a simple title: 'Redmill 1994: The Evidence They Hid'.
By two in the morning, one thousand people had read it. By six, ten thousand. People in the town sent it to their friends. Telephones began to ring in the newsroom.
At seven, Mr. Collins walked in. He looked at Priya. He looked at the telephones. Then he said, in a tired voice: "Change the front page."
A2.q: What did Mr. Collins decide at the end?
o: To fire Priya.
To publish the story in his own newspaper after the public reaction.
To close the newspaper.
To delete the article.
A2.hint: Mr. Collins sonunda ne karar verdi?
A2.why: Halkın tepkisini görünce haberi kendi gazetesinde de yayımlamaya karar verdi.

text: On Wednesday night Priya did not go home. She sat in the empty newsroom with the grey file and her laptop. Mr. Collins had left, saying only, 'I need to think.' She knew exactly what that meant.

At eleven she made her decision. She scanned every document: the letter, the draft, the slips, Mr. Reed's statements. She wrote a clear article with her own name at the top and sent it to an independent news website that was not afraid of anybody.
At midnight it went online under a plain title: 'Redmill 1994: The Evidence They Hid'.
By two in the morning a thousand people had read it. By six, ten thousand. Townspeople forwarded it to their friends, and the telephones in the newsroom began to ring.
At seven Mr. Collins walked in. He looked at Priya, and then at the ringing telephones. "Change the front page," he said in a tired voice.

B1.q: What made Mr. Collins change his mind?
o: A threat from Varley.
A holiday.
The huge public interest after the article was published elsewhere.
A new poster.
B1.hint: Mr. Collins'in fikrini değiştiren şey ne?
B1.why: Haber başka bir yerde yayımlanınca ortaya çıkan büyük halk ilgisi.

text: On Wednesday night Priya did not go home. She sat in the empty newsroom with the grey file and her laptop. Mr. Collins had left, saying only, 'I need to think.' She knew exactly what that meant, having heard the same sentence from three previous editors.

At eleven she made her decision. She scanned every document: the letter, the draft, the slips, Mr. Reed's statements. She wrote a clear article with her own name at the top and sent it to an independent news website that was not afraid of anybody.
At midnight it went online under a plain title: 'Redmill 1994: The Evidence They Hid'.
By two in the morning a thousand people had read it. By six, ten thousand. Townspeople forwarded it to their friends, and the telephones in the newsroom began to ring.

At seven Mr. Collins walked in. He looked at Priya, and then at the ringing telephones. "Change the front page," he said in a tired voice. It was not courage that had moved him, she thought, but something more useful: the discovery that silence had stopped being safe.
B2.proof: the discovery that silence had stopped being safe
B2.q: What does the narrator say actually moved Mr. Collins?
o: Pure bravery.

text: On Wednesday night Priya did not go home. She sat in the empty newsroom with the grey file and her laptop. Mr. Collins had left, saying only, 'I need to think.' She knew exactly what that meant, having heard the same sentence from three previous editors.

At eleven she made her decision. She scanned every document: the letter, the draft, the slips, Mr. Reed's statements. She wrote a clear article with her own name at the top and sent it to an independent news website that was not afraid of anybody.
At midnight it went online under a plain title: 'Redmill 1994: The Evidence They Hid'.
By two in the morning a thousand people had read it. By six, ten thousand. Townspeople forwarded it to their friends, and the telephones in the newsroom began to ring.

At seven Mr. Collins walked in. He looked at Priya, and then at the ringing telephones. "Change the front page," he said in a tired voice. It was not courage that had moved him, she thought, but something more useful: the discovery that silence had stopped being safe. Priya did not say that she had acted without permission, and Mr. Collins did not mention it. Some agreements in newspapers are made entirely without words, and those are usually the ones that last.
C1.proof: Some agreements in newspapers are made entirely without words
C1.q: What does the final remark suggest about Priya and Collins?
o: That they reached a silent understanding that the unauthorised act was justified.
That they argued loudly.
That Priya was punished.
That Collins resigned.
C1.hint: Priya ile Collins arasında nasıl bir anlaşma var?
C1.why: İzinsiz yayının doğru olduğu konusunda sözsüz bir anlayışa varmışlar.

eps.title: The Council Acts
eps.recap: Haber yayımlandıktan iki gün sonra belediye meclisi olağanüstü toplandı. Meclis, 1994 yangınını bağımsız bir komisyona soruşturturken Varley'in adaylığı hakkında karar vermeyi ertelemeyi reddetti.

text: On Friday evening, the Redmill town hall was full. There were more than three hundred people in the big room. Some stood in the corridor. There were cameras at the back.

The chairwoman of the council hit the table with a small hammer. "Order, please," she said. "We have a serious matter to discuss. Yesterday's articles in the Herald raise questions about the Redmill fire of 1994."

She looked at the papers in front of her. "The council will start an independent investigation. A commission of three outside experts will read all the documents. And the council will not wait for the commission to decide about Mr. Varley's candidacy. We will discuss it on Monday."
The room made a loud noise. Some people clapped. Some people shouted. In the third row, Sarah Hale held Mrs. Okafor's hand.
Ivo stood at the back, next to the wall. For the first time in a week, he could breathe.
A2.q: What did the council decide?
o: To close the case.
To burn the documents.
To start an independent investigation and discuss Varley's candidacy.
To give Varley a prize.
A2.hint: Kasaba meclisi toplantıda ne karar verdi?
A2.why: Bağımsız bir soruşturma başlatmaya ve Varley'in adaylığını görüşmeye.

eps.title: Withdrawal
eps.recap: Pazartesi sabahı Alan Varley, 'ailevi nedenlerle' belediye başkanlığı adaylığından çekildiğini açıkladı. Kısa açıklamasında yangın, mektup ya da sigortadan hiç söz etmedi. Redmill'de bunu herkes bir itiraf gibi okudu.

text: On Monday morning, a short message appeared on the front page of the Redmill Herald. It was a statement from Mr. Alan Varley. It was printed in a small black box.
'Due to family reasons,' it said, 'I have decided to withdraw from the election for mayor. I thank all who supported me. I ask for privacy in this difficult time.'
Mrs. Okafor read it at her kitchen table with a cup of tea. She read it twice. Then she put the newspaper down and looked at Ivo, who was sitting opposite her.

"Do you notice what is missing?" she asked. "Not one word about the fire. Not one word about the letter or the insurance. A man who is innocent defends himself. A man who is not, hides in the word 'family'."
Ivo smiled. "In Redmill," he said, "everybody will read it like a confession."
A2.proof: Not one word about the fire.
A2.q: Why does Mrs. Okafor find the statement suspicious?
o: It is too long.
It is written in red.
It is about food.
It does not defend Varley or mention the accusations at all.
A2.hint: Mrs. Okafor açıklamayı neden şüpheli buluyor?
A2.why: Açıklama suçlamalardan hiç söz etmiyor ve Varley kendini savunmuyor.

text: On Monday morning a short statement appeared on the front page of the Redmill Herald, printed in a small black box. It came from Mr. Alan Varley.

That all statements are true.

eps.title: The Court Decides
eps.recap: Üç ay sonra bağımsız komisyonun raporu çıktı ve yüksek mahkeme, 1994 mahkûmiyetini kaldırdı. Mahkeme, Tom Hale'in 'hiçbir suçu olmadığını' ve yangının sigorta amacıyla kasten çıkarıldığına dair güçlü kanıtlar bulunduğunu açıkladı.

text: Three months later, the commission finished its work. Its report was four hundred pages long. On a cold Tuesday, the High Court opened a special hearing about the case of Tom Hale.
Sarah sat on the first bench. She wore her mother's black coat. Next to her, in a wheelchair, sat her old mother. She was eighty-one years old and she held a small handkerchief.

The judge was a tall woman with white hair. She read the decision slowly, in a calm voice. "The 1994 conviction of Thomas Hale is cancelled. The court finds that he committed no crime. The court also finds strong evidence that the fire was started deliberately for an insurance claim."
There was a moment of complete silence. Then Sarah's mother whispered, "Thirty years." Sarah put her arm around her.
"Mr. Hale's name," said the judge, "is cleared."
A2.proof: The court finds that he committed no crime
A2.q: What did the court decide?
o: Tom Hale was innocent, and the fire was probably set for insurance money.
Tom Hale was guilty.
The case was closed with no decision.
Sarah was arrested.
A2.hint: Yüksek mahkeme Tom Hale hakkında ne karar verdi?
A2.why: Tom Hale'in suçsuz olduğuna ve yangının büyük olasılıkla sigorta için çıkarıldığına.

text: Three months later the commission finished its work. Its report ran to four hundred pages. On a cold Tuesday the High Court opened a special hearing on the case of Tom Hale.

o: That she is thirty years old.

That she dislikes the judge.

B1.hint: Annenin 'otuz yıl' sözü neyi anlatıyor?

eps.title: The Letter at the Grave
eps.recap: Mahkeme kararından sonraki pazar Sarah, babasının mezarına gitti. Yanında arşivdeki mektubun resmî kopyası vardı. Mektubu yüksek sesle okudu ve mezarın yanına küçük bir taş kutuya koydu.

text: On Sunday morning, the sky was blue, and the wind was light. Sarah walked alone into the old cemetery at the top of the hill. In her hand there was a white envelope.
She stopped in front of a grey stone. On the stone, there were three words: 'Thomas Hale, 1951–1994'. The grass around it was short and neat. Her mother came here every week.
Sarah knelt. She opened the envelope. Inside was a copy of the letter from the archive, now stamped by the court: 'Official copy. Evidence in the case of Thomas Hale.'
She began to read aloud. Her voice was soft. "Dear Mr. Varley, I am writing to tell you that I have seen the insurance papers..." She read the whole letter, to the last line.
Then she folded it and put it into a small stone box near the grave. "Dad," she said. "They read it. They read it at last."
A2.q: Why does Sarah read the letter at the grave?
o: To forget him.
To share with her father that his warning was finally heard.
To lose the letter.
To practise reading.
A2.hint: Sarah mektubu neden mezarın başında okuyor?
A2.why: Babasına uyarısının sonunda duyulduğunu ve haklı çıktığını bildirmek için.

eps.title: Corrected
eps.recap: Redmill arşivinde, 1994 yangın dosyasının kutusuna yeni bir etiket yapıştırıldı: 'Düzeltildi' (Corrected). Ivo işine geri döndü ve etiketi kendi eliyle yerleştirdi. Mektup artık dosyanın ilk sayfasıydı.

text: Six months later, Ivo came back to work in the archive. The same cold basement. The same smell of old paper. But now, a new director sat in the office upstairs: a young woman who loved books.

On his desk, there was the grey box labelled 'Redmill Fire, 1994'. He opened it. Inside, the folder was thick. It had many more documents now. On top lay the letter from Tom Hale, in a clear plastic cover.
Next to the box, there was a small white label. A printer had made it that morning. Ivo took it in his fingers. It had one word, in big black letters: 'CORRECTED'.
He peeled off the paper behind it. He pressed the label firmly on the front of the grey box, over the old date. He smoothed it with his thumb.
Then he took a step back and looked at it. It was a very small label. But he knew that it would be there for fifty years.
A2.proof: It had one word, in big black letters: 'CORRECTED'.
A2.q: What is the purpose of the new label?
o: To decorate the box.
To hide the box.
To record that the archive's story of the fire has been corrected.
To mark the box as lost.
A2.hint: Arşivdeki yeni etiketin asıl amacı nedir?
A2.why: Arşivdeki yangın hikâyesinin düzeltildiğini kayda geçirmek.
