B2.why: 1994'te olduğu gibi belgelerin gizlice kaldırılmasına karşı.

text: Six months later Ivo returned to work in the archive: the same cold basement, the same smell of old paper. But upstairs there was a new director, a young woman who loved books and who had personally signed a rule that no document in the building could be removed without two signatures.

On his desk stood the grey box labelled 'Redmill Fire, 1994'. He opened it. The folder inside was thick, with many more documents than before, and on top lay Tom Hale's letter in a clear plastic cover.
Beside the box was a small white label, printed that morning. Ivo picked it up. It carried a single word in large black letters: 'CORRECTED'.
He peeled off the backing and pressed the label firmly on the front of the grey box, over the old date, smoothing it with his thumb.

Then he stepped back and looked at it. It was a very small label. But it would be there for fifty years. Archives, he thought, are often described as the memory of a society, but a memory is only worth having if it can be corrected: a record that cannot admit its own errors is not a memory but a monument. He switched off the basement light and, for the first time in his career, left the door open behind him.
C1.proof: a record that cannot admit its own errors is not a memory but a monument
C1.q: What is the main idea of Ivo's reflection?
o: That monuments are better than archives.
That an archive is valuable only if it is able to correct its mistakes.
That archives should be closed.
That errors are never found.
C1.hint: Ivo'nun düşüncesindeki ana fikir nedir?
C1.why: Bir arşivin, hatalarını düzeltebildiği ölçüde değerli olduğu.

title: The Missing Manuscript
hero: Doktora öğrencisi Noah Kaya, büyük bir konferanstan iki gün önce danışmanının makalesinin silindiğini fark ediyor ve suçluyu aramaya başlıyor.
intro: Üniversite laboratuvarında sabah. Konferansa iki gün var ve Prof. Alder'in yıllardır çalıştığı makale dosyası bilgisayardan kayboluyor. Doktora öğrencisi Noah Kaya, kayıt dosyalarını, yedekleri ve hakem yazışmalarını inceleyerek gerçeği arıyor. Akademik İngilizcenin kullanıldığı bu hikâyede YDS/YDT tarzı metinlere alışacaksın.
outro: Noah ve arkadaşları makalenin gerçek sahibini ortaya çıkardı ve çalıntı veriyi geri aldı. Otuz gün boyunca akademik İngilizceyle okudun, çıkarım yaptın ve bir gizemi çözdün. Başka bir tefrikaya geçmeye hazırsın.

eps.title: Empty Folder
eps.recap: Konferansa iki gün kala Prof. Alder'in makale dosyası bilgisayardan kayboldu. Noah klasörü boş buldu; dosyanın gece 3.12'de silindiğini gösteren bir kayıt gördü.

text: Noah Kaya arrived at the laboratory at seven in the morning. The corridor was empty. He wanted to finish his work before the others came.

Professor Alder was already in her office. Her face was white. "Noah, come here. My manuscript is gone." The manuscript was the paper about her new research. In two days, she was going to present it at a big conference.
Noah looked at her computer. He opened the folder called 'Conference'. It was empty. He checked the trash. It was empty too.
"Look at this," he said. He clicked on the folder's properties. The screen said: 'Last changed: 3.12 a.m.'
"Three in the morning?" said Professor Alder. "Nobody is in the lab at that time." Noah looked at the door. The lock was not broken.
A2.q: What does the time on the screen suggest?
o: The computer made a mistake while it was updating.
Someone deleted the file in the middle of the night, when the lab was empty.
Professor Alder deleted the file before she went to sleep.
Noah deleted the file by accident in the morning.
A2.hint: Dosyanın değiştirildiği saat ve laboratuvarın o saatteki durumu ne anlatıyor?
A2.why: Klasör gece 3.12'de değiştirilmiş; o saatte laboratuvarda kimse olmaması gerekiyor. Demek ki biri dosyayı gece, sessizce silmiş.

text: Noah Kaya arrived at the laboratory at seven in the morning. The corridors were empty, and he hoped to finish his work before the others came.

Professor Alder was already in her office, and her face was pale. "Noah, come here. My manuscript has disappeared." The manuscript was the paper about her new research, three years of work. In two days she was due to present it at the biggest conference of her career.
Noah sat at her computer. He opened the folder named 'Conference' and found it empty. He checked the trash, and that was empty too.
"Look at this," he said. He right-clicked the folder and read the properties aloud: "Last modified, 3.12 a.m."
"Three in the morning?" said Professor Alder. "There's nobody in the laboratory at that time." Noah looked at the office door. The lock was intact, and there was no sign that anyone had forced it.
B1.proof: Last modified, 3.12 a.m.
B1.q: What can we infer from the intact lock and the 3.12 a.m. time?
o: A thief broke in during the night and left no traces.
The file was deleted by the computer's own error.
Whoever deleted the file probably had legitimate access to the building.
Professor Alder forgot to lock her office.
B1.hint: Kilidin kırılmamış olması içeri nasıl girildiğine dair ne düşündürür?
B1.why: Kilit sağlam ve saat gece 3.12; silen kişinin binaya yasal bir erişimi (anahtar ya da şifre) olması muhtemel.

text: Noah Kaya arrived at the laboratory at seven in the morning. The corridors were deserted, and he hoped to finish his analysis before the others came in.

Professor Alder was already in her office, and her face was pale. "Noah, come here. My manuscript has disappeared." The manuscript was the paper on her new research, the result of three years of work. In two days she was due to present it at the most important conference of her career.
Noah sat at her computer. He opened the folder named 'Conference' and found it empty. He checked the recycle bin, and that was empty too.
"Look at this," he said. He right-clicked the folder and read the properties aloud: "Last modified, 3.12 a.m."

"Three in the morning?" said Professor Alder. "There's no one in the laboratory at that hour." Noah looked at the office door. The lock was intact, and there was no sign of forced entry. Either the file had been deleted by someone with a key, or by someone who had never needed to be in the room at all.
B2.proof: no sign of forced entry
B2.q: What does the last sentence suggest about how the file may have been deleted?
o: It must have been deleted by Noah himself.
It was deleted by the cleaning staff.
It disappeared because of a power cut.
It could have been done remotely, without entering the room.
B2.hint: 'Odada olması gerekmeyen biri' ifadesi dosyanın nasıl silinmiş olabileceğini anlatıyor.
B2.why: Zorla giriş izi yok; Noah'ya göre dosyayı ya anahtarı olan biri ya da hiç odaya girmesi gerekmeyen biri (uzaktan) silmiş olabilir.

text: Noah Kaya arrived at the laboratory at seven in the morning. The corridors were deserted, and he hoped to finish his statistical analysis before the rest of the group came in.

Professor Alder was already in her office, and her face was drained of colour. "Noah, come here. My manuscript has disappeared." The manuscript was the paper on her new research, the culmination of three years of work. In two days she was due to present it at the most important conference of her career, and the department had been talking about little else for a month.
Noah sat at her computer. He opened the folder named 'Conference' and found it empty. He checked the recycle bin, and that was empty too. Nothing had been misplaced; it had been removed.
"Look at this," he said. He right-clicked the folder and read the properties aloud: "Last modified, 3.12 a.m."

"Three in the morning?" said Professor Alder. "There's no one in the laboratory at that hour." Noah looked at the office door. The lock was intact, and there was no sign of forced entry. Either the file had been deleted by someone with a key, or by someone who had never needed to be in the room at all, and he was not sure which possibility disturbed him more.
C1.proof: or by someone who had never needed to be in the room at all
C1.q: Why is Noah disturbed by the two possibilities he considers?
o: Both suggest the deletion was deliberate and carried out by a person with access.
Both prove that the computer was infected by a virus.
Both mean that Professor Alder will not attend the conference.
Both show that the laboratory should be closed at night.
C1.hint: Anahtarı olan kişi ile uzaktan erişen kişi arasındaki ortak noktayı bul.
C1.why: İki ihtimalde de silme işlemi bilinçli ve erişimi olan biri tarafından yapılmış; Noah'ı rahatsız eden de bu ortak sonuç.

eps.title: No Backup
eps.recap: Noah yedekleri kontrol etti ama laboratuvarın otomatik yedek sunucusunda da klasör boştu. Her iki dosyanın aynı gece silinmiş olması, bunun bir kaza olmadığını gösteriyordu.

text: "Don't worry," said Noah. "There is a backup." Every night, the lab computers copy their files to a big server in the university's main building.
He opened the server on his own laptop. He found Professor Alder's folder. It was there! But when he opened it, the same thing happened. It was empty.
Noah looked at the date. It was the same: 3.12 a.m. The same minute, the same night.
"Two places," he said slowly. "Your computer and the server. Both were cleaned in the same minute."
Professor Alder sat down. "A computer can break," she said. "A server can break. But not both, in the same minute." Noah nodded. "That is not an accident."
A2.proof: Both were cleaned in the same minute
A2.q: Why does Noah decide that it was not an accident?
o: The server is too old to work properly.
The professor forgot to make a backup.
Two different places were emptied at exactly the same time.
The files were too big for the computer.
A2.hint: Hem bilgisayarın hem sunucunun aynı dakikada boşaltılması neyi gösterir?
A2.why: İki ayrı yer aynı dakikada boşaltılmış. İki cihazın aynı anda bozulması çok olası değil, bu yüzden Noah kazadan şüpheleniyor.

text: "Don't panic," said Noah. "We have the backup." Every night the laboratory computers copied their files to a large server in the university's main building.
He connected to the server from his own laptop and found Professor Alder's folder. It was there. But when he opened it, he saw the same thing as before: nothing.
He checked the date. It was the same minute, 3.12 a.m., on the same night.

He scrolled back through the server's history for the last month. Every night the backup had run without a single error, and every folder had been copied at two o'clock. Only this night was different. The deletion had started seventy-two minutes after the last copy was finished, as though someone had waited for the backup to be safe before destroying it.
"Two places," he said slowly. "Your computer and the server. Both emptied at exactly the same minute."

Professor Alder sat down heavily. "A computer can fail," she said. "A server can fail. But they can't both fail in the same minute." Noah nodded. "Which means somebody did it on purpose, and somebody who knew the backup existed."
B1.proof: Both emptied at exactly the same minute
B1.q: What does the identical time on both systems prove?
o: That the backup system is not working at night.
That the professor deleted the files herself.
That the server was disconnected from the internet.
That one person or action probably emptied both locations.
B1.hint: Aynı dakikada gerçekleşen iki silme işleminin ortak bir nedeni olabilir mi?
B1.why: İki sistemin aynı dakikada boşalması, tek bir kişinin ya da tek bir işlemin ikisini birden silmiş olabileceğini gösteriyor.

text: "Don't panic," said Noah. "We have the backup." Every night the laboratory computers copied their files to a large server in the university's main building, and Professor Alder had never lost a document in twelve years.
He connected to the server from his own laptop and found her folder. It was still there. But when he opened it, he saw exactly what he had seen on her computer: nothing.
He checked the date. It was the same minute, 3.12 a.m., on the same night.

He scrolled back through the server's history for the last month. Every night the backup had run without a single error, and every folder had been copied at two o'clock. Only this night was different, and the change had been made seventy-two minutes after the last copy finished.
"Two places," he said slowly. "Your computer and the server. Both emptied at exactly the same minute."

Professor Alder sat down heavily. "A computer can fail," she said. "A server can fail. They can't both fail in the same minute." Noah nodded. "Which means somebody did it on purpose. And it was somebody who knew the backup existed, and knew how to reach it."
B2.proof: knew how to reach it
B2.q: What can be concluded about the person who deleted the files?
o: They had technical knowledge and knew how the backup system worked.
They were a stranger who entered by chance.
They were a student who made an error while copying files.
They worked for the company that built the server.
B2.hint: Hem bilgisayarı hem sunucuyu silmek için kişinin neyi bilmesi gerekir?
B2.why: Failin yedeğin var olduğunu ve ona nasıl ulaşılacağını biliyor olması gerekiyor; bu da teknik bilgisi ve erişimi olduğunu gösteriyor.

text: "Don't panic," said Noah. "We have the backup." Every night the laboratory computers copied their files to a large server in the university's main building, and Professor Alder had not lost a single document in twelve years.

He connected to the server from his own laptop and found her folder. It was still there, which for a moment made him smile. But when he opened it he saw exactly what he had seen on her computer: nothing.
He checked the timestamp. It was the same minute, 3.12 a.m., on the same night.

He scrolled back through the server's history for the last month. Every night the backup had run without a single error, and every folder had been copied at two o'clock. Only this night was different. The deletion had begun seventy-two minutes after the last copy finished, as though someone had waited for the backup to be safe before destroying it, and had wanted to be certain that nothing was left.
"Two places," he said slowly. "Your computer and the server. Both emptied at exactly the same minute."

Professor Alder sat down heavily. "A computer can fail," she said. "A server can fail. They can't both fail within the same sixty seconds." Noah nodded. "Which means somebody did it on purpose. And it was somebody who knew the backup existed, who knew how to reach it, and who knew which folder mattered." He did not say what he was beginning to suspect: that the person had known the manuscript better than a stranger could.
C1.proof: who knew which folder mattered
C1.q: What is Noah beginning to suspect at the end of the passage?
o: That the manuscript contained a serious mistake.
That the person who deleted the files was close to the research.
That Professor Alder had asked someone to delete it.
That the server had been replaced recently.
C1.hint: Hangi klasörün önemli olduğunu bilmek, faili kimlere yaklaştırır?
C1.why: Fail hangi klasörün önemli olduğunu da biliyordu; bu, makaleye yakın biri olduğunu, yani yabancı olmadığını düşündürüyor.

eps.title: The Access Log
eps.recap: Mei sistemin erişim kayıtlarına baktı. Silme işlemi Prof. Alder'in kendi hesabıyla yapılmış görünüyordu, ama bu işlem idari binadaki bir bilgisayardan gelmişti ve Alder o sırada evde uyuyordu.

text: Mei was a friend of Noah. She worked in the same lab and she knew computers very well. At ten o'clock, Noah showed her the empty folder.
"I will check the access log," said Mei. "The server writes down every login." She typed for five minutes. Then she was quiet.
"This is strange," she said at last. "At 3.12 a.m., the account of Professor Alder deleted the files."
Professor Alder shook her head. "I was at home. I was asleep. I never use my account at night."
Mei pointed to the screen. "And look at the computer name. It is not your lab computer. It says ADMIN-07." Noah asked, "Where is ADMIN-07?" Mei answered, "In the administration building."
A2.proof: At 3.12 a.m., the account of Professor Alder deleted the files
A2.q: What does the log suggest?
o: Professor Alder deleted her files by mistake.
The server made a mistake in the log.
Mei deleted the files to test the system.
Someone used Professor Alder's account from another place.
A2.hint: Hesap Alder'e ait ama bilgisayar adı laboratuvardan farklı; ve Alder o saatte evde uyuyordu.
A2.why: Silme, Alder'in hesabıyla yapılmış görünüyor ama bilgisayar laboratuvardan değil, idari binadan; Alder evde uyuyordu. Biri onun hesabını kullanmış.

text: Mei was Noah's friend and fellow doctoral student, and she knew more about computers than the rest of the department put together. At ten o'clock Noah showed her the empty folder.
"I'll check the access log," she said. "The server records every login." She typed for five minutes without speaking. Then she stopped.
"This doesn't make sense," she said at last. "At 3.12 a.m., the files were deleted by Professor Alder's own account."
Professor Alder shook her head. "I was at home, asleep. I never use my account at night."
Mei looked at her. "Who else knows your password?" Professor Alder thought for a moment. "Nobody. Well, the computer office set up the account for me, but that was years ago."

Mei pointed to the screen. "And look at the machine name. It isn't any computer in this lab. It says ADMIN-07." Noah frowned. "Where is ADMIN-07?" Mei took a breath. "In the administration building. Second floor."
B1.proof: Professor Alder's own account
B1.q: What problem does the access log create?
o: The account is Alder's, but the computer and the time do not fit her.
The log shows that nothing was deleted.
The log was written by Professor Alder.
The administration building has no computers.
B1.hint: Hesap sahibi, saat ve bilgisayar adı birbiriyle uyuşuyor mu?
B1.why: Hesap Alder'e ait ama silme gece 3.12'de, laboratuvar dışındaki bir bilgisayardan yapılmış; Alder ise evde uyuyordu. Bilgiler birbirini tutmuyor.

text: Mei was Noah's friend and fellow doctoral student, and she understood computers better than the rest of the department put together. At ten o'clock Noah showed her the empty folder.
"I'll check the access log," she said. "The server records every login." She typed for five minutes without speaking. Then she stopped.
"This doesn't make sense," she said at last. "At 3.12 a.m., the files were deleted by Professor Alder's own account."
Professor Alder shook her head. "I was at home, asleep. I never use my account at night."

Mei looked at her. "Who else knows your password?" Professor Alder thought for a moment. "Nobody. Well, the computer office set up the account for me, years ago, and they have always been able to reset it. But that is a very small department."

Mei pointed to the screen. "And look at the machine name. It isn't any computer in this laboratory. It says ADMIN-07." Noah frowned. "Where is ADMIN-07?" Mei took a breath. "In the administration building. Second floor. Staff only, behind a card reader." Nobody said anything. The list of people who could enter that room, Noah realised, was a short one.
B2.proof: behind a card reader
B2.q: What is Noah's realisation at the end?
o: That the culprit is Professor Alder herself.
That the culprit must belong to a small group with access to that room.
That the card reader is broken.
That the log has been copied to Mei's laptop.
B2.hint: Kart okuyucunun arkasındaki odaya kimler girebilir?
B2.why: Oda kart okuyucuyla korunuyor; içeri girebilecek kişi listesi kısa. Noah, failin bu küçük grubun içinde olduğunu fark ediyor.

text: Mei was Noah's friend and fellow doctoral student, and she understood computers better than the rest of the department put together. At ten o'clock Noah showed her the empty folder, and she set her coffee aside with the look of someone about to be disappointed by a machine.
"I'll check the access log," she said. "The server records every login." She typed for five minutes without speaking. Then she stopped.
"This doesn't make sense," she said at last. "At 3.12 a.m., the files were deleted by Professor Alder's own account."
Professor Alder shook her head. "I was at home, asleep. I never use my account at night. I couldn't even tell you what my password is without looking at the card in my wallet."

Mei pointed to the screen. "And look at the machine name. It isn't any computer in this laboratory. It says ADMIN-07." Noah frowned. "Where is ADMIN-07?" Mei took a breath. "In the administration building. Second floor. Staff only, behind a card reader." Nobody spoke. The list of people who could enter that room, Noah realised, was a short one, and the password card in the professor's wallet suddenly seemed less important than the person who might have copied it.
C1.proof: the person who might have copied it
C1.q: What is the most logical conclusion about the culprit?
o: They were a hacker from a foreign country.
They were Professor Alder's family member.
They had access to the administration room and found a way to use Alder's login.
They worked in the library of the university.
C1.hint: Alder'in şifresini kullanabilen ve idari odaya girebilen kişi kimdir?
C1.why: İdari binadaki kart okuyuculu odaya girebilen biri, Alder'in şifresine de ulaşıp hesabını kullanmış olmalı.

eps.title: A Calm Face
eps.recap: Prof. Alder dışarıdan sakin görünüyordu ama gözlerinde korku vardı. Noah'a iki hafta önce birine son veri tablolarını e-postayla gönderdiğini söyledi, fakat kimin olduğunu söylemeyi reddetti.

text: Professor Alder was a calm woman. In the lab, she never shouted. When a machine broke, she only said, "We will fix it." Noah admired her for this.
That afternoon, she asked Noah to sit in her office. She poured two cups of tea. Her face was calm, but her hands were not. The cup made a small noise on the plate.
"Noah," she said, "this paper is two years of our work. Your analysis, my ideas. If we lose it before the conference, the money for our laboratory will stop."
Noah nodded. "We can write it again," he said. "I remember the analysis."

"Two weeks ago," she said slowly, "someone asked me for the final tables of numbers. I sent them by email." "Who?" asked Noah. Professor Alder looked at the window. "I do not want to say," she said. "Not yet."
A2.proof: I do not want to say
A2.q: Why is Professor Alder afraid?
o: She may suspect someone she trusts.
She does not like her student's analysis.
She is angry about the broken machine.
She wants to leave the university.
A2.hint: Alder kimin e-posta aldığını söylemiyor; bunu neden saklıyor olabilir?
A2.why: Alder iki hafta önce birine tabloları göndermiş ve adını söylemek istemiyor; güvendiği birinden şüphelendiği için korkuyor olabilir.

text: Professor Alder was a calm woman. In the laboratory she never raised her voice, and when a machine broke she simply said, "We'll fix it." Noah had always admired that about her.
That afternoon she asked him to sit in her office and poured two cups of tea. Her face was calm, but her hands were not. The cup rattled gently against its saucer.
"Noah," she said, "this paper represents two years of work. Your analysis, my ideas. If we lose it before the conference, our funding will stop and the laboratory will close."
Noah nodded. "We can rewrite it. I remember the analysis."

"There's something else," she said slowly. "Two weeks ago, someone asked me for the final tables of results. I sent them by email." "Who was it?" asked Noah. Professor Alder looked out of the window. "I would rather not say. Not yet."
B1.proof: I would rather not say
B1.q: What does Alder's refusal to name the person suggest?
o: She has forgotten the person's name.
She is unsure whether her suspicion is fair, or she fears the consequences.
She is going to send the tables again.
She wants Noah to write the paper alone.
B1.hint: Adı söylemek istememesi onun ruh hali hakkında ne söyler?
B1.why: Alder adı söylemekten çekiniyor; ya şüphesinin haksız olmasından ya da sonuçlarından korkuyor.

text: Professor Alder was a calm woman. In the laboratory she never raised her voice, and when a machine broke she simply said, "We'll fix it." Noah had always admired that about her.
That afternoon she asked him to sit in her office and poured two cups of tea. Her face was composed, but her hands were not. The cup rattled gently against its saucer.
"Noah," she said, "this paper represents two years of work. Your analysis, my ideas. If we lose it before the conference, our funding will stop and the laboratory will close."
Noah nodded. "We can rewrite it. I remember the analysis."

"There's something else," she said slowly. "Two weeks ago, a colleague asked me for the final tables of results. I sent them by email without a second thought." "Who was it?" asked Noah. Professor Alder looked out of the window for a long time. "I would rather not say. Not until I'm certain I'm not being unfair to someone." Noah did not push her. He had learned long ago that she said things when she was ready.
B2.proof: Not until I'm certain I'm not being unfair to someone.
B2.q: Why does Alder hesitate to name the colleague?
o: She wants to protect the colleague from the police.
She has lost the colleague's email address.
She does not want to accuse someone without being sure.
She does not remember who sent the request.
B2.hint: 'Haksızlık etmediğimden emin olmadıkça' ifadesi neyi gösterir?
B2.why: Alder, yeterli kanıtı olmadan birini suçlamaktan çekiniyor; kimseye haksızlık etmek istemiyor.

text: Professor Alder was a calm woman. In the laboratory she never raised her voice, and when a machine broke she simply said, "We'll fix it." Noah had always admired that about her, and had never once seen her afraid.

That afternoon she asked him to sit in her office and poured two cups of tea. Her face was composed, but her hands were not. The cup rattled gently against its saucer, and she put it down as though it had insulted her.
"Noah," she said, "this paper represents two years of work. Your analysis, my ideas. If we lose it before the conference, our funding will stop and the laboratory will close."
Noah nodded. "We can rewrite it. I remember the analysis."

"There's something else," she said slowly. "Two weeks ago, a colleague asked me for the final tables of results. I sent them by email without a second thought." "Who was it?" asked Noah. Professor Alder looked out of the window for a long time. "I would rather not say. Not until I'm certain I'm not being unfair to someone I have trusted for twenty years." Noah did not push her. He had learned long ago that she spoke when she was ready, and that a silence from her was usually the beginning of a sentence.
C1.proof: someone I have trusted for twenty years
C1.q: What does the final phrase tell us about the person Alder suspects?
o: That it is a new student in the laboratory.
That it is a stranger from another university.
That it is Noah himself.
That it is someone she has known and trusted for a long time.
C1.hint: Alder'in 'yirmi yıldır güvendiği' ifadesi şüphelinin kim olduğuna dair ne söyler?
C1.why: Alder'in şüphelendiği kişi onun yirmi yıldır güvendiği biri; yani uzun zamandır tanıdığı, yakın bir meslektaş.

eps.title: A Helpful Man
eps.recap: Dekan yardımcısı Dr. Voss, laboratuvara gelip dosyaların kurtarılması için çok istekli bir şekilde yardım teklif etti. Noah, Voss'un soruların çok ayrıntılı olduğunu ve verilerle yardımdan daha çok ilgilendiğini fark etti.

text: On Tuesday morning, Dr. Voss came to the laboratory. He was the deputy dean, a tall man with a warm smile and an expensive grey coat. He shook Professor Alder's hand with both of his.
"I heard about your problem," he said. "What a disaster. Please let me help. I can send the university's computer experts. I can give you an assistant."
Professor Alder thanked him. Noah was surprised. The deputy dean never came to the laboratory.

Dr. Voss asked many questions. "Where did you keep the analysis? Which version was it? How many tables were there? Did you use the new statistical method?" Noah answered slowly. The questions were very exact.
At the door, Dr. Voss smiled. "Do not worry," he said. "If the experts find anything, I will take the files to my office myself."
A2.q: What does Noah notice about Dr. Voss?
o: He does not want to help at all.
He asks more about the data than a person who only wants to help.
He does not know anything about computers.
He is angry with Professor Alder.
A2.hint: Voss'un sorularının 'çok kesin' olması ne anlama gelir?
A2.why: Voss'un soruları çok ayrıntılı ve veriye yönelik; yalnızca yardım etmek isteyen birinin soracağından fazlası.

text: On Tuesday morning Dr. Voss came to the laboratory. He was the deputy dean, a tall man with a warm smile and an expensive grey coat, and he shook Professor Alder's hand with both of his.
"I heard about your trouble," he said. "What a disaster. Please, let me help. I can send the university's best computer specialists, and I can lend you an assistant."
Professor Alder thanked him warmly. Noah was surprised. In four years he had never seen the deputy dean in the laboratory.

Dr. Voss asked a great many questions. "Where did you store the analysis? Which version was it? How many tables were there? Did you use the new statistical method?" Noah answered slowly. The questions were unusually precise for someone who was only trying to be kind.
At the door Dr. Voss smiled again. "Don't worry. If the specialists recover anything, I'll take the files to my own office personally."
B1.proof: unusually precise for someone who was only trying to be kind
B1.q: What is Noah beginning to feel about Dr. Voss's visit?
o: That Voss is too busy to help.
That Voss does not know the university rules.
That Voss is more interested in the data than in helping.
That Voss is angry because nobody called him.
B1.hint: Noah'a göre bu sorular 'yalnızca kibar olmaya çalışan biri için' nasıl?
B1.why: Noah, soruların yalnızca nazik olmaya çalışan biri için fazla ayrıntılı olduğunu düşünüyor; Voss'un veriyle asıl ilgilenmiş olabileceğini sezmeye başlıyor.

text: On Tuesday morning Dr. Voss came to the laboratory. He was the deputy dean, a tall man with a warm smile and an expensive grey coat, and he shook Professor Alder's hand with both of his.
"I heard about your trouble," he said. "What a disaster. Please, let me help. I can send the university's best computer specialists, and I can lend you an assistant."
Professor Alder thanked him warmly. Noah was surprised. In four years he had never seen the deputy dean in the laboratory, and he had not known that Voss and Alder were on first-name terms.

Dr. Voss asked a great many questions. "Where did you store the analysis? Which version was it? How many tables were there? Did you use the new statistical method?" Noah answered slowly. The questions were unusually precise for someone who had come only to be kind, and one of them, the one about the new method, concerned something Noah had told almost nobody.
At the door Dr. Voss smiled again. "Don't worry. If the specialists recover anything, I'll take the files to my own office personally."
B2.proof: concerned something Noah had told almost nobody
B2.q: Why does the detail about the 'new method' matter?
o: It proves that Noah told Voss about it last week.
It shows that the new method has failed.
It means that Voss wants to change the method.
It suggests that Voss already knows details about the research.
B2.hint: Noah neredeyse kimseye söylemediği bir konuyu Voss nasıl biliyor?
B2.why: Voss'un yeni yöntemi sorması, Noah'ın neredeyse kimseye söylemediği bir konuyu zaten bildiğini düşündürüyor.

text: On Tuesday morning Dr. Voss came to the laboratory. He was the deputy dean, a tall man with a warm smile and an expensive grey coat, and he shook Professor Alder's hand with both of his, as if she had been bereaved.
"I heard about your trouble," he said. "What a disaster. Please, let me help. I can send the university's best computer specialists, and I can lend you an assistant."
Professor Alder thanked him warmly. Noah was surprised. In four years he had never seen the deputy dean in the laboratory, and he had not known that Voss and Alder were on first-name terms.

Dr. Voss asked a great many questions. "Where did you store the analysis? Which version was it? How many tables were there? Did you use the new statistical method?" Noah answered slowly. The questions were unusually precise for someone who had come only to be kind, and the last one, about the new method, concerned something Noah had told almost nobody. He noticed that Voss never asked about the conclusions, only about the numbers behind them.
At the door Dr. Voss smiled again. "Don't worry. If the specialists recover anything, I'll take the files to my own office personally."
C1.proof: Voss never asked about the conclusions, only about the numbers behind them
C1.q: What does Voss's choice of questions suggest?
o: That he cares about the raw data, which is what someone could reuse as his own.
That he is a statistician who is simply curious.
That he finds the conclusions unimportant for the university.
That he has already read the whole paper.
C1.hint: Sonuçlar yerine sayılarla ilgilenen biri neye ihtiyaç duyar?
C1.why: Voss sonuçları değil sayıları soruyor; ham veri, başkası tarafından yeniden kullanılabilecek en değerli kısım olduğu için asıl ilgi alanı bu olabilir.

eps.title: An Automatic Email
eps.recap: Noah, e-posta kutusunda bir hakem sistemi bildirimi buldu: makale üç hafta önce hakemlere gönderilmiş görünüyordu. Ne Noah ne de Prof. Alder bunu yapmıştı.

text: That evening, Noah was alone in the laboratory. He opened his email to write to a friend. Under the new messages, there was one with a strange title: "Notification: Manuscript received."

He almost deleted it. Then he read the first line. "Thank you for submitting your manuscript, Memory Effects in Polymer Films, to the Journal of Materials Science. Your paper has been sent to reviewers."
Noah read it again. The paper had the same name as their paper. It was the same title. He looked at the date. The email was three weeks old.
Three weeks ago! Noah did not send the paper to any journal. He called Professor Alder. She was silent for a long time. "I did not send it, either," she said.
"Then somebody did," said Noah. "And they put our names on it. Or maybe they did not." He looked again at the email. His name was not in the list of authors.
A2.proof: His name was not in the list of authors.
A2.q: What does the email show?
o: The journal rejected the paper.
Noah sent the paper but forgot it.
Someone sent a copy of the paper to a journal without telling them.
The paper was written by a different laboratory.
A2.hint: Makale üç hafta önce gönderilmiş ve ne Noah ne de Alder göndermemiş: bu ne demek?
A2.why: Başlık aynı, ama ne Noah ne de Alder göndermiş. Yani onların haberi olmadan birisi makalenin bir kopyasını dergiye yollamış.

text: That evening Noah was alone in the laboratory. He opened his email to write to a friend, and among the new messages he noticed one with an odd subject line: "Notification: Manuscript received."

He almost deleted it. Then he read the first sentence. "Thank you for submitting your manuscript, 'Memory Effects in Polymer Films', to the Journal of Materials Science. Your paper has been assigned to reviewers."
Noah read it again. It was the title of their paper, word for word. He checked the date. The email was three weeks old, and it had been sent to him automatically, as if he were an author.
Three weeks! Noah had submitted nothing to any journal. He phoned Professor Alder, who was silent for a long moment. "I didn't submit it either," she said.

"Then somebody did," said Noah. "And before the files were deleted." He scrolled down to the list of authors. His name was not on it, and neither was hers. He sat in the empty laboratory and listened to the hum of the machines.
B1.proof: His name was not on it, and neither was hers.
B1.q: What is the most important detail in the email?
o: The paper was accepted by the journal.
The journal asked for new data.
The title was spelled incorrectly.
The paper was submitted before the deletion and without their names.
B1.hint: Yazar listesinde kimlerin olmadığına ve tarihe bak.
B1.why: Makale dosyalar silinmeden üç hafta önce gönderilmiş ve yazarlar arasında Noah ile Alder yok; bu çok önemli bir ipucu.

text: That evening Noah was alone in the laboratory. He opened his email to write to a friend, and among the new messages he noticed one with an odd subject line: "Notification: Manuscript received."

He almost deleted it. Then he read the first sentence. "Thank you for submitting your manuscript, 'Memory Effects in Polymer Films', to the Journal of Materials Science. Your paper has been assigned to reviewers."
Noah read it again. It was the title of their paper, word for word. He checked the date. The email was three weeks old, and it had landed in a folder he almost never opened.
Three weeks! Noah had submitted nothing to any journal. He phoned Professor Alder, who was silent for a long moment. "I didn't submit it either," she said.

"Then somebody did," said Noah. "And before the files were deleted." He scrolled down to the list of authors. His name was not on it, and neither was hers. Instead, there was a single institutional account, with no personal name at all. Whoever had done this had wanted to stay invisible.
B2.proof: a single institutional account, with no personal name at all
B2.q: What can be concluded from the author information?
o: The submission was made in a way that hides the real person.
The paper has too many authors.
The journal made a mistake with the names.
The paper belongs to the university library.
B2.hint: Kişisel ad yerine kurumsal bir hesap kullanılması neyi gizler?
B2.why: Gönderim kişisel isimsiz bir kurum hesabıyla yapılmış; bu, gerçek göndericinin kimliğinin gizlendiğini gösteriyor.

text: That evening Noah was alone in the laboratory. He opened his email to write to a friend, and among the new messages he noticed one with an odd subject line: "Notification: Manuscript received."

He almost deleted it. Then he read the first sentence. "Thank you for submitting your manuscript, 'Memory Effects in Polymer Films', to the Journal of Materials Science. Your paper has been assigned to reviewers."

Noah read it again. It was the title of their paper, word for word. He checked the date. The email was three weeks old, and it had landed in a folder he almost never opened, which could not have been a coincidence.
Three weeks! Noah had submitted nothing to any journal. He phoned Professor Alder, who was silent for a long moment. "I didn't submit it either," she said.

"Then somebody did," said Noah. "And before the files were deleted." He scrolled down to the list of authors. His name was not on it, and neither was hers. Instead, there was a single institutional account, with no personal name at all, and the more he looked at it, the more he suspected that the file had not been destroyed that night. It had been moved.
C1.proof: It had been moved
C1.q: What new idea does Noah have by the end?
o: That the file was completely destroyed.
That the deleted paper may have been copied and submitted elsewhere.
That the journal will return the paper.
That Professor Alder submitted it by mistake.
C1.hint: Dosya silinmedi de 'taşındı' ise nereye gitmiş olabilir?
C1.why: Noah, dosyanın o gece yok edilmediğini, başka bir yere taşınıp dergiye gönderildiğini düşünüyor; yani silme, kopyayı gizlemek için yapılmış olabilir.

eps.title: Version Three
eps.recap: Mei, dergiye gönderilen dosyanın makalenin üçüncü taslağı olduğunu fark etti. Bu taslağı üç hafta önce Prof. Alder yalnızca beş meslektaşına dahili inceleme için göndermişti; demek ki gönderen kişi bu beş kişiden biriydi ya da onlardan birine ulaşmıştı.

text: On Wednesday morning, Mei opened her laptop in the laboratory. She was angry and excited. "I have found something," she said to Noah. "I looked at the file name in the journal's email. It says: Manuscript_v3."
"Version three," said Noah. "That is an early draft. We changed the paper many times after that."
"Exactly," said Mei. "Professor Alder sent version three to five people in the department. It was three weeks ago. She asked them to read it and give comments. I remember the email."
Noah counted on his fingers. "So the person who sent the paper to the journal had version three," he said. "That means he was one of the five people. Or he had a friend who was."
"Who were the five?" asked Mei. She opened the old email. She read five names, one by one. Noah listened. One of the names made his stomach turn cold.
A2.proof: Professor Alder sent version three to five people in the department.
A2.q: What does the version number tell Noah and Mei?
o: The paper was submitted by Professor Alder herself.
The paper was finished and perfect.
The journal changed the file name.
The person who submitted the paper probably got the draft from the group of five readers.
A2.hint: Dergiye giden dosya 'v3' ve bu taslak yalnızca beş kişiye gönderilmişti.
A2.why: Gönderilen dosya üçüncü taslak ve bu taslak yalnızca beş kişiye gönderilmişti; yani gönderen kişi bu beş kişiden biri ya da onlara ulaşabilen biri.

text: On Wednesday morning Mei opened her laptop in the laboratory, angry and excited at once. "I've found something," she told Noah. "I looked at the file name in the journal's email. It says Manuscript_v3."
"Version three," said Noah. "That's an early draft. We rewrote half of it after that."
"Exactly. Professor Alder sent version three to five colleagues in the department, three weeks ago, for internal comments. I remember the email because I was copied."
Noah counted on his fingers. "So whoever submitted the paper had version three. Either he was one of those five, or he knew somebody who was."

"Who were the five?" asked Mei. She opened the old message and read the names aloud, one at a time. Noah listened. When she reached the fourth, he felt his stomach turn cold. He said nothing yet, because he wanted to be sure before he accused anyone, and because the corridor outside was suddenly full of footsteps.
B1.proof: Either he was one of those five, or he knew somebody who was.
B1.q: What does Noah's cold feeling at the end suggest?
o: He recognises a name that he suspects.
He is sick from the coffee.
He forgot his own name.
He is afraid of Mei.
B1.hint: Dördüncü isim okunduğunda Noah'ın midesinin soğuması ne anlama gelir?
B1.why: Noah, dördüncü isim okunduğunda tanıdık ve şüpheli bir isim duymuş gibi tepki veriyor.

text: On Wednesday morning Mei opened her laptop in the laboratory, angry and excited at once. "I've found something," she told Noah. "I looked at the file name in the journal's email. It says Manuscript_v3."
"Version three," said Noah. "That's an early draft. We rewrote half of it after that, and the final tables didn't even exist yet."
"Exactly. Professor Alder sent version three to five colleagues in the department, three weeks ago, for internal comments. I remember the email because I was copied."
Noah counted on his fingers. "So whoever submitted the paper had version three. Either he was one of those five, or he knew somebody who was. And since then, he asked her for the final tables."

"Who were the five?" asked Mei. She opened the old message and read the names aloud, one at a time. Noah listened carefully. When she reached the fourth, he felt his stomach turn cold. It was a name that had been wearing a very warm smile only the day before. Mei saw his face and stopped reading, and for a long moment the two of them just looked at each other in silence.
B2.proof: a name that had been wearing a very warm smile only the day before
B2.q: Which person is Noah probably thinking of?
o: Professor Alder, who was in her office.
Dr. Voss, who visited the laboratory the day before.
The librarian of the university.
A friend from another country.
B2.hint: Bir gün önce sıcak gülümsemesiyle laboratuvara kim gelmişti?
B2.why: Bir gün önce sıcak bir gülümsemeyle laboratuvara gelen kişi dekan yardımcısı Dr. Voss'tu; Noah onun adını duyunca irkiliyor.

text: On Wednesday morning Mei opened her laptop in the laboratory, angry and excited at once. "I've found something," she told Noah. "I looked at the file name in the journal's email. It says Manuscript_v3."
"Version three," said Noah. "That's an early draft. We rewrote half of it after that, and the final tables didn't even exist yet."
"Exactly. Professor Alder sent version three to five colleagues in the department, three weeks ago, for internal comments. I remember the email because I was copied."

Noah counted on his fingers. "So whoever submitted the paper had version three. Either he was one of those five, or he knew somebody who was. And two weeks ago somebody asked Professor Alder for the final tables, which means that the person wanted the numbers as well as the words."

"Who were the five?" asked Mei. She opened the old message and read the names aloud, one at a time. Noah listened carefully. When she reached the fourth, he felt his stomach turn cold. It was a name that had been wearing a very warm smile only the day before, and had asked, with such kindness, about the new statistical method. Noah said nothing at first, because an accusation without proof is only another kind of theft, and he wanted his next step to be a careful one.
C1.proof: had asked, with such kindness, about the new statistical method
C1.q: How does the final sentence connect to earlier events?
o: It shows that Mei asked about the method.
It proves that Noah invented the new method.
It links the fourth name to the person who asked suspicious questions in the laboratory.
It suggests that the method was published already.
C1.hint: Yeni istatistik yöntemi hakkında nezaketle soru soran kişi kimdi?
C1.why: Yeni yöntemi sorup laboratuvarı ziyaret eden kişi Dr. Voss'tu; cümle dördüncü ismi onun adıyla ilişkilendiriyor.

eps.title: An Account With No Name
eps.recap: Noah ve Mei, makalenin dergiye 'FAC-ADM-02' adlı kurumsal bir hesapla yüklendiğini öğrendi. Bu hesap fakülte idaresine aitti ve yalnızca birkaç kişi şifresini biliyordu.

text: Mei found a link in the journal's email. It said: 'Check the status of your submission.' She clicked on it. A page opened. It showed the title of the paper and a date. Under the date, there was a line: 'Submitted by: FAC-ADM-02'.
"What is that?" asked Noah. "It is not a name. It is a code."
"It is an account of the university," said Mei. "I know this kind of account. FAC means Faculty. ADM means Administration. It is a shared account. It does not belong to one person."
"Who can use it?" asked Noah. Mei thought for a moment. "Only people in the Faculty office," she said. "Maybe four or five people."
Noah remembered the computer in the administration building: ADMIN-07. "The same word," he said. "Admin. First the deleted files, and now the submitted paper. It is the same place."
A2.proof: First the deleted files, and now the submitted paper.
A2.q: What does the code FAC-ADM-02 suggest?
o: The submission came from the faculty administration, like the deletion.
The paper was submitted by a student.
The journal made a mistake.
The paper was sent from a foreign country.
A2.hint: FAC-ADM ve ADMIN-07 arasındaki ortak noktayı bul.
A2.why: Her iki olayda da 'idare' (admin) var; dosyanın silinmesi ve makalenin gönderilmesi aynı yerden, fakülte idaresinden gelmiş olabilir.

text: Mei found a link in the journal's email. It said: 'Check the status of your submission.' She clicked it, and a page opened. It showed the title of the paper, a date, and under the date a line: 'Submitted by: FAC-ADM-02'.
"What on earth is that?" asked Noah. "It's not a name. It's a code."
"It's a university account," said Mei. "I know this kind. FAC for Faculty, ADM for Administration. It's a shared login. It doesn't belong to any one person."
"Who can use it?" Mei thought for a moment. "Only people in the Faculty office. Four or five at most. But they'd all have to sign in with their own passwords first, so there's a record somewhere."

Noah thought of the computer in the administration building. "ADMIN-07," he said. "The same word again. First the deleted files, and now the submitted paper. They came from the same corner of the university."
B1.proof: They came from the same corner of the university.
B1.q: What does Noah conclude?
o: The shared account is used by all students.
Both the deletion and the submission were probably done by someone in the faculty office.
The journal is run by the university.
The files were deleted by Mei.
B1.hint: İki olayın ortak kaynağı hakkında Noah ne söylüyor?
B1.why: Silme ve gönderim 'admin' ile ilgili hesaplardan yapılmış; Noah ikisinin de fakülte idaresindeki biri tarafından yapıldığını düşünüyor.

text: Mei found a link in the journal's email. It said: 'Check the status of your submission.' She clicked it, and a page opened. It showed the title of the paper, a date, and under the date a line: 'Submitted by: FAC-ADM-02'.
"What on earth is that?" asked Noah. "It's not a name. It's a code."

"It's a university account," said Mei. "I know this kind. FAC for Faculty, ADM for Administration. It's a shared login. It doesn't belong to any one person, which is exactly why somebody would use it if they didn't want to be found."
"Who can use it?" Mei thought for a moment. "Only people in the Faculty office. Four or five at most. But they'd all have to sign in with their own passwords first, so there's a record somewhere."

Noah thought of the computer in the administration building. "ADMIN-07," he said. "The same word again. First the deleted files, and now the submitted paper. They came from the same corner of the university, and I'd bet from the same hands." Mei closed the laptop halfway. "If we're right," she said, "then somebody in a position of authority just stole from a professor and used the university's own computers to do it."
B2.proof: somebody in a position of authority just stole from a professor
B2.q: What serious accusation does Mei make at the end?
o: That Professor Alder stole from the university.
That the journal stole from the students.
That a person with official power used university systems to steal the research.
That Noah deleted his own paper.
B2.hint: 'Yetkili bir kişi' ifadesi kimi ima ediyor?
B2.why: Mei, fakülte idaresinde yetkili bir konumda olan birinin üniversitenin kendi bilgisayarlarını kullanarak bir profesörün çalışmasını çaldığını ima ediyor.

text: Mei found a link in the journal's email. It said: 'Check the status of your submission.' She clicked it, and a page opened. It showed the title of the paper, a date, and under the date a line: 'Submitted by: FAC-ADM-02'.
"What on earth is that?" asked Noah. "It's not a name. It's a code."

"It's a university account," said Mei. "I know this kind. FAC for Faculty, ADM for Administration. It's a shared login. It doesn't belong to any one person, which is exactly why somebody would use it if they didn't want to be found. Everything done through it is attributed to an office, never to a human being."

"Who can use it?" Mei thought for a moment. "Only people in the Faculty office. Four or five at most. But they'd all have to sign in with their own passwords first, so there's a record somewhere, assuming nobody has cleaned that up as well."

Noah thought of the computer in the administration building. "ADMIN-07," he said. "The same word again. First the deleted files, and now the submitted paper. They came from the same corner of the university, and I'd bet from the same hands." Mei closed the laptop halfway. "If we're right," she said, "then somebody in a position of authority just stole from a professor, and used the university's own computers to do it. Which means that going to the university to complain may be the one thing we cannot do."
C1.proof: going to the university to complain may be the one thing we cannot do
C1.q: Why does Mei think they cannot simply complain to the university?
o: Because the university has no complaint office.
Because complaints are only accepted by email.
Because Professor Alder forbade it.
Because the person responsible may belong to the university's own administration.
C1.hint: Şikâyet etmenin neden zor olduğunu düşün.
C1.why: Sorumlu kişi üniversite idaresinin içinden biri olabilir; bu yüzden aynı kurumdan yardım istemek riskli.

eps.title: Reviewer Two
eps.recap: Mei, dergiden gelen hakem yorumlarını buldu. İkinci hakem, yalnızca Noah ve Prof. Alder'in bildiği 'tau yıldız' adlı parametreden söz etmişti; bu, hakemin bağımsız olmadığını gösteriyordu.

text: On Thursday, Mei found another email. It was also three weeks old, and it came from the journal. The title was: 'Reviewers' comments'. She opened it and read it aloud to Noah.
Reviewer One wrote a short and friendly text. "This is a good paper. I recommend publication." Reviewer Two wrote a very long text. It had many questions about the analysis.
Then Mei stopped. She read one line again. "Please explain more clearly the parameter that the authors call tau-star."
Noah jumped from his chair. "Tau-star?" he said. "That is not in the paper! It is only my private name for a number. I invented it in the laboratory. Only Professor Alder and I use it."
"Then how does Reviewer Two know it?" asked Mei. Noah did not answer. Outside the window, the clouds were becoming dark.
A2.proof: That is not in the paper!
A2.q: Why is the word 'tau-star' important?
o: It is a famous word in physics.
It is a private name that an independent reviewer could not know.
It is the name of the journal.
It is the title of the paper.
A2.hint: 'Tau-star' kelimesi makalede yoksa hakem bunu nereden biliyor?
A2.why: 'Tau-star' Noah'ın laboratuvarda uydurduğu özel bir isim ve makalede geçmiyor; bu ismi bilen hakem gerçekten bağımsız olamaz.

text: On Thursday Mei found another email, also three weeks old, from the journal. Its subject line was 'Reviewers' comments'. She opened it and read it aloud to Noah.
Reviewer One had written a short, friendly note: "A good paper. I recommend publication." Reviewer Two had written pages, full of detailed questions about the analysis.
Then Mei stopped. She read one sentence again. "Please explain more clearly the parameter the authors call tau-star."
Noah jumped out of his chair. "Tau-star? That isn't in the paper! It's just my private nickname for a number. I invented it in the laboratory. Only Professor Alder and I use it."

"Then how does Reviewer Two know it?" asked Mei. Noah did not answer. Outside the window the clouds were turning dark, and the laboratory lights hummed above them. Mei quietly copied the sentence into her notebook and underlined it twice, as if the line might disappear.
B1.proof: That isn't in the paper!
B1.q: What does the reviewer's knowledge of 'tau-star' suggest?
o: The reviewer read the paper more carefully than others.
The reviewer is Professor Alder.
The reviewer is not independent and has seen the laboratory's internal work.
The reviewer is a student of Noah.
B1.hint: Makalede olmayan, yalnızca laboratuvarda kullanılan bir kelime nasıl hakeme ulaşmış?
B1.why: Hakem makalede olmayan özel bir ismi biliyor; bu, laboratuvarın iç çalışmalarını görmüş birinin yazdığını düşündürüyor.

text: On Thursday Mei found another email, also three weeks old, from the journal. Its subject line was 'Reviewers' comments'. She opened it and read it aloud to Noah.

Reviewer One had written a short, friendly note: "A good paper. I recommend publication." Reviewer Two had written pages, full of detailed questions about the analysis, in a tone that was courteous, firm and slightly too confident.
Then Mei stopped. She read one sentence again. "Please explain more clearly the parameter the authors call tau-star."
Noah jumped out of his chair. "Tau-star? That isn't in the paper! It's just my private nickname for a number. I invented it in the laboratory. Only Professor Alder and I use it."

"Then how does Reviewer Two know it?" asked Mei. Noah did not answer. Outside the window the clouds were turning dark. He was thinking that a real reviewer sees only the manuscript, and that the only people who could have seen the nickname were those who had seen the notes behind it. Mei wrote the sentence into her notebook and underlined it twice, as though the evidence might vanish.
B2.proof: those who had seen the notes behind it
B2.q: What reasoning does Noah follow?
o: A true reviewer always knows nicknames.
The nickname was published in a newspaper.
The reviewer is a friend of Mei.
A true reviewer would know only what is in the paper, so this reviewer had extra access.
B2.hint: Gerçek bir hakem hangi bilgiyi görür?
B2.why: Gerçek bir hakem yalnızca makaleyi görür; takma adı bilen kişi makalenin arkasındaki notlara da erişmiş olmalı.

eps.title: Borrowed Words
eps.recap: Mei, ikinci hakemin yorumlarının dilini inceledi ve Prof. Alder'in eski makalelerindeki ifadelerle şaşırtıcı biçimde örtüştüğünü gördü. Birinin Alder'in yazım alışkanlıklarını çok iyi tanıdığı anlaşılıyordu.

text: On Friday, Mei could not stop thinking about the reviewer's text. She is a person who notices small things in language. She read the comments three times.
Then she opened four old papers by Professor Alder. She put them next to the reviewer's text on her screen. Slowly, she began to circle words with a red pen.

"Look," she said to Noah. "Reviewer Two writes: 'It is worth stressing that…'. Professor Alder writes the same words in every paper. And look at 'one might reasonably ask'. She loves that sentence. And the spelling: behaviour, not behavior. She is the only person in the lab who writes it in this way."
Noah looked at the circles. There were twenty-three of them. "The reviewer is not only reading her style," he said. "He is copying it."
"Yes," said Mei. "Someone who knows Professor Alder very well wrote these comments."
A2.q: What does Mei discover about the reviewer's text?

It was written by Mei herself.
It copies Professor Alder's way of writing.
It is too short to study.
A2.hint: Mei hakem yorumunda hangi ortak ifadeleri buluyor?
A2.why: Hakem metni, Prof. Alder'in sık kullandığı kalıpları ve yazım biçimini taklit ediyor; onu çok iyi tanıyan biri yazmış olmalı.

text: On Friday Mei could not stop thinking about the reviewer's text. She was the kind of person who notices small things in language, and she read the comments three times.

eps.title: The Security Desk
eps.recap: Noah, idari binanın güvenlik masasından o gecenin giriş kayıtlarını istedi. Görevli Mr. Dalton, aynı çıktıyı bir gün önce dekanlık ofisinden birinin alıp götürdüğünü söyledi.

text: On Saturday, Noah went to the administration building. At the front, there was a small desk with a security guard. His name was Mr. Dalton. He was a heavy man, and he was eating a sandwich.
"Excuse me," said Noah. "I need to see the entry list for the second floor. For the night of the twelfth. Between two and four in the morning."
Mr. Dalton put down his sandwich. "We keep a record of every card," he said. "But I cannot show it to a student. Only the office of the dean can ask for it."

Noah said, "Please. It is important." Mr. Dalton looked at him for a long time. Then he spoke more quietly. "It is funny. Yesterday, a person from the dean's office came for the same list. He asked for the printed paper. And he took it with him."
"Who was it?" asked Noah. "He did not give his name," said Mr. Dalton. "But he was very polite. And he had a warm smile."
A2.q: Why is Mr. Dalton's story important?
o: Mr. Dalton wants to eat his sandwich in peace.
The list does not exist.
The dean's office is closed on Saturdays.
Someone from the dean's office took the same record the day before.
A2.hint: Bir gün önce aynı listeyi kim almış?
A2.why: Dekanlık ofisinden biri bir gün önce aynı kaydı alıp götürmüş; bu, izlerin silinmeye çalışıldığını düşündürüyor.

eps.title: The Editorial Board
eps.recap: Noah, dergi sitesindeki hakem kurulu listesini açtı ve üçüncü satırda 'Dr. Henrik Voss' adını gördü. Makalenin gönderildiği dergide Voss'un hakem olduğu ortaya çıktı.

text: On Sunday night, Noah could not sleep. He sat on his bed with his laptop. He opened the website of the Journal of Materials Science. He wanted to know more about the people who work for it.

He clicked on a page called 'Editorial Board and Reviewers'. It had a long list of names with small photographs. Noah began to read from the top. He knew some of the professors. He did not know many others.
On the third line, a name stopped him. He read it once. He read it again. The photograph showed a tall man with a warm smile. The name was: 'Dr. Henrik Voss'.
Noah's heart was loud in the quiet room. Dr. Voss, the deputy dean. Dr. Voss, who wanted to help. Dr. Voss, who asked about the new method.
He picked up his phone and wrote a message to Mei: "Come early tomorrow. I have found the journal's reviewer. It is the man who brought us coffee."

He is the editor of Noah's school newspaper.
He wrote the paper with Noah.
He wants to buy the journal.

eps.title: The Same Number Twice
eps.recap: Prof. Alder'in eski öğrencisi Dr. Chen, Noah'a telefonda Voss'un bir kongre bildirisinde 'tau yıldız' değerini kullandığını söyledi. Aynı sayı, Alder'in kapalı dahili toplantısında ilk kez gösterilmişti.

text: On Tuesday, Noah received a phone call. It was from a woman with a kind voice. "I am Dr. Chen," she said. "Professor Alder was my teacher many years ago. Mei wrote to me. She said you have a problem."
Noah told her the story. It took ten minutes. Dr. Chen listened. Then she was silent for a few seconds.
"Noah," she said slowly, "you mentioned a special number. Tau-star. Is it 0.37?"
Noah almost dropped the phone. "Yes! How do you know?"
"Because I saw it on a slide last month at a small conference," said Dr. Chen. "The speaker was Dr. Voss. He said it was his own new result. I thought it was strange. But I did not say anything."
A2.proof: He said it was his own new result.
A2.q: What did Dr. Voss do at the conference?
o: He thanked Professor Alder.
He asked a question.
He showed Noah's number as his own result.
He did not speak at all.
A2.hint: Dr. Chen'in anlattığına göre Voss konferansta ne yapmış?
A2.why: Noah'ın bulduğu sayıyı kendi yeni sonucuymuş gibi sunmuş.

Noah nearly dropped the phone. "Yes! How do you know that?"

B1.proof: he presented it as his own new result
B1.q: What does Dr. Chen's story prove about Voss?
o: That Voss is a brilliant researcher.
That Chen is Voss's friend.
That the conference was cancelled.
That he had already used Noah's result publicly under his own name.
B1.hint: Dr. Chen'in görüntüsü Voss hakkında neyi gösteriyor?
B1.why: Voss, Noah'ın sonucunu daha önce kendi adıyla halka açık olarak sunmuş.

o: Because it is difficult to challenge someone with so much authority.
Because she did not see the slide.
Because she was asleep.
Because she agreed with him.
B2.hint: Dr. Chen neden konferansta sessiz kaldı?
B2.why: Bir dekan yardımcısına itiraz etmek zor; konumunun gücü onu susturmuş.
